Now that I have your attention... The client is one Baron Von Hess. Pompous fellow with more money than sense. Seems a tribe of goblins has taken up residence in his logging woods and are 'disrupting his vital economic endeavors'.
Goblins. You're giving us a B-Rank for *goblins*. That's pest control, Gabe. You hired S-Rank and A-Rank talent to go squash some green rats.
But goblins can be dangerous in large numbers! And it's for a Baron! It's a classic adventurer quest! This is great!
The Baron's involvement is what concerns me. A task's rank is often inflated by a wealthy client's ego. Goblins are a nuisance, but they are rarely a B-Rank threat on their own.
Hey, his money is good. He's paying B-Rank price, so it's a B-Rank job. All you have to do is go to the logging camp east of here, find the tribe, and... persuade them to leave. Permanently.
Fine. Let's go get this farce over with. But if I get even one drop of goblin guts on my boots, you're paying for a new pair.
It is our duty. Let us hope this Baron is not as trying as his reputation suggests.
The Strays' first B-Rank mission! Let's go!
Heh. 'Classic adventurer quest'. This is gonna be good.
Doesn't smell like a warzone. I was expecting more screaming and... well, goblins.
Look. Tracks. Dozens of them. They are small, chaotic... and lead deeper into the woods. But there are no signs of a struggle. No blood, no broken weapons. Strange.
They must have a hidden base! A goblin fortress! We've got to be careful.
Sure, kid. A 'fortress'. Let's go find your fortress. Just try not to trip over any roots on the way.
Following Lyrel's plan, the party approached with open hands. The goal: reason with their admirers.
Greetings! We are the Strays! We come in peace!
The goblins stopped their play, their jaws agape. Their heroes were here! In their excitement, they swarmed forward to greet them.
They tried to bow like Lyrel, but being goblins, they just ended up headbutting each other and falling over.
In the commotion, several goblins tripped backwards into the stage's main support beam. It groaned, swayed, and then collapsed.
The wiggling worm log rolled off its platform and flattened the cabbage-water bucket. The badger, finally free, went on a vengeful rampage through the goblin audience.
Following Eve's plan, the party prepared for a show of force. The goal: scare the goblins, don't slaughter them.
Alright, watch a master at work. I'm just going to dismantle their little stage. They'll get the message.
Eve shot forward like a shadow. But as she vaulted onto the stage, the goblins didn't scream or flee. They gasped in awe.
WOOOW! THE SHADOW-STAB!
The large 'Goblin Eve' saw her idol in action and decided to join in. He copied her leap... but with none of her grace.
The brutish goblin landed squarely on the stage's weakest point, which collapsed with a splintering crack, starting a chain reaction.
The wiggling worm log rolled off its platform and flattened the cabbage-water bucket. The badger, finally free, went on a vengeful rampage through the goblin audience.
Well... that didn't go according to plan.
This is a disaster! If you'd just let me handle it properly...
Me?! Your 'plan' resulted in the exact same outcome! This is what happens when you refuse to consider the honorable path!
The two women squared off amidst the wreckage, their patience completely gone. The comedic music fades out, replaced by a tense silence.
My methods are efficient. Your methods are naive.
My methods have integrity. Yours have none.
That's it, elf. You and me. Right now.
Just as they were about to come to blows, a familiar, loud, rumbling growl echoed through the clearing.
You have got to be kidding me.
Lyrel clutched her stomach, her face a mask of pure mortification. It had happened again.
I... had a light breakfast.
YAY! THE WARDEN'S ROAR!
HAHAHA! Not again! The timing! It's too perfect!
The tension shattered instantly. But before anyone could say another word, a new, pompous voice cut through the air.
What is the meaning of this disaster?!
I hired you to eliminate these pests, not throw a festival with them! Look at this mess! Guards, kill every last one of these vile creatures!
Wait! You can't!
And why not? They are goblins! Worthless! Now, out of my way!

steps.prompt: How do we stop the Baron without a bloodbath?

options.text: Eve's Plan: Deception. (This will earn a heart for Eve)
Lyrel's Plan: Honor. (This will earn a heart for Lyrel)

steps.text: (Whispering) Eve, can you create a distraction?
(Whispering) Better. Watch.
Baron, I would not take another step if I were you. We didn't destroy their camp. We were forced to quarantine it.
Quarantine? What nonsense is this?
They're afflicted with Scrofulous Pox. Highly contagious. Causes boils in... very embarrassing places. We were trying to contain it when you arrived.
The Baron, a man who clearly valued his vanity, turned pale and took a step back.
P-Pox?! Disgusting! Very well, burn the whole forest! I don't care, just keep them away from me! I'm leaving!
(Whispering) Lyrel, can you reason with her?
(Whispering) Reason is for reasonable men. He understands only reputation.
Baron Von Hess! These goblins are now under the official protection of the Adventurer's Guild. Any hostile action against them will be considered a direct assault on the Guild itself.
The Guild? You can't be serious!
I am. Word of a nobleman who hires adventurers and then tries to slaughter them while they work travels fast. Your reputation would be in tatters. Is that truly worth it?
The Baron sputtered, her face turning red with fury and indignation. He valued his reputation more than anything.
This is an outrage! An insult! Fine! Keep your filthy pets! But I am NOT paying you!
Well, we saved them. Now what?
Cyan stepped forward, facing the Goblin Chief. He pointed a finger at her, then deep into the forest, away from the logging camp.
LEAVE.
Then he pointed at their stage props.
AND STOP COPYING US.
The goblins, finally getting a command simple enough to understand, nodded frantically, gathered their things, and scurried off into the deep woods.
Well... that's that. You think they'll actually stop?
Nope. Not a chance.
I am less concerned with *if* they will stop, and more concerned with *what* their next performance will entail.
They have just witnessed two spectacularly failed strategies, a direct confrontation, and a... a biological interruption.
Great. I can't wait to hear the goblin tribute ballad of 'The Warden's Roar'.
Please, do not call it that.
Let's just... let's just go home.
Late afternoon. Heat presses down on the palace garden.
Peach juice drips from his fingers.
Worth it.
Those are sour.
You scared me.
The red ones taste better.
Those haven’t ripened.
…You’re not going to yell?
Why would I?
Because I’m stealing.
Oh.
That makes sense.
It does?
Watch.
See?
Much better.
Ha—!
Oh. That sound.
I’m Eclia.
…Cyan.
You should eat before the guards come back.
The garden is too quiet.
Okay.
You eat like you’re racing someone.
Because I am.
Hunger.
Is that a person?
No.
Oh.
You can have more.
You’re pretty generous for a palace kid.
You think so?
footsteps.ogg
…Lady Eclia.
Vera! I was just—
Playing.
And you are?
He’s with me.
He didn’t do anything wrong.
…Is that so?
I invited him.
Of course you did.
You shouldn’t be here.
…But you don’t look dangerous.
Eat.
Then go home.
And you—
—you know better.
Can he come back?
…If he behaves.
I can behave!
We’ll see.
Laughter fades into the warm light.
A tower window glows faintly red.
Late afternoon. The sun presses down on the palace garden. Guards move slowly in the heat.
Cyan crouches behind a trimmed hedge, fingers already sticky with peach juice. Heart pounding — but in a good way.
Those are sour.
…You scared me.
The red ones taste better.
Those haven't ripened properly yet.
…You're not going to yell?
Why would I?
Because I'm stealing.
Oh.
That makes sense.
Watch.
See? Much better.
Oh. That sound.
I'm Eclia. What's your name?
…Cyan.
Well, Cyan — you should eat before the guards come back.
The garden is too quiet. Not peaceful — quiet. The kind where birds don't chirp.
Okay.
You eat like you're racing someone.
Because I am. Hunger.
Is that… a person?
No. It's when you don't eat.
Oh.
…You can have more. There's plenty.
You're pretty generous for a palace kid.
You think so?
…Lady Eclia.
Vera! I was just—
Playing. I can see that.
And you are?
She's with me. She didn't do anything wrong.
I invited her.
…Is that so?
…Of course you did.
You shouldn't be here.
…But you don't look dangerous.
Eat. And when you're done, go home.
Lia — you know better than to run off without telling me.
Can she come back?
Something flickers across Vera's face — something heavy and far away.
…If she behaves.
I can behave!
We'll see.
Goodbye!
Laughter fades into the warm light.
Behind them, unseen — a tower window glows faintly red.
The garden no longer felt stolen.
You're late.
I came as fast as I could.
Okay. Follow me.
Are we allowed—
The door creaked open.
This place is huge.
I know.
They keep telling me where I can't go.
So I remember all the places I can.
Their footsteps echoed.
Palace kids do this for fun?
Lady Eclia? You're not supposed to be here.
Vera said I could walk today.
...Did she?
Yes.
Don't go far.
You're really brave.
I didn't lie.
...You kind of did.
Only a little.
Lights drifted like glowing dust.
This place is amazing!
It's just where they teach me things.
Like magic?
Like listening.
We should go.
Why?
Vera doesn't like it when I stay here too long.
I turn my back for five minutes—
And you've discovered half the palace.
Cyan gets bored easily.
That's not a good excuse.
Thanks.
Are we in trouble?
No.
Behind them, a door sealed shut.
None of the children noticed.
The outer wall hadn't changed.
That was the first thing Cyan noticed.

The stone was still worn smooth near the base, where rainwater pooled and guards used to slip when they weren't careful. The ivy still crept up the western side, thinner now, scorched in places, but alive.
Cyan crouched behind a collapsed cart and studied the wall, heart beating fast but steady.
Same height, she thought. Same cracks.
She waited for the patrol to pass.
Boots echoed along the parapet above, measured and disciplined. These weren't the lazy palace guards from her memories. These were soldiers—alert, armored, sharp.
When the footsteps faded, Cyan moved.
She climbed where she used to, fingers finding old grooves without thinking. Her body remembered before her mind did. A small ledge. A shallow notch. The loose stone she never trusted her weight on.
She pulled herself up and rolled quietly onto the inner path.
No alarm.
She lay still, listening.
Nothing.
Cyan exhaled slowly and almost laughed.
Guess you never really forget.
Voices drifted nearby.
"…north supply lines again—"
"—keep moving, don't stop—"
Cyan pressed flat against the wall, heart spiking.
Two soldiers rounded the corner ahead.
She ducked into a shadowed recess, the same one she used to hide in when she stole bread from the kitchens. It still smelled faintly of damp stone and old grain.
The soldiers slowed.
Cyan held her breath.
"…Thought I saw something," one said.
The other glanced around, then shrugged. "Probably nothing. We're behind schedule."
They moved on.
Cyan stayed still for a long moment after their footsteps faded.
Busy, she told herself. They're stretched thin. That's all.

She slipped out of the recess and moved deeper into the palace grounds, keeping to the edges, avoiding torchlight. The palace felt alive around her—too alive. Messengers hurried past without looking her way. Doors opened and closed in careful rhythm.
No one stopped her.
That should have worried her.
Instead, Cyan felt a strange, fragile comfort settle in her chest.
It's still my home, she thought. At least a little.
She paused at the edge of the inner courtyard and looked up at the towers beyond.
Somewhere inside, Lia was waiting.
She didn't notice the guard on the far parapet watching her go.
She didn't see the runner slip away in the opposite direction.
And when the patrol routes shifted moments later—just slightly—Cyan chalked it up to luck.
Cyan didn't head for the throne wing.
Not yet.
Old habits pulled her elsewhere.

She moved through side passages and narrow corridors that most people forgot existed, places servants once used and children were never meant to know. Her feet turned on their own, following paths carved into muscle memory long before the war.
The kitchen wing came into view.
The smell hit her first—warm bread, oil, something spiced and sharp. It made her stomach tighten painfully. She hadn't realized how hungry she was until then.
Still works, she thought, almost amused.
She waited by the corner, counting breaths. On the third, a group of kitchen hands passed, talking too loudly, arguing about rations. Cyan slipped in behind them, head down, invisible in the noise.
No one noticed.
The pantry door stood ajar.
That alone should have been suspicious.
Cyan eased it open and slipped inside, heart racing with the familiar thrill. Shelves lined the walls, stacked with loaves wrapped in cloth. Fewer than she remembered. Smaller.
She reached out, hesitated, then took one.
Warm.
For a moment, the war vanished.
She leaned against the shelf and tore off a piece, chewing quickly, quietly. The taste grounded her in a way nothing else had since she crossed the wall.
This was a bad idea.
She smiled anyway.
Footsteps approached.
Cyan froze.
The pantry door opened wider, light spilling in. A soldier stepped inside—young, tense, armor too new.
Their eyes met.
For a heartbeat, neither of them moved.
Cyan braced herself.
The soldier frowned slightly, as if trying to place her.
"…We're short on flour," the soldier said, not to Cyan, but to someone outside. "Tell them to ration again."
A voice answered from the hall. "Already doing it."
The soldier closed the door and left.
Just like that.
Cyan stood there, breath shallow, pulse roaring in her ears.
Did he see me? Did he recognize me?
She waited, counting again.
Nothing.
I really shouldn't try that again.
She wrapped the bread carefully and tucked it into her pack, just like she used to.
When she stepped back into the corridor, she noticed something odd.
The patrol route had shifted.
Where there should have been two guards, there was only one. Where the corridor usually bottlenecked, the way was clear.
Cyan frowned, then shook her head.
They're reorganizing, she reasoned. War does that.
She moved on, quicker now, confidence creeping in. Each corner she turned without incident fed the same dangerous thought.
I can still do this.
Above, unseen, a quiet signal passed between watchers.
Let her roam.
The inner corridors were quieter.
Not empty — just restrained, like a held breath.

Cyan slowed her pace as she moved deeper into the palace, loaf of bread tucked under her arm like a guilty secret. The stone beneath her boots felt cleaner here, less worn, the walls lined with newer runes etched with care and purpose.
She knew this wing.
That knowledge tugged at her.
She stopped in front of a familiar door.
Vera's old room.
The plaque beside it was gone.
Cyan frowned and stepped closer. She knocked once, lightly.
No answer.
Vera?
Silence.
She tried the handle.
Locked.
That wasn't unusual. Vera had always locked her door. But something about the lock felt… final. Reinforced. New.
A servant passed at the far end of the corridor, arms full of folded cloth.
Hey.
The servant paused, eyes flicking to her, then away.
"Yes?" she said politely. Too politely.
Vera. Is she around?
The servant hesitated — just long enough to be noticed.
"I don't have that information," she replied. "Please don't linger here."
Before Cyan could ask more, she turned and walked away, footsteps quickening.
Cyan stared after her.
Busy, she told herself again. War.
She moved on.

The corridors bent and branched in ways that felt subtly wrong. Turns she remembered now led somewhere else. Doors that used to creak opened soundlessly. She passed guards who didn't look at her — and that bothered her more than being challenged would have.
Once, she stopped abruptly, certain someone was behind her.
No one was there.
Still, the feeling didn't fade.
She reached the old garden overlook — the one Vera used to scold her for sneaking into. The stone bench was still there. The ivy had been cut back harshly, replaced with angular metal supports.
The fireflies were gone.
Cyan swallowed.
This place really changed.
A soft click echoed behind her.
She turned.
A guard stood at the far archway, helmet shadowing her face. She wasn't blocking the path. She wasn't advancing either.
Just… there.
Cyan waited.
After a moment, the guard shifted her stance and stepped aside, clearing the way forward.
No words.
No challenge.
Cyan nodded awkwardly and walked past.
Her skin prickled as she did.
They're watching everything, she thought. They're just choosing not to watch me.
That thought should have frightened her.
Instead, it made her straighten her shoulders.
Lia wouldn't let them hurt me.
She followed the corridor as it widened, light pooling ahead.
Somewhere beyond, the heart of the palace waited.
And behind her, unseen, the quiet watchers adjusted their positions once more.
The corridor widened.
That alone felt wrong.

Cyan slowed as she stepped forward, bread forgotten beneath her arm. The ceiling rose higher than the rest of the palace, arches stretching overhead in a way meant for ceremony, not servants or thieves.
She had never been here as a child.
This was new territory.
The light ahead was steady and white, spilling from tall windows that overlooked the inner city. Beyond the glass, banners of the South hung unmoving, heavy with purpose.
Cyan paused at the threshold.
No guards barred the way.
No locks. No runes flared. No voice challenged her.
The doors stood open.
She scanned the space carefully, instincts screaming that this was a mistake. She searched for shadows, for patrols, for anything that made sense.
Nothing.
They must be distracted, she thought. Everyone's focused on the war.
She stepped inside.
The hall beyond was vast and quiet, its floor polished smooth enough to reflect her silhouette. Footsteps echoed too loudly, every sound suddenly impossible to hide.
Halfway across, she stopped.
A single figure stood near the far end of the hall — a guard, unmoving, weapon lowered. Not blocking the path. Not watching her.
Waiting.
Cyan swallowed.
She considered turning back.
Just for a second.
Then she shook her head and continued forward, forcing herself to walk normally, as if this were all part of the plan.
As she passed the guard, the man inclined his head slightly.
Not a bow.
Not respect.
Acknowledgment.
Cyan felt something cold settle in her stomach.
The guard did not follow.
At the end of the hall, a final set of doors waited.
They were familiar.
Too familiar.
Cyan stared at them, breath catching.
This is it, she thought. I did it.
She reached for the handle.
It opened at her touch.
Warm air spilled out, carrying with it a scent she hadn't expected — metal, incense, and something faintly floral beneath it all.
Cyan stepped inside.
The doors closed behind her without a sound.
The room was not a throne room.
At least, not the kind Cyan remembered from stories.

There were no raised steps, no towering chair meant to dwarf whoever stood before it. The space was wide and open, its ceiling lost in shadow, its walls lined with banners and rune arrays that pulsed faintly like a living thing.
At the center stood a circular platform.
And on it—
Cyan.
Her name was spoken gently.
She froze.
Eclia stood facing her, hands folded behind her back. She wore no crown. No heavy armor. Just dark, layered garments threaded with faint crimson runes that shifted slowly, like breath beneath skin.
She looked older.
Not taller. Not stronger.
Just… settled.
Beside her stood another figure: a tall man in military attire, posture straight, eyes sharp. He said nothing.
Sol.
Cyan's heart slammed against her ribs.
…Lia?
She smiled.
It wasn't wide. It wasn't warm.
But it was real.
You came alone. That was wise.
I— I had to see you. I heard things. They said—
I know what they said.
Her voice was calm, steady, carrying easily through the chamber.
She gestured lightly.
Sol.
The man inclined his head and stepped back, stopping just short of the platform's edge. He did not leave. He simply became part of the room.
Eclia's eyes never left Cyan.
You used the outer wall. The old ivy route.
How did you—
You stole bread from the kitchens. Third shelf from the left. You always avoided the corner loaves. Too dry.
Her mouth went dry.
You hid in the recess near the pantry. And you paused at Vera's door.
Her tone didn't change.
Cyan felt the ground tilt beneath her.
I… didn't think anyone noticed.
I noticed.
Silence stretched.
Then Cyan straightened, forcing the feeling down.
You let me in.
Yes.
You could've stopped me.
Yes.
Why didn't you?
Eclia studied her for a moment longer than before.
Because you wanted to save me. And because you still believe you can.
You need help.
Eclia's smile faded — not into anger, but into something firmer.
No. I need you to understand where you are.
She turned, gesturing toward the banners, the runes, the maps etched faintly into the stone floor.
This is the heart of the South. Not a cage. Not a laboratory.
She faced her again.
A command.
They used you. The experiments— the monsters—
I authorized them.
The words were quiet.
Final.
You were a child.
I was. And then I wasn't.
Sol shifted slightly. Not in threat. In acknowledgment.
Eclia stepped closer, stopping just within arm's reach.
You remember me as I was. That is why I allowed you to walk these halls.
Her gaze hardened — not cruel, not kind.
But do not mistake memory for truth.
Cyan opened her mouth.
No words came out.
Eclia turned away from her, facing the chamber once more.
Stay. Listen. Ask your questions.
Then, without looking back—
After that, you will choose.
The chamber felt suddenly very small.
And Cyan understood, for the first time since crossing the wall—
She had not come here to rescue anyone.
Eclia did not return to the platform.
She stepped down from it, moving across the chamber with unhurried grace, as if this were a place she crossed every day—which, Cyan realized, it was.
Walk with me.
Cyan hesitated.
Then followed.
The chamber opened into a long gallery lined with glass panels. Behind them, rune-lit mechanisms hummed softly, each etched circle connected to the next by thin crimson lines.
Are these… conduits?
Yes.
For monsters?
For commands.
She stopped before one panel. Inside, a projection shimmered—an image of the southern front. Markers moved slowly, deliberately.
Those aren't random attacks. They're too clean.
You always noticed patterns quickly.
The compliment hit harder than it should have.
If you stop this—just for a moment—if you give them space, they'll calm down.
They won't. You've seen enough to know that.
Cyan opened her mouth, then closed it.
She had seen it. Berserk monsters. Broken chains. Instinct overriding control.
That's because the North pushed them too far. If we remove their pressure—
You still think this is reactive.
She moved to the next panel.
This one showed lists. Names. Numbers. Resource tallies.
Cyan glanced at them and quickly looked away.
They turn everything into math. Just like the North.
Eclia stopped again.
Yes. That is why they will lose.
You sound like them.
The words slipped out before she could stop them.
For the first time, Eclia paused.
Not in anger.
In consideration.
Do you remember the day you told me heroes always arrive too late?
What?
You said, 'If they were really heroes, they'd come before everything broke.'
I was a kid.
So was I.
They walked on.
You don't have to carry all of this alone. If you step away—if you let someone else—
No one else can.
She gestured toward the far end of the gallery.
Through the glass, Cyan could see the city below. Smoke rose in thin lines. People moved in ordered patterns. Not panicked. Not free.
Organized.
You think I am afraid to stand beside you. I am not.
She turned to face her fully.
I am afraid of what happens if I stop.
Cyan felt something slip.
Just a little.
You're tired. That's all this is. Anyone would be.
Eclia studied her with something close to pity.
You're still speaking to the girl who cried over fireflies.
Her voice remained even.
That girl does not exist.
The words landed softly.
And broke something anyway.
Cyan looked away first.
For a moment, neither spoke.
Then Eclia gestured toward the inner doors ahead.
You may continue. Ask what you came to ask.
Sol's eyes met Cyan's briefly.
There was no hostility there.
Only confirmation.
Cyan nodded stiffly and walked on, heart pounding for reasons she refused to name.
Behind her, the gallery lights dimmed slightly.
And the hairline cracks in her certainty began to spread.
The battlefield stretched beneath a crimson moon, churned mud reeking of blood and smoke. Cyan was on her knees, gasping, armor battered, face streaked with dirt and tears.
(Internal, frantic) No... not like this. I was supposed to be the hero. I was supposed to...
(Internal) Where is she? Where is Eve?! She went after Anne... alone. Always alone.
The player gets control. Only forward, stumbling through the mud toward a point on the battlefield.
(Voice trembling) I told her not to. I told her we'd do it together! She never listens. She never...

Cyan crests a small, muddy hill. In a small clearing: Anne, the resurrected hero, lies dead, her head a few feet from her body. Her massive greatsword is planted in the earth. Impaled on it, slumped against the crossguard, is Eve. Her dual daggers lie in the mud. She is unnervingly still.
(Voice-acted, a choked scream) EVE!
Cyan stumbles, falls, crawls the last few feet to her side, reaching out with a trembling hand.
(Voice-acted, a weak raspy cough) Heh... Took you long enough... rookie.
Cyan touches her arm. She's cold.
Don't talk! I can... my runes... I can fix this!
Eve gives a faint, tired smile — the most genuine Cyan has ever seen from her.
Save your mana... It's too late for... ghosts...
Finally... put her to rest. My last... loose end.
Don't say that! Don't... what about our promise? The tavern by the sea... you promised you'd teach me how to cheat at cards!
The first rule... kid... is never play a game... you can't win...
Cyan grips her hand, desperately trying to channel weak healing magic. It flickers and dies.

A bustling city market in the North, warm sunlight. A younger Cyan has tears streaming from her eyes, mouth wide open after trying a notoriously spicy skewer. Eve stands beside her, arms crossed, exasperated — then her composure breaks. A rare, genuine laugh. She fidgets with a tarnished silver coin.
(Flashback, clear and amused) You are, without a doubt, the biggest idiot I've ever met. What did you think 'Dragon's Breath' meant?
(Flashback, choking) I thought it was just a cool name!
Back on the battlefield. The silver coin slips from Eve's loosening grasp and falls into the mud. Cyan catches it instinctively. It's cold.
Cyan... The monsters... Lyrel... She's...
Go... Don't let my win... be for nothing.
(Sobbing) No... Eve, please...
Eve's head lolls to the side. Her eyes are empty. The music swells to a heartbreaking crescendo then fades.

KEY CG: Cyan on her knees, cradling Eve's lifeless head in her lap. The body still impaled on the massive dark greatsword. The beheaded Anne forgotten in the background. The Blood Moon casts a tragic light.
Cyan gently closes her eyes. Grief turns to cold, horrifying dread.
(Internal) Lyrel... She went to hold them back. The monsters... Eclia's monsters...
Cyan lays Eve down, clutching the silver coin in her fist. She forces herself to her feet and runs — no longer clumsy, but fueled by terror.

Ahead: an unnaturally alive patch of battlefield. A massive circle of glowing green vines and ethereal pulsing flora holds back a tide of snarling berserk monsters. A sanctuary of life in a field of death.

At the center, Lyrel floats just above the ground. Her body is wracked with spasms. Green energy pours from her, feeding the barrier, but black corrupted veins crawl up her arms and neck. Her life force is burning out.
LYREL!
Cyan sprints into the circle. The barrier flickers, letting her pass. She reaches Lyrel just as the light begins to dim. Lyrel falls into her arms, shockingly frail.
(Voice-acted, weak and strained) Cyan...? You came...
Stop this! Lyrel, you have to stop! It's killing you!
(A sad smile, face blood-streaked) It's okay... Look. The forest... can be born anew... even here.
I just... wish I could have seen... our forest... healthy again.
We will! We'll fix it together! Like we planned!

The Eldertide Forest before the worst of the poisoning. Sunlight through a lush green canopy. Lyrel, radiant and joyful, leads Cyan by the hand toward a hidden sparkling waterfall. Eve in the background, leaning against a tree, trying to look annoyed.
(Flashback, full of life) Isn't it amazing, Cyan? This is a Heartwood grove! The whole forest listens to this place. As long as the Heartwood is strong, there's always hope!
She reaches into a hollow in the ancient tree and pulls out a single smooth faintly glowing seed.
(Flashback, soft and sincere) Here. A promise. So you'll always have a piece of my home with you.
Back in Cyan's arms. She reaches into a pouch at her belt and pulls out the Heartwood seed. It's no longer glowing. It's dull, grey, and cracked.
Don't... make that face... It doesn't suit a hero...
Being deemed a traitor... it hurt. But with you... with Eve... it didn't feel so lonely...
Her hand weakly comes up to touch his cheek — then falls. Her breathing stops.

KEY CG: Cyan holding Lyrel's body. Her head tilted back over his arm. Face bloodied, eyes half-open and lifeless, a single bloody tear on her cheek. In the background her barrier of life shatters, and the tide of monsters begins to surge forward unopposed.
Cyan holds her tight, a silent guttural scream tearing from her throat. She has failed. She has lost everything. She holds Eve's cold coin in one hand and Lyrel's dead seed in the other.
She looks up and sees Princess Eclia in the distance, eyes glowing with power, monsters converging. There is no escape. There is no hope.
(Voice-acted, a whisper of absolute despair) I would give anything... anything... to do it all again.
As the first monster lunges, a blinding white light erupts from Cyan. Her rune magic, overloaded by grief and despair, goes nova.
A simple room in a small village. Cyan is sitting bolt upright in a cheap bed. Morning sun streams through the window. She's back where her journey started, just after her exile.
She frantically clutches her chest. Her hands come back empty. No coin. No seed.
(Internal) It... it was a dream? A nightmare?
She gets up and looks into a cracked mirror. Her face is younger, more naive... but her eyes are not. They hold the reflection of a burning battlefield and two dying friends.
FINAL CG: A close-up on Cyan's face. Expression of dawning horror, grief, and a new terrifyingly cold determination. Not the boy who was exiled. A survivor.
So. The great heroes return from the big B-Rank goblin hunt. Judging by your faces, I'm guessing you don't want a celebratory drink.
We failed, Gabe. The job's a bust. The Baron walked. We're not getting paid.
Hold on. There's a difference between 'failing a job' and 'not getting paid by a cheapskate nobleman'. Are the goblins still causing a problem at his logging camp?
No. We... convinced them to relocate.
And you did it without a massacre?
Yes. But the Baron wanted us to kill them, so when we refused...
So let me get this straight. You were hired to solve a pest problem. You went there, found out the 'pests' were just a bunch of brain-dead fans putting on a terrible play...
Cyan, Eve, and Lyrel recounted the entire absurd story. With every detail—the badger teleportation, the cabbage water, the 'Warden's Roar'—Gabe's amusement grew.
Hahaha! So you solved the problem, stood up to a pompous noble, and accidentally started a goblin cargo cult. That's not a failure! That's the most Strays-ass victory I've ever heard of!
It doesn't feel like a victory when we don't get paid for it.

Good thing I know my clients. I took a 'non-refundable security deposit' from the Baron before you even left. For 'potential property damage'. He was so furious he forgot to ask for it back. This should cover your fee.
And speaking of a job well done... Eve, Lyrel. Your report mentioned the kid handled herself.
He didn't panic when the plan went up in flames. And she stood his ground against the Baron. That takes guts.
His judgment in a chaotic social situation was sound. He chose a path that, while unconventional, prevented bloodshed. It was commendable.
A few days later...
A nervous-looking delivery boy entered the guild, dragging a large object covered by a burlap sack. He dropped it in the middle of the room, handed Gabe a note, and ran.
Huh. It's for 'The Strays'.
Cyan pulled off the sack. Underneath was, without a doubt, the single ugliest statue ever created.

It was a lopsided, life-sized sculpture of the three of them, made of mud, twigs, and stolen junk. The 'Eve' was a lump with two bent spoons for daggers. The 'Lyrel' had a ridiculous cape made of leaves. The 'Cyan' was just a smaller lump holding a shiny rock.
And at their feet, represented by a particularly spiky pinecone, was 'Anne the badger'.
I'm getting the firewood.
While aesthetically... challenging... it is a testament to the impact we have on the world. A terrible, terrible testament.
They... sent us a gift.
Major Arc Summary: "The Silent Forest"
Overall Arc Goal: Driven by their own initiative, the Strays will investigate the monster scarcity, uncover a single piece of a massive conspiracy, and be recruited by Inquisitor Brandt.
Together, they will unravel the South's audacious, multi-stage "Withering War" plan, ending the Common Route with the full, terrible truth.
Phase 1: The Local Problem (3 Scenes)
Goal: To establish the crisis and motivate the Strays to begin their own unsanctioned investigation.
Scenes:
1. An Echo in the Guild: Elara the Hunter explains that "the hunt is dead."
2. A Walk Through the Rot: The Strays witness the economic decay in Porthumming.
3. The Unsanctioned Hunt: The Strays, driven by what they've seen, get a lead from Elara about the strange, monster-less Whisperwood and decide to investigate on their own.
Phase 2: The Tip of the Iceberg (3 Scenes)
Goal: To have the Strays stumble upon the first layer of the conspiracy (the Capture Squad) and attract Brandt's attention.
Scenes:
1. The Wrong Tracks: In the Whisperwood, the Strays find evidence of a hunt, but the clues (like the tranquilizer dart) are all wrong.
2. The Ambush: The Beastman Capture Squad ambushes them to retrieve the evidence and eliminate witnesses. The Strays are forced into a desperate fight.

3. The Investigator: Inquisitor Brandtappears after the fight. He reveals he has been monitoring the region for "anomalous activity." He confiscates the dart and, impressed by their survival, offers them a private contract to help her find the enemy's base of operations.
Phase 3: The Money Grubbers (2 Scenes)
Goal: Guided by Brandt, the Strays will find the enemy's forward base and uncover the first two stages of the Southern plan, as well as the black market splinter group.
Scenes:
1. The Hidden Camp: Brandt's intelligence leads them to the Beastmen's hidden forward operating base. They infiltrate the camp, which is focused on trapping and transport logistics.
2. The Smugglers' Ledger: Inside the command tent, they find two crucial pieces of evidence.

Evidence A (The Official Plan):Maps detailing the Luring and Trapping Zones (Stages 1 & 2) and routes leading to a location marked "Subterranean Access Point," confirming their suspicions of a massive capture operation.

Evidence B (The Corruption): A separate, coded ledger detailing secret sales of high-quality monster parts to a black market contact in the North. This confirms the existence of the "Money Grubbing" Beastman faction, operating against their own mission for personal profit.
Phase 4: The Saboteurs (The Final 2 Scenes)
Goal: To use the smugglers' ledger to find the final piece of the puzzle—the Saboteurs—and uncover the full, horrifying truth of the "Withering War."
Scenes:

1. The Poisoned Honey Pot: The Strays report back to Brandt. He is shocked by the scale of the capture operation but fascinated by the smugglers' ledger. He recognizes the black market contact as a known front for a shadowy organization.
He devises a plan: use the ledger to set up a fake "buy" and lure the masterminds out. This leads them to the abandoned silver mine.

2. The Withering War (Common Route Finale): The "buy" is a trap. The silver mine is not a simple hideout; it's the main laboratory of the Saboteurs (the Lizardmen/Foxians). Here, they witness the final stages of the plan:
They see the high-quality parts from the Money Grubbers being received.
They see those same parts being analyzed and then used as templates to create the toxic, low-quality synthetics.

The Lead Saboteur confronts them, explaining their brilliant, parasitic strategy: they let the Beastmen do the dirty work, buy the real parts, and then sell poisonous fakes back to the North, profiting while accelerating the enemy's decay.

The arc ends with the Strays' desperate escape from the lab, now holding proof of the entire, multi-layered conspiracy. This leads directly into the final scene where Eve confronts Brandt, knowing he is far more than a simple magistrate.
The Aftermath: A World on the Brink
What the Player and the Strays See:
1. The Counter-Sabotage (Objective 1 & 2):
This should be the most visible consequence. A few weeks after the Strays' report, news will trickle into the guild. Not from official channels, but from rumors.

The Rumor Mill: Travelers will speak of a "catastrophic earthquake" that collapsed the old silver mine. Others will talk of a "freak fire" that destroyed a huge swathe of the Whisperwood where the Beastman camp was.

The Punchline: Then, the most exciting rumor: sightings of rare monsters—a lone Griffon, a pair of Basilisks—are being reported for the first time in years. It's confusing and chaotic, but for adventurers like Elara, it's a flicker of hope.

The Strays' Reaction: The Strays will know the truth. These weren't accidents; they were surgical strikes. They will understand that Brandt's report immediately led to decisive, covert action. This confirms they are now part of a much larger, more dangerous game.
2. The "Gold Rush" (The Effect of Objective 4):
You are right, showing the North borrowing money is probably too high-level. What the Strays would see is the direct result of that money flooding the system.

Brandt's New Quests: Brandt will return to the Strays, but this time with a different kind of contract. He'll explain that "private investors" (the allied nation) are funding a major initiative to rebuild the North's strength. He will hire the Strays for high-paying missions that support this:
"An old dwarven forge has been rediscovered. We need you to clear it of squatters and secure it." (Securing new production facilities).
"A reclusive but brilliant alchemist needs rare herbs from a dangerous swamp. Escort and protect her." (Rebuilding the potion supply chain).
"We need you to guard a massive shipment of high-quality steel being transported from the coast." (The influx of new resources).

The Effect on the World: The Strays will see the atmosphere in Porthumming and other towns begin to change. Guilds are busier. Adventurers have better gear. There's a sense of cautious optimism in the air. The North is actively, visibly getting stronger.
What is Kept Hidden (But Drives the Plot):

The Border Containment (Objective 3):This happens completely in secret. The Strays won't know that the Underground Road has been sealed. The player doesn't need to see this, but it's the critical action that forces the South's hand.
The South's Desperation: This is the most important consequence. You are 100% right. The South's leadership receives three devastating reports at once:
1. Their primary forward base has been destroyed.
2. Their main R&D lab has been annihilated.

3. Their primary infiltration route, the Underground Road, has been sealed. Their long-term "Withering War" plan is in ashes. They have lost the element of surprise. They know the North is now aware of them and is rapidly re-arming.
Setting Up the Next Grand Arc: "The Southern Gambit"
The South's conclusion is simple and terrifying: "We must strike now."

Their patient, multi-year plan has failed. They are forced to switch to a desperate, high-risk, high-reward strategy. They still have one trump card: the army of monsters they've already captured and the experimental bio-alchemical weaponsthey were developing.
The next phase of your visual novel will not be a cold war. It will be the frantic, final days before an inevitable invasion. The South will begin making overt moves:
Probing Attacks: Small squads of elite Southern soldiers (perhaps accompanied by a captured monster) will begin attacking Northern border forts to test their defenses.
Assassination Attempts: Key Northern figures who are helping the rebuilding effort (like the reclusive alchemist the Strays are hired to protect) will be targeted.
The Search for a New Path: The South will desperately search for a new way to invade, perhaps by sea or through a dangerous, forgotten mountain pass.

The Strays, as Brandt's trusted field team, will be on the front lines of every one of these incidents, unknowingly fighting to delay an invasion that their own actions accidentally accelerated. This creates a fantastic sense of forward momentum and rising tension.
The next morning, the air in Eve's inn was thick with the smell of stale ale and silence.
A massive, bearded man with the physique of a bear was fast asleep, her head pillowed on her arms at a corner table. His snores sounded like a distant thunderstorm.
Eve stood behind the bar, methodically cleaning a mug with a worn rag.
Morning, Eve! Ready for our debriefing at the guild?
Should we not wait? You seem to be... working.
Lyrel gestured vaguely at the empty, silent room.
This is it. This is the morning rush. Her.
She nodded toward the snoring drunk.
That's Borin. He's my best customer. Pays his tab once a month and serves as a free security system.
(mumbling in sleep)...I'll fight the whole lot o' ya...
See? Low maintenance.

Eve finished cleaning the mug, hung it up, and pulled a small, dusty wooden sign from under the counter. She flipped it over. On it, crudely painted, were the words: GONE HUNTING. POUR YOUR OWN. LEAVE COIN IN JAR.
Wait, that's it? You're just... leaving?
This place doesn't make money, kid. It's a place for me to drink in peace. If anyone wants a room, they can fight Borin for it. If they win, they've earned it.
She walked to the front door, flipped the 'Open' sign to 'Closed,' and hung her new sign on the inside.
She turned to them, completely deadpan.
Let's go. I'm missing out on valuable time I could be spending getting lectured by Gabe.
The guild hall was moderately busy. The Strays, still covered in grime from the basement, walked up to the counter where Gabe was sorting papers.
She looked up and did a visible double-take.
You're back already? And the town's still standing?
What did you break? Did you burn it down? I know you burned it down, Eve.
My professional integrity is wounded.
You don't have any. Report.
Cyan, standing a little taller than before, stepped forward.
Mission complete, Guild Master. The nest has been eradicated.
He proceeded to explain their 'Trinity Strike' strategy, detailing each member's role.
Huh.
Gabe leaned back, genuinely impressed.
A three-pronged synergistic assault... for rats. You three don't do anything halfway, do you?
The kid's scouting rune saved us from walking in blind. It's a solid strategy. He's not as useless as he looks.
Cyan beamed at the backhanded compliment.
And we couldn't have done it without Lyrel! Her spore magic was incredible! She handled the whole horde by herself!
Lyrel, unaccustomed to such direct praise, looked away, a faint blush on her cheeks.
It was a team effort... And... I suppose... Helmet Hair's final strike was... undeniably efficient.
Damn right it was.
Gabe was speechless for a moment, a rare sight. He expected them to fail, or worse, succeed by causing thousands in property damage.
She shook her head, a real smile breaking through his usual cynicism, and slid a heavy pouch of coins across the counter.
I'll be damned. You didn't kill each other. That's a first.
Go get a drink. My treat. You look like you've earned it.
A short while later, the four of them were gathered at a corner table. The mood was lighter than it had ever been.
So she really got drenched? The whole 'cabbage water' thing?
Completely! You should have seen her face!
Keep talking, kid, and I'll show you again up close.
I must admit, for a moment, I believed justice had been served.
Even Eve cracked a small, reluctant smile. For the first time, it felt less like a business arrangement and more like... a party.
From a nearby table, a loud, drunken voice cut through the chatter.
And then the bastard... my own partner... took the Eye of the Gorgon and ran! Left me for dead in that goblin nest! Can you believe it? Betrayed by my own friend of ten years!
The mood at their table instantly shifted.
Happens all the time. Never trust your partner more than you trust your own blade.
How could someone do that? A bond of trust is sacred. To break it is unforgivable.
Sounds like you picked a bad partner, old man.
Cyan was quiet. He wasn't cynical like Eve or morally outraged like Lyrel. She looked genuinely, deeply confused by the concept itself.
She turned to the group, her voice quiet and earnest.
But... why? Why would a friend do that to someone they trust?
The question hung in the air, heavy and out of place. It wasn't philosophical; it was personal and painful.
Eve's faint smile vanished. She gave Cyan a long, searching look, sensing again that there was a deeper wound there.
Lyrel saw his genuine pain and offered a reassuring smile, though she didn't understand its source.
Gabe, completely missing the subtext, just clapped her on the back.
Because people are bastards, kid. Welcome to the real world.
The laughter from the other table seemed distant and hollow.

They were closer now, yes. But Cyan's simple, painful question was a stark reminder that the greatest dangers they faced weren't in monster-filled basements, but in the pasts they were all running from.
Okay, first official quest as 'The Strays'! Let's make a good impression!
I am still formally protesting the name.
Protest denied. It's on the paperwork.
It is an affront to my dignity as a Warden of the Eldertide.
Good. Builds character.
Anne the cat, perched on Cyan's shoulder, flicked her tail in what could have been agreement or complete indifference.
Come on, you two. We're a team now. We have to at least pretend to get along.
Pretending is for nobles and people who aren't getting paid. I'm just here to make sure you don't Blink into a tree.
They walked on, the bickering eventually fading into a reluctant silence. After a half-hour, a small, well-kept cottage came into view, a thin trail of alchemical smoke curling from its chimney.
The door opened before they could knock. A man in his fifties, with kind eyes and a weary slump to his shoulders, stood in the doorway.
He wore a scholar's robe stained with chemicals.
You must be from the guild. Thank you for coming so quickly. I am Master Valerius.
Yes, sir! We're here for the subjugation quest. I'm Cyan, and this is...
Cyan hesitated, realizing she had to say the name out loud.
...we're 'The Strays'.
Valerius didn't laugh. He didn't even smile. He just nodded slowly, a deep, tired acceptance in her eyes.
An honest name. We are all strays from something, are we not? Please, come in.
The party exchanged glances. His reaction was somehow funnier than any joke would have been.
The cottage was tidy but cluttered. Books on magical theory were stacked next to half-eaten plates of food. The air smelled of dried herbs and something faintly metallic.
I apologize for the state of things. The... infestation has made work difficult.
You mentioned overgrown rats?
An understatement. Some of my reagents seem to have had an adverse effect on the local vermin. They're larger, more aggressive. Unpleasant.
Don't worry, Master Valerius! That's why we're here. We became adventurers to help people with problems just like this!
Cyan's voice was full of earnest, youthful energy. He truly believed it.
I was inspired, actually. By the stories of the great heroes of the North. People who fight for what's right.
A strange expression crossed Valerius's face. He let out a short, hollow chuckle, completely devoid of humor.
Heroes.

Heroes are what the capital calls the men who sign the paychecks, boy. The rest of us who did the work for them... we were just equipment. To be used, and then discarded when we were no longer convenient.
Cyan's smile faltered. She looked to Eve, who gave a slow, almost imperceptible nod of agreement. Lyrel frowned, sensing the bitter history behind the alchemist's words.
Forgive an old man his cynicism. I was a researcher for the army, once. A long time ago. Now I prefer a quiet life.
The problem is in the basement. I've sealed the door, but... the sounds are getting worse.
He led them to a heavy, reinforced door at the back of the cottage. He unbolted three heavy locks.
As the door creaked open, a wave of foul air washed over them. The smell of filth, acrid chemicals, and a thick, cloying scent of fear.
Valerius handed them a glowing crystal for light.
Be careful. They are not just rats anymore.
She closed the door behind them, the bolts sliding shut with a heavy thud. They were locked in.
Cyan held the light crystal high. The beam cut through the darkness, illuminating a stone staircase leading down.
And at the bottom of the stairs, visible in the dim, wavering light, were rows of cages.
Most were empty, their doors bent and broken from the inside. But one was not.
Inside it, a small creature whimpered. It looked like a fox, but two mismatched, leathery wings were crudely stitched to its back with thick, black thread.
Eve's hand went to her sword. Lyrel gasped, her face a mask of horror.
But Cyan... Cyan just stared. The eager adventurer was gone. Her face went pale, her eyes wide, fixed on the caged, broken animal.
The light from the crystal in her hand trembled.
By the Ancients... what has he done?
Lyrel's voice was a choked whisper. She took a step toward the cage, her hand outstretched as if to offer comfort.
Forget the creature. The mission is rats. And this place is a stone box.
Eve's voice was cold, pragmatic. The eager adventurer in Cyan was gone, replaced by a quiet, chilling stillness. The sight of the cage seemed to lock something down inside her.
There are vents near the ceiling. We seal the door crack, start a fire with some of this alchemical junk, and smoke them out. Fast, clean, and we get paid.
Absolutely not!
Lyrel spun around, her horror shifting to righteous fury.
We will not harm that innocent creature or resort to such mindless brutality! There is a life in that cage!
It's a failed experiment. A casualty. We have a job to do.
Eve drew two wicked-looking daggers from her belt, spinning them deftly.
You use daggers? I thought you used a sword.
A sword is for battlefields. Daggers are for tight, dirty places like this. And for getting a job done without any fuss.
Cyan finally spoke, her voice unnervingly flat.
We're not burning anything.
Exactly! I will use calming spores. We can pacify the aggressive ones without bloodshed and free that poor creature.
No.
Both women looked at her, surprised by his firm tone.
We don't know what we're fighting. Scouting first.
I'll use a rune. 'Rivira'. It will show us their numbers and where the nest is. Then we make a plan.
We don't have time for arts and crafts, kid. My way is faster.
And my way is merciful!
And my way isn't stupid! We go in blind, we get ambushed.
They stared at each other, a triangle of stubborn pride. No one was willing to compromise.
Fine. Have it your way.

Before Eve could even react, a torrent of frothy, foul-smelling water erupted from the grates directly above her." play sound "audio/water_splash_heavy.ogg
Lyrel ignored her, striding deeper into the basement.
Now, witness a proper solution.
She opened a pouch at her belt, tossing a fine powder into the air. It shimmered, creating a wave of soft, green light.
The sound of scuttling and squeaking rats immediately softened. Several normal-sized rats wobbled out from the shadows, yawned, and fell asleep.
It is done. Simple, and humane.
Then, a hiss echoed from the darkness. A rat the size of a wolfhound, with glowing red veins on its back, lunged from a pile of crates. It opened its mouth and spat a glob of green acid.
What?!
Lyrel threw up a thorny barrier just in time, the acid sizzling against the wood.
They're immune!
While they were distracted, Cyan found a clear space on the floor.
You two are impossible. I'll get us the intel.
She knelt, placing her hand on the stone. She began to chant, runes glowing around his palm.
Rivira... show me what hides in the dark...
A map of light spread across the floor, showing dozens of small dots... and one massive, pulsing cluster deep within a crack in the foundation.
The nest... it's in the wall...
Suddenly, a black blur shot out from under a shelf. One of the mutated rats, moving with unnatural speed, lunged for her throat.
Before it could connect, Anne the cat's eyes glowed. The world snapped.
Cyan found herself ten feet away, the scouting rune shattering into nothing. The rat crashed into the wall where he'd been kneeling.
Whoa! Thanks, Anne.
Acid sizzled behind them. Fast-moving shapes darted in the shadows. The sleeping rats were beginning to stir.
They were forced back to the staircase, dirty, frustrated, and having achieved nothing.
Well, that was a complete disaster.
If you had just let me handle the mutated ones—
With what? More sleepy dust? We need to eliminate the nest.
And we can't do that if we're fighting them one by one!
They stood in the dim light of the crystal, glaring at each other.
Their first mission as a team, and they had failed. Utterly.
I'm telling you, if you'd just let me handle it—
And bring the whole cottage down on our heads? Your solution to everything is overwhelming force!
It works, doesn't it? Better than your sleepy dust.
At least my methods don't cause collateral damage, you brute!
Cyan slammed her hand against the cold stone wall. The sharp sound echoed in the small space, cutting through their argument.
ENOUGH!
Eve and Lyrel stopped, both turning to look at her, surprised by his sudden fire.
Arguing isn't going to work. Your plan failed, Eve. My plan failed. And Lyrel, your plan failed too. We can't do this alone. So let's stop trying to.
Let's just... talk. What do we actually know?
She took the lead, not as a commander, but as a moderator trying to stop a fight.
My scouting rune worked for a second. There are dozens of small ones, four or five of those big mutated ones, and one huge nest deep in a crack in the back foundation. The nest is the source.
The smaller creatures are no threat if they can be pacified. My spores will work on them, but they had no effect on the mutated ones. Their magical resistance is too high.
And those mutated ones are the real problem. They're fast, and that acid can melt steel. The wards on this place prevent any large-scale attacks.

I could fight them all, but I can't guarantee this place would still be standing. If I'm dodging acid and fighting off a horde, I can't afford to hold back. Gabe's 'no S-rank solutions' rule goes out the window.
Okay... so we have a horde that needs to be controlled, and elites that need to be distracted, all so we can hit a single target without bringing the house down.
Lyrel closed her eyes, thinking.
If I could focus just on the horde, I could create a 'path of peace' through them. But I'd be completely exposed to the mutated ones.
And if I had a clear path, I could get to that nest and finish this in under five seconds. But I can't do that while fending off those acid-spitters. I need a diversion.
A moment of silence hung in the air as the pieces of the puzzle clicked into place. Cyan looked at Eve, then at Anne the cat, who was watching them with intelligent eyes.
A diversion... Eve, you need something that can get their attention but can't be easily hit, right?
Yeah. Something impossibly fast.
A slow grin spread across Cyan's face. She looked at Anne.
We can do that. Anne and I. We'll be the diversion. We'll Blink around, keep the big ones busy. They can't hit a moving target.
Lyrel's eyes widened as she saw the full picture.
It could work! While you have the elites' attention, I will pacify the horde. That will give Eve...
...a clean run straight to the nest.
Eve finished the thought. A rare glint of professional respect flickered in her eyes as she looked from Cyan to Lyrel.
It's a risky plan. If your timing is off by a second, kid, you're acid-bait.
We can do it. Together.
They looked at each other, a silent agreement passing between them. No one was giving orders. It was their plan.

They moved as one. Lyrel went first, casting her spores in a wide, sweeping arc. A wave of calming green energy washed over the basement, and the horde of smaller rats instantly slowed, their aggression fading.
The mutated rats hissed, unaffected. Just as they were about to lunge at Lyrel, the air snapped.
Cyan appeared directly in front of them. 'Hey, ugly!' he yelled, waving her arms.
As they spat acid, he vanished again, reappearing safely on the other side of the room. Anne and Cyan became a blur of blue light, a constant, impossible-to-hit distraction.
It was all the opening Eve needed. With the horde pacified and the elites distracted, she exploded into motion.
She was a silver streak, her twin daggers a blur. She ran through the path Lyrel had cleared, vaulted over a sleeping rat, and reached the back wall.
Without hesitating, she plunged both daggers deep into the pulsating, fleshy nest.
A piercing shriek echoed through the basement. The mutated rats froze, their glow fading, and collapsed. The magic holding them together was gone.
The silence that followed was absolute. The basement was still, the threat neutralized.
Cyan leaned against a wall, breathing heavily. Lyrel was already kneeling, checking on the sleeping rats.
Eve calmly wiped her daggers clean.
Job done.
Before they left, Lyrel walked to the cage at the back of the room. She placed a hand on the whimpering creature, a soft green light flowing from her palm, healing the worst of its wounds.
Cyan followed her. He didn't say a word. He just lifted his boot and brought his heel down hard on the cage's rusty lock.
The door swung open. The small creature looked at her for a long moment before scurrying into a dark crack in the wall, and to freedom.
Eve watched from the stairs, rolling her eyes. But she didn't stop them.
They met Valerius outside. He handed them a pouch of coins without asking for details.
As they took the money, Cyan looked the alchemist directly in the eye. He didn't say anything, but his cold, disappointed stare said everything that needed to be said.
You're right, boy. I should have been more careful.
The old man turned and went back inside his quiet cottage, closing the door on his secrets.
The Strays walked back to Porthumming. They didn't talk much on the way.
They weren't friends yet. But the silence between them was no longer hostile. It was the quiet of a team that had survived its first test.
The morning after the goblin statue's arrival was heavy with an unspoken question.
The sheet-covered lump in the corner served as a silent, ugly monument to their chaotic existence.
Eve stared at it, her breakfast untouched. The weariness of the past few weeks seemed to finally settle on her shoulders.
What are we doing?
What do you mean?
This. The Strays. Stumbling from an alchemist's disaster to a goblin fan club. We almost get killed, we barely get paid... What is the *point* of all this?
The point? Eve, we're helping people! The ones nobody else will. We freed that creature, we saved those goblins from being slaughtered.
Isn't this what real adventurers do? It's exactly what a hero like Anne would have done!
The name hit the air like a shard of glass. A flicker of raw pain crossed Eve's face before a cold, bitter mask slammed down in its place.
You have no idea what you're talking about, kid.
You think being a hero like Anne is a storybook? It's being a weapon for other people's wars until you break. That's the 'point'.
He is naive. Dangerously so.
But his naivete provides an unexpected tactical advantage.
Consider our recent missions. An illegal alchemy lab and a dispute with a minor noble. We operated completely beneath the notice of the military or any major political power.
Our reputation is not that of efficient mercenaries, but of chaotic, unpredictable eccentrics.
This... foolishness... is the perfect camouflage. By following his idealistic crusade to 'help the forgotten,' we become invisible.
No one of power would ever see 'The Strays' as a threat or a tool worth controlling. It grants us the freedom to move and act without scrutiny.
And so, an unspoken agreement was forged. It was not a shared goal, but a fragile symbiosis.
Cyan would get to be the hero he always dreamed of being.
And in doing so, he would provide the perfect shield for the two deeply wounded people following in his wake.
Fine. Do whatever you want.
Just... don't use her name like that again.
The air was thick with the things left unsaid. Eve's warning to never use Anne's name like that again hung between them, heavy and cold.
Cyan opened her mouth, the shape of an apology on his lips, but Lyrel spoke first, her voice cutting cleanly through the tension.
The issue of our 'camouflage' is settled. However, the mission at the Baron's logging camp revealed a significant tactical flaw in our operational structure.
Eve, your power is overwhelming but indiscriminate. My own skills are for precision and defense. In both of our recent missions, we have been a sledgehammer and a scalpel.
We lack versatility. We lack a proper vanguard.
We are a liability because you cannot keep up.

She's right, kid. The goblin thing was a joke, but if that Baron had been a real commander, you'd be dead. Your Blink is a great trick, but in a real fight, you're a glass cannon with a five-second fuse.
We need to get you to B-Rank proficiency. Not on paper, but in practice. If you're going to run with this circus, you need to be able to pull your own weight when things get real.
Okay... so how do I do that? What does a B-Rank test even look like?

There is no single test. One is recognized as B-Rank when one has survived a B-Rank threat. My own recognition came during the border skirmishes. My unit was tasked with holding a mountain pass against a full legion of Southern regulars for three days.
It was not about killing. It was about controlling the terrain, managing dwindling supplies, and outlasting a superior force. B-Rank, for a Warden, is about endurance and strategy.
And... and you, Eve?
A distant, almost fond look entered her eyes. It was a startlingly open expression, a brief glimpse of a person Cyan had never met.
My test was... messier. Less strategy, more chaos.

It was before the war. Back when monster subjugation quests were still common. A whole clan of Orcs had migrated down from the Dragon's Tooth mountains and were terrorizing the northern farmlands. A real B-Rank threat.
A ghost of a smile touched her lips, tinged with a deep, unspoken sadness.
There were three of us. A loudmouthed warrior who was better at taking hits than planning...
She means Gabe.
...the shield of the party, calm and focused, the one who actually kept the warrior from getting herself killed...
She means Anne.
...and me.
The smile turned a little more real, a little more weary.

We were young, stupid, and thought we were invincible. The plan went to hell in the first five minutes. We were supposed to ambush them in a ravine, but our warrior tripped a rockslide and we ended up in a full-blown brawl with fifty angry orcs.

It wasn't elegant. It wasn't clean. We won because we refused to lose. He held the line, she picked off their shaman, and I just... caused chaos. Traps, smoke bombs, hamstringing their biggest brutes from the shadows. B-Rank, for us... it was about pure, stubborn teamwork. Watching each other's backs and pulling a win out of a complete disaster.
The room was silent. Cyan was left with two starkly different images of strength: Lyrel's disciplined military operation, and Eve's chaotic, friendship-fueled trial by fire.
So... I just need to survive something impossible?
Pretty much. You're not a Warden and you don't have a party of idiots to watch your back... well, you've got two idiots now, I guess.
We'll have to find a job that tests *your* limits as a Rune Mage.
Indeed. A standard subjugation will not suffice. We need a mission that requires a unique application of your skills.
The weight in the inn's common room had been lifted, replaced by a new, tangible sense of purpose. For the first time, they weren't just reacting to chaos; they were actively seeking it.
As they walked through the streets of Porthumming, the morning sun casting long shadows, Eve broke the comfortable silence.
Alright, kid. Before we go looking for a B-Rank suicide mission, let's get one thing straight. What are you even trying to be?
Huh? I'm a Rune Mage.
That's not a thing. That's a title. I'm talking about your class. Your path.
My... path?
Your combat discipline. Most adventurers begin by mastering one of the Four Pillars. The Warrior, the Rogue, the Archer, or the Mage.
From there, one can either perfect their Pillar or walk an Advanced Path by combining two.
So a Mage can become something else?

Correct. A Mage who devotes themselves solely to the arcane arts may become a Wizard, a master of complex, learned magic. Conversely, a Warrior who studies magic can become a holy Paladin. That was Anne's path.
My own class, Arcane Archer, is the fusion of the Archer and Mage Pillars.
And some people are just born with it. They're Sorcerers. Magic in their blood from some long-dead dragon ancestor or whatever. They don't learn it, they just... are.
Wow. So what about you, Eve? You're a Rogue, but you fight more like a Warrior.
A pure Rogue is a backstabber hiding in the dark. Too fragile. I walk the path of the Duelist. It's a fusion of the Warrior's resilience and the Rogue's speed.
I even use a little magic, but not for light shows. Just enough to harden my skin or make my muscles fire faster. It's about ending a fight before the other guy even knows what hit her.
Wizards, Sorcerers, Paladins, Duelists... Cyan felt a growing sense of unease. He didn't fit into any of these molds.
Which brings us back to you, Cyan. Your 'Rune Magic' does not seem to be a Pillar, an Advanced Path, or a Sorcerous bloodline. What is its origin?
He was in exile, hiding from his past. But these two were his team. They deserved to know something.
It's... it's a Southern art.
From the Southern Alliance?
Yes. It was developed by the Rune Weaver tribe. I learned the basics from a guard I knew when I was younger.

It's not like your magic. We don't channel power from the world. The spells are pre-woven into runes, and we just... activate them. It requires high intelligence and a certain... compatibility. That's why not many can use it, even in the South.

The North's propaganda painted the Southern Alliance as a horde of savages. But Lyrel knew their military was brutally effective. To learn of a rare and powerful Southern magic from the boy in front of her was a paradigm shift.
Fascinating. A form of prepared, activated magic... The tactical applications are immense.
The Southern Alliance... The Five Tribes. The Rune Weavers are one... The Beastmen are another, aren't they?
Yes. The wolf-kin and the bear-kin are the strongest.
For the first time since he'd met her, Cyan saw a look of genuine, almost childish wonder in Eve's eyes. It was completely unguarded.
So... you've seen them? The wolf-kin who walk the Warrior's path?
The Werewolves? Uh, yes. I have.
Hmph. In my younger days, I would always dream of being able to do that.
To just... let go. Transform into something else. Something wild and strong that no one could hurt.
Ho ho...
So the stray dog dreams of being a wolf.
Eve's head snapped back towards them, her face flushing a deep, embarrassed red as she realized how much she'd just revealed.
Shut it, elf!
Anyway. Southern magic, Beastmen... you're full of surprises, aren't you?
Great. So you really are in a class of your own. Class: 'Secret Southern Weirdo'.
Hey! Keep your voice down!
And I'm not a weirdo!
Oh, right. Gotta protect your little secret. My mistake, 'Mister Not-From-Around-Here'.
But the name doesn't matter. The path does. So forget the title for a minute, 'Secret Southern Weirdo'...
And tell me what you're going to *do*. You can't just be 'the guy with the cat' forever. You need a focus.
Are you going to learn how to take a hit like a Warrior? Use dirty tricks like a Rogue? Shoot magic from afar like an Archer? Or double down on that rune stuff like a proper Mage?
