steps.text: If I'm going to protect people, I need to be able to stand on the front line. I'll focus on the Warrior's path. A Rune Knight.
Heh. A frontline magic-user. Bold. I can work with that.
A sound tactical choice. Your defensive capabilities will be a great asset.
Brute force isn't everything. I'll focus on the Rogue's path. Control the fight before it even begins. A Rune Trickster.
Smart. A battlefield is just a big trap waiting to be sprung. I like the way you think.
An unconventional but potentially devastating choice. Your ability to disable opponents without lethal force will be valuable.
You two are masters of close combat. The party needs someone who can provide cover from afar. I'll focus on the Archer's path. A Rune Caster.
Safe. Practical. Can't argue with it.
An excellent decision. A ranged fighter who can coordinate with a Warden is a powerful combination.
This power is my heritage. I need to understand it, not just imitate other styles. I'll focus on the Mage's path. A true Rune Weaver.
Doubling down on the weird, huh? Ambitious. Don't blow yourself up.
A bold path, and perhaps the most powerful. To master an entirely different school of magic... I will be observing your progress with great interest.
Alright. You've got your goal.
Now, c'mon. Let's go see if Gabe has a quest weird enough to test it.
He wasn't just a boy with a cat anymore. He was a Rune {cyan_path}. And she had work to do.
The fire had burned down to coals.
Cyan stopped speaking.
The silence that followed wasn’t empty. It pressed in, thick and heavy, like the air before a storm. Ash drifted lazily upward, carried by a wind that didn’t care what it disturbed.
Lyrel was the first to move.
She stepped away from the fire and wrapped her arms around herself, ears pinned back, eyes fixed on the dark beyond the ruins.
“…They called her Mother of Monsters,” she said quietly.
Cyan flinched at the title.
Lyrel continued, voice strained but steady. “The soldiers whisper it like a curse. Like she’s something that chose this.”
“She didn’t,” Cyan said immediately.
Eve didn’t respond right away. She crouched near the fire and picked up the folded report again, scanning it once more even though she already knew what it said.
“This intelligence is real,” she said at last. “I hate the North. You know that. But this?” She tapped the page. “This is how they operate when they’re certain.”
Cyan shook his head. “They lie.”
“They manipulate,” Eve corrected. “They exaggerate. They reframe.”
She looked up at him. “But they don’t invent command structures mid-war. Not without proof.”
Lyrel turned back toward them. “The monsters are moving together. Not just attacking — coordinating. Retreating. Surrounding.”
“That doesn’t mean it’s her,” Cyan said. “That just means someone’s controlling them.”
Eve stood.
“And the report says she is.”
Cyan’s fists clenched. “Then the report is wrong.”
Eve studied him, eyes sharp but not unkind. “You think the South just picked a random girl and put a crown on her?”
“She was taken,” Cyan snapped. “Experimented on. Used. You heard what they did to her.”
“I heard what happened to a child,” Eve said. “I’m looking at what exists now.”
Lyrel stepped between them slightly, her voice softer.
“Cyan… even if she didn’t choose this,” she said, “she’s still at the center of it. Monsters are dying. People are dying.”
“She wouldn’t want that,” Cyan said. “She hated hurting things.”
Eve’s jaw tightened. “People change.”
“No,” Cyan said. “They’re changed.”
The words hung there.
Lyrel looked down. “The rumor says she commands them by blood.”
Cyan’s head snapped up. “That’s not how it works.”
Eve narrowed her eyes. “You know that?”
Cyan hesitated — just for a moment.
“…Yes.”
Eve didn’t press. She didn’t need to.
“So what,” Eve said slowly, “you think we march into the South, past Fenrir, past an army of monsters, and pull her out?”
Cyan didn’t answer immediately.
“I think,” he said, voice lower now, “that if I can reach her, she’ll stop.”
Lyrel’s breath caught. “Cyan—”
“She listened to me,” he insisted. “She trusted me.”
Eve shook her head. “You were children.”
“She’s still her,” Cyan said. “Somewhere.”
The fire popped, sending sparks into the air.
Lyrel looked between them, torn. “If you’re wrong—”
“I’m not,” Cyan said.
Eve turned away, staring into the dark.
“Then you’re asking us to gamble the war on a memory,” she said. “And if you’re right… we still have to deal with everything else.”
Cyan’s voice was quiet. “I’m not asking you to follow me.”
Eve glanced back at him sharply. “That’s worse.”
Lyrel swallowed. “We can’t stay like this,” she said. “If we split—”
“We already are,” Eve replied.
The words settled like ash.
Eve folded the report once, carefully, then tossed it into the fire. The paper curled and blackened, Eclia’s name vanishing first.
“I’ll help stop the worst of it,” Eve said. “Heroes. Weapons. Things that shouldn’t exist.”
Lyrel nodded slowly. “I’ll try to calm what can still be calmed.”
They both looked at Cyan.
He didn’t look away from the fire.
“I’m going to her,” he said.
No one argued.
Above them, the sky remained dark and unmoved.
The Strays were still together.
But for the first time, they were no longer walking the same road.
The fire burned low.
Not because there was no wood left, but because no one had bothered to add more.

Cyan sat with his back against a broken pillar, watching embers collapse into ash. Across from him, Eve wiped her blade clean with slow, practiced motions, scraping dried blood from the edge as if it were no different from mud.
Lyrel stood a little apart, hands wrapped around a chipped cup she hadn’t drunk from.
The town behind them was quiet in the wrong way.
No shouting.
No movement.
Just smoke drifting lazily from places that should not have burned.
“They’re calling it a success,” Eve said at last.
Lyrel’s ears twitched. “Who is they?”
“The relay,” Eve replied. “Northern command. Supply routes intact. Monster pressure reduced.”
“Reduced?” Lyrel asked softly. “They tore through the eastern quarter.”
Eve slid the blade back into its sheath. “War doesn’t care where people live.”
Cyan lifted his head. “We weren’t supposed to be part of this.”
Eve looked at him. “We stopped it from becoming worse.”
“That’s what they always say,” Lyrel murmured.
Footsteps crunched through the rubble.
Brandt emerged from the smoke like he always did — clean, composed, untouched by the destruction around him. His coat bore no dust. His gloves were pristine.
“You’ll redeploy at dawn,” he said, stopping just outside the firelight. “Further south.”
Eve exhaled slowly. “We’re not soldiers.”
“No,” Brandt agreed. “You’re deniable.”
Lyrel looked up sharply.
“Independent. Mobile. Difficult to replace,” Brandt continued calmly. “That makes you useful.”
Cyan stood. “You said this was stabilization.”
“It was,” Brandt replied. “Before the situation changed.”
Eve crossed her arms. “Define changed.”
Brandt reached into his coat and produced a folded document, sealed with a thin strip of wax. He placed it on a flat stone near the fire.
“Updated intelligence,” he said. “Read it carefully. Everything you need is there.”
Eve picked it up immediately, eyes scanning the page.
“…Monster coordination confirmed,” she read. “Previously independent packs now acting in sequence.”
Lyrel leaned closer. “That’s new.”
“Yes,” Brandt said. “And unsustainable.”
“And the source?” Eve asked without looking up.
Brandt adjusted his gloves.
“Identified. Classified. Recorded.”
Lyrel frowned. “So we don’t even get a name?”
“You don’t need clarification,” Brandt replied. “You need compliance.”
He glanced at the fire.
“You move at first light,” he continued. “Burn the report after.”
Then he turned and walked away, boots disappearing into the smoke without another word.
Silence followed him.
Eve kept reading.
“…Mother of Monsters,” she said quietly. “Field designation.”
Cyan stiffened. “That’s just a rumor.”
Lyrel’s gaze dropped to the page. Her expression changed.
“It lists Fenrir,” she said. “And the missing monster cases.”
Eve’s voice slowed.
“…Confirmed leadership of the Southern coalition,” she read.
“…Primary control vector for non-human forces.”
Her thumb stopped.
“…Name recorded.”
The fire crackled.
Cyan shook his head. “No.”
Lyrel looked at Eve. “Read it.”
Eve hesitated — just a fraction — then spoke.
“Eclia.”
The word landed heavy and final.
Cyan laughed once, sharp and wrong. “That’s not who she is.”
Eve looked up at him. “You know her.”
Cyan swallowed. “They’re lying.”
Lyrel stepped closer, voice gentle.
“You always avoid talking about the South,” she said. “You always have.”
She met his eyes.
“You knew her, didn’t you?”
Cyan stared into the embers.
“That’s not who she is,” he said again, quieter.
Lyrel’s voice barely carried.
“Then who is she?”
The fire dimmed.
The night receded.
And Cyan remembered.
The palace changed overnight.
Cyan noticed it in the little things first.
The rugs in the hallways were gone. The curtains were tied back. Servants walked in pairs now, whispering to each other and stopping whenever someone important passed by.
Even the air felt different—too clean, like after a storm.
“Did they lose something?” she asked as they crossed the courtyard.
Eclia shook her head. “I don’t think so.”

They reached the outer garden, only to find a line of adults standing near the entrance. Not guards—these ones wore plain robes marked with thin silver stitching, their expressions calm and sharp at the same time.
“Who are they?” she whispered.
Eclia didn’t answer.

One of the robed figures was speaking quietly to a Rune Weaver. The Weaver nodded too many times, hands folded tight in front of him. Another figure took notes on a thin slate that glowed faintly as symbols rearranged themselves.
She leaned closer. “Are they teachers?”
Eclia hesitated. “…Observers.”
That word didn’t sound fun.
As they turned away, Vera appeared, moving faster than usual.
“Not today,” she said softly but firmly. “You can’t play here.”
“But—“ she started.
“I said not today.”
Her voice wasn’t angry.
That made it worse.
She guided them down a different path, one Cyan hadn’t taken before. Doors that were usually open were sealed now, runes glowing faintly along their edges. Some flickered when Eclia passed.
Cyan noticed Vera’s hand tighten around Eclia’s wrist—not rough, but protective, like she was afraid to let go.
They reached a small sitting room near the back of the palace. It was plain and quiet.
“Stay here,” Vera said. “I’ll come get you.”
Eclia looked up at her. “For how long?”
Vera paused.
“…I don’t know,” she said honestly.
That made Cyan’s chest feel funny.
“Is this about the test?” she asked brightly. “She did really good last time.”
Vera’s eyes flicked to him.
“Yes,” she said after a moment. “She did.”
A knock sounded at the door before Cyan could ask more.
A man in a silver-stitched robe bowed slightly. “Lady Eclia. They’re ready.”
Eclia stood.
She smoothed her dress, then hesitated and looked back at Cyan.
“I’ll come find you later,” she said.
“Okay,” Cyan replied immediately. “I’ll wait.”
She smiled at that.
As she followed the man down the corridor, Cyan watched the door close behind her. The runes flared briefly, then dimmed.
Vera didn’t move.
For a long moment, she just stood there, staring at the door like she could see through it.
Finally, she knelt in front of Cyan.
“You listen very well,” she said quietly. “Do you know that?”
Cyan blinked. “I do?”
She nodded. “That’s a good thing. But sometimes… it’s better not to listen too closely.”
She laughed. “Then how will I learn anything?”
Vera smiled, but it didn’t reach her eyes.
“That,” she said, standing again, “is something we’ll talk about another day.”
From the other side of the palace, a low hum began—deep, steady, and wrong.
Cyan decided it was just another machine starting up.
He waited.
Cyan woke up because the palace was too quiet.
Not the normal quiet. This one felt stretched thin, like a held breath.

She rolled over on the small cot Vera had insisted she use whenever she stayed late. Moonlight slipped through the narrow window, painting the floor in pale silver. For a moment, he considered going back to sleep.
Then he heard it.
A soft scrape. Then another.
Cyan sat up.
The door to the hallway was open just a little.
She padded out barefoot, careful not to make a sound. The palace at night felt different—bigger, emptier. Even the runes along the walls glowed dimmer, like they were tired too.
Light spilled from the kitchen.

Vera stood at the counter, sleeves rolled up, hair loose around her shoulders. A small candle burned beside her, its flame steady and low. Papers were spread across the stone surface—thin sheets etched with symbols Cyan half-recognized and half didn’t.
She didn’t notice him at first.
Vera read one page, then another. Her face didn’t change much, but her hands trembled slightly as she folded the paper in half. Then again. Smaller. Tighter.
She moved to the hearth and fed it to the fire.
The paper burned fast.
Cyan frowned. “Is something broken?”
Vera startled.
She turned so quickly the candle flickered.
“…Cyan,” she said, relief and something else crossing her face. “You should be asleep.”
“I heard noises,” she said apologetically. “Are we in trouble?”
“No,” she said at once. Too quickly. “No one’s in trouble.”
She shuffled closer, peering at the remaining papers. “Are those lessons?”
Vera stepped between her and the counter without thinking.
“Yes,” she said. Then, more softly, “No.”
She sighed and knelt so they were eye level.
“Sometimes,” she said, choosing her words carefully, “adults have to clean up messes before they become disasters.”
She brightened. “Like heroes!”
Her mouth twitched.
“…Yes,” she said. “Like that.”
She reached out and smoothed her hair, lingering a moment longer than usual.
“You’ve been very good,” she added. “Staying where I tell you. Not asking too many questions.”
She beamed. “I’m practicing.”
“I know.”
She stood again and gathered the last of the papers. This time, she didn’t burn them. She tucked them into a small metal box instead and locked it with a soft click.
Cyan watched, curious. “What’s in there?”
“Things I don’t want to forget,” Vera replied.
From somewhere deep in the palace, a dull vibration passed through the floor. Not loud enough to be a sound. Just enough to be felt.
She laughed nervously. “Is the palace snoring?”
Vera closed her eyes for half a second.
“Yes,” she said. “Something like that.”
She guided her back toward her cot, pulling a blanket up around her shoulders.
“Sleep,” she said. “Tomorrow will be easier.”
“Will Eclia be okay?” she asked, suddenly.
Vera paused.
Then she smiled—the real one, warm and familiar.
“She’s strong,” she said. “Stronger than she knows.”
That was enough for him.
As Cyan drifted back to sleep, Vera returned to the kitchen alone. She opened the metal box once more, stared at its contents, then closed it without touching anything.
Outside, the moon slid behind a cloud.
And for the first time, Vera allowed herself to whisper into the empty room:
“…This is getting out of hand.”
No one heard her.
Cyan found the book under his mattress.
He’d hidden it there weeks ago, folded carefully so the corners wouldn’t bend. The cover was faded, the title barely legible, but he knew every picture by heart.
Great Deeds of the Free Adventurers.
He lay on his stomach and opened it anyway.

The pages smelled like dust and ink. Illustrations filled the margins—figures standing atop ruins, swords raised, cloaks snapping dramatically in the wind. Monsters lay defeated at their feet, always larger than life, always unmistakably evil.
Cyan traced one picture with his finger.
“This one crossed the sea,” he murmured to himself. “And this one fought a dragon. And this one saved a city.”
He liked that one best.
He glanced up when footsteps passed outside the room. Voices murmured, then moved on. Cyan waited until the sound faded before returning to the book.
Heroes were simple.
They saw something wrong.
They got stronger.
They fixed it.
No secrets. No confusion.
Eclia sat beside him on the floor, knees pulled to her chest. She watched the pictures without comment, her chin resting on her arms.
“Do they ever lose?” she asked.
Cyan shook his head immediately. “Nope.”
“What if they get hurt?”
“They get back up.”
“What if they’re scared?”
He smiled at her. “Then they’re brave.”
She considered this.
“…I don’t think I’d be very good at that,” she said.
Cyan frowned. “Why not?”
“I don’t like fighting,” she admitted. “And I don’t like hurting things.”
“That’s why you’d be good,” he said, as if this were obvious. “Heroes don’t like it. They just do it when they have to.”
Eclia looked away, staring at nothing.
“Would you save me?” she asked suddenly.
Cyan didn’t hesitate. “Of course.”
From anything. From anywhere.
She smiled faintly at that and leaned closer, her shoulder brushing his.
Outside the window, a line of smoke drifted briefly into view from the far wing of the palace before dissipating into the air.
Cyan didn’t notice.
He turned the page.
“When I’m an adventurer,” he continued eagerly, “I’ll go everywhere. The North, the South, the places in between. I’ll help people so nobody has to be scared.”
Eclia listened quietly.
“That sounds nice,” she said.
“It’ll work,” Cyan insisted. “Stories wouldn’t lie.”
She closed her eyes.
For a moment, the world felt as simple as the pages in Cyan’s hands.
Eclia waited until the palace was fully asleep.
Not quiet—asleep.
There was a difference, and she knew it now.
She counted the guards by sound alone. The rhythm of their boots. The pause near the stairwell. The longer stop by the west wing where someone always yawned too loudly.
Only then did she turn to Cyan.
“It’s clear,” she whispered.
Cyan blinked. Then grinned.
“Oh?” he said softly. “Listen to you.”
She frowned. “What?”
He leaned closer, voice teasing. “Last time you were shaking.”
“I was not.”
“You absolutely were.”
“I was cautious,” Eclia corrected, lifting her chin. “That’s different.”
Cyan laughed silently, covering his mouth. “Careful, Princess. Next thing I know, you’ll be dragging me into trouble.”
She didn’t deny it.
Eclia opened the door.
This time, she didn’t hesitate.
She led them through the corridor, choosing turns without stopping, guiding them past shadows and light with quiet confidence. When Cyan lagged behind once, she reached back and tugged his sleeve.
“Keep up,” she whispered.
He raised both hands in surrender. “Yes, yes. Very scary.”
They reached the kitchen without incident.
Eclia climbed onto the crate first.
Cyan stared. “Wow. Didn’t even wait for me.”
She glanced down at him. “You said the window sticks on the left.”
He blinked again.
“…I did say that.”
She pushed exactly where she needed to. The window opened without a sound.
Cyan shook his head in disbelief. “You’re terrifying.”
She smiled—just a little.
Inside, they moved quickly. Confidently.
Too confidently.
The door behind them opened.
Light spilled into the kitchen.
“Interesting,” a calm voice said.
Eclia froze.
Cyan turned slowly.
Vera stood in the doorway, arms crossed, expression unreadable.
The world seemed to collapse inward.
“I—” Eclia started, breath hitching. “I can explain—”
Cyan stepped forward immediately.
“It was my idea,” he said. Loud. Clear. “All of it.”
Vera’s gaze shifted to him.
“Oh?”
“I showed her the route,” Cyan continued, standing straighter than he ever had. “I told her when to go. I wanted cookies. She just… followed.”
Eclia stared at him.
That wasn’t true. Not anymore.
Vera studied them both for a long moment.
Then she sighed.
“Sit,” she said, gesturing to the table.
They obeyed instantly.
Vera placed the plate of cookies between them. Untouched.
“You two,” she said evenly, “are very bad at being subtle.”
Cyan winced.
Eclia’s hands trembled in her lap.
“But,” Vera continued, softer now, “you are very good at working together.”
Eclia looked up sharply.
Vera met her eyes.
“Next time,” Vera said, “you will tell me beforehand.”
Cyan blinked. “There’s a next time?”
Vera gave him a look.
“One that does not involve guards, broken windows, or heart failure,” she said. “Yes.”
Eclia let out a shaky breath she hadn’t realized she was holding.
Vera turned to Cyan again.
“And you,” she added, “will understand this.”
Her tone sharpened—not angry, but firm.
“Bravery is not stealing cookies,” Vera said. “Bravery is taking responsibility when someone weaker might suffer.”
Cyan nodded, serious now. “I know.”
Vera watched him closely.
She believed him.
After Vera left, the room felt different. Smaller. Quieter.
Eclia stared at the table.
“You didn’t have to do that,” she said.
Cyan shrugged, trying to smile. “Sure I did.”
She looked at him.
“What if she punished you?”
He tilted his head. “Then she punishes me.”
That answer settled somewhere deep inside her.
Not loud.
Not dramatic.
Just solid.
That night, as Eclia lay awake listening to the palace breathe, she held onto that moment.
Not the cookies.
Not the sneaking.
But the way Cyan stepped forward without fear—
not to break rules,
but to protect someone else.
That day, Eclia learned what bravery looked like.
And years later, when she stood alone before the North and chose war over obedience,
she did not tremble.
She had learned long ago
how to step out first.
Vera waited until the palace settled.
That meant after the last bells, after the guards changed shifts, after the runes dimmed to their night-glow. Only then did she knock softly on Cyan’s door.
She opened it immediately.
“You’re late,” she said cheerfully.
“I know,” Vera replied. “May I come in?”
She stepped aside.

The room was small and plain, borrowed space meant for convenience, not comfort. Cyan’s few belongings were stacked neatly in one corner: spare clothes, a chipped cup, the adventure book she always reread.
Vera noticed that too.
She sat on the edge of the bed, hands folded in her lap. For a moment, she didn’t speak.
Cyan waited.
“You listen well,” she said finally. “And you remember things.”
She brightened. “I do!”
“I’ve seen it,” Vera continued. “The way you notice patterns. The way you copy them without thinking too hard.”
She scratched her cheek. “I just… look.”
“That’s enough,” she said quietly.

She reached into her sleeve and drew out a thin object wrapped in cloth. When she unwrapped it, Cyan saw a small, worn book. Not large. Not impressive. Its cover was plain wood, etched with faded symbols so old they’d almost smoothed away.
She held it for a second longer than necessary.
“This isn’t a storybook,” Vera said.
Cyan leaned forward anyway.
“It’s a reference,” she continued. “About runes. Old ones. Simple ones.”
“Like the stove?” she asked.
“…Yes,” Vera said.
She placed the book into her hands.
It was heavier than it looked.
“You’re not to show this to anyone,” she said calmly. “Not Eclia. Not the servants. No one.”
She’s excitement dimmed just a little. “Is it dangerous?”
Vera hesitated.
“Only if you misunderstand it,” she said at last.
She nodded, solemn. “I won’t.”
She met his eyes. “You don’t need to understand everything in it. Most of it won’t make sense. That’s fine.”
“Then why—”
“Because one day,” Vera said, interrupting herself, “you might need to recognize when something is wrong.”
That sounded important.
Cyan held the book like a secret.
“Is this for being good?” she asked.
Vera smiled faintly. “Something like that.”
She stood, smoothing her sleeves. “Hide it well. And if anyone ever asks where you learned something—anything—you tell them you guessed.”
“Guessed what?”
“Everything.”
She grinned. “I’m good at guessing.”
“I know,” Vera said.
She paused at the door, hand resting on the frame.
“…Cyan,” she added softly. “If someone ever tells you that knowing things makes you dangerous—“
She stopped.
Then shook her head.
“Never mind,” she said. “Sleep.”
After she left, Cyan sat on the bed and opened the book.
The first page showed a single curved line.
Nothing else.
He frowned, then smiled.
“I can do that,” he whispered.
Far away, Vera locked the metal box in her room and pressed her forehead against the door.
She had just ensured that if the world broke, Cyan might survive it.
The door had never been locked before.

Cyan knew that because he’d leaned against it once, laughing, while Eclia tried to shove him away so she could peek inside. It had been just another door then—plain stone, faint runes along the frame, nothing special.
Now it glowed.
They stopped in front of it together, both of them staring.
“That’s new,” Cyan said.
Eclia didn’t answer.
The runes along the doorframe pulsed slowly, red light tracing careful patterns that didn’t quite repeat. The air nearby felt tight, like the moment before a storm.
She leaned closer, squinting. “Did they break it?”
“No,” Eclia said softly. “They fixed it.”
That didn’t sound better.
She reached out without thinking, stopping her hand just short of the glowing line. The rune nearest her fingers reacted instantly, flaring brighter in warning.
Cyan yelped and jumped back. “Okay! Okay. I won’t.”
Eclia’s shoulders relaxed a little.
“They don’t want anyone going in,” she said. “Not today.”
“Is something inside?”
She hesitated.
“…Something important.”
That word again.
She nodded, accepting it the way she always did. Important things were everywhere in palaces.
A pair of guards stood at the end of the hall now, watching them openly. Not bored. Not distracted.
She waved.
Neither guard waved back.
“Well,” she said, forcing a grin, “guess we’ll have to play somewhere else.”
Eclia smiled at her, but it was tired.
They turned away together.

As they walked, Cyan felt a strange itch in her fingers—the same restless sensation she’d felt near the wounded creature. She slipped her hand into her pocket, brushing against the small, hidden book.
The feeling eased.
Behind them, the locked door hummed softly, runes cycling through containment patterns Vera had not authorized.
Elsewhere in the palace, a schedule was rewritten.
The incident was getting closer
