Part I: Vera and Cyan (Private)
Vera stopped Cyan in a side corridor just before the servants’ wing.
Eclia had already gone ahead, her soft footsteps fading around the corner.
Vera waited until they were alone.
Then she reached into her sleeve and produced a small hairpin, resting it on her palm.
Plain. Functional. Forgettable.
“You drop things,” Vera said mildly.
Cyan frowned. “What?”
“You leave traces,” she corrected. “Footprints. Noise. Attention.”
She opened her mouth to argue. She continued.
“This,” she said, lifting the hairpin slightly, “will not.”
She squinted at it. “Is that… for fixing clothes or something?”
“Hair,” Vera replied. “Yours would never stay in place.”
“Hey—“
She closed her fingers around it.
“Give it to her,” Vera said.
She stiffened. “Why?”
Vera did not answer immediately.
“She is learning too quickly,” she said at last. “And she learns best when she believes something was her choice.”
She swallowed. “You think this helps?”
“I think,” Vera said calmly, “that people who remember being children hesitate before becoming monsters.”
She stepped back, already done with the conversation.
“Or don’t give it to her,” Vera added. “It will make no difference to me.”
She walked away.
Cyan stood there for a long moment, staring at the hairpin in her palm.
It felt heavier than it should have.
Part II: Cyan and Eclia
Later that night, Eclia was sitting on the edge of her bed, brushing her hair slowly, carefully.
Cyan hovered near the door.
“…Hey,” he said.
She glanced up. “What is it?”
He hesitated, then held out his hand.
“I found this,” he said too quickly. “Well—found is probably not the right word. But it was just there.”
Eclia looked at the hairpin.
“For me?”
“Yeah,” Cyan said, scratching his neck. “You don’t have to wear it. I just thought… it wouldn’t get in your way.”
She took it gently.
It was simple. Light. Unimportant.
And yet—
Her fingers curled around it as if it might disappear.
No one had ever given her something without asking for something back.
Her lips curved upward before she could stop them.
A real smile. Small, bright, unguarded.
“…Thank you,” she said.
Cyan blinked. “You like it?”
She nodded, then slid it into her hair, movements tentative, uncertain.
“How does it look?” she asked.
Cyan stared for a second too long.
“…It fits,” he said.
Eclia touched it once more, smiling wider now.
She wore it to sleep.
She wore it the next day.
And long after the palace stopped being a place where gifts existed at all,
the hairpin remained.
They came back at dusk.

The garden was the same as before—same walls, same vines, same worn stones—but it felt smaller somehow. Or maybe quieter. The fireflies rose from the grass slowly, fewer than last time, their glow dimmer, like they were tired too.
Cyan noticed immediately.
“There’s less of them,” she said.
Eclia nodded. “Sometimes they don’t like coming out.”
“Why not?”
“They get scared.”
Cyan frowned. “Of what?”
She didn’t answer.
They sat on the stone bench where they always did, shoulders nearly touching. Eclia kept her hands folded in her lap, fingers laced tightly together.
“You’ve been busy,” she said, trying to sound normal.
Eclia smiled. “A little.”
“You’re always busy now.”
That smile faltered.
For a while, they just watched the fireflies drift and fade.
“…Cyan,” Eclia said softly.
She turned toward her immediately. “Yeah?”
She hesitated, eyes fixed on the lights.
“When it’s just us,” she said, carefully, “you don’t have to call me Eclia.”
She blinked. “I don’t?”
She shook her head. “Vera doesn’t.”
Cyan remembered. The way Vera’s voice softened. The way the name sounded different when she said it.
“…What should I call you, then?”
Eclia finally looked at her.
“Lia,” she said.
The word felt fragile, like glass.
She smiled slowly. “Okay.”
She said it once, testing it.
“Lia.”
She smiled back—really smiled this time, like something unknotted inside her.
“Only when it’s just us,” she added quickly.
“Deal,” she said.
They bumped their fists together, solemn as knights swearing an oath.
The fireflies pulsed brighter for a moment, then began to disappear one by one.
“Do you think,” Eclia asked quietly, “that heroes ever get tired?”
She thought about it. “Maybe. But they don’t stop.”
She nodded, satisfied with that answer, even if it wasn’t true.
She leaned her head lightly against his shoulder.
Cyan didn’t move.
From the far edge of the garden, Vera watched without interrupting.
She closed her eyes for just a second.
Then she turned away, knowing this moment would be impossible to undo.
Cyan shouldn’t have been there.
She knew that, vaguely, the way children know rules they don’t fully respect.
But she had pastries.

Warm ones, wrapped carefully in cloth so they wouldn’t crumble. She’d stolen them fair and square from the kitchen when no one was looking. It felt important to bring them today. Lia had looked tired yesterday. Quieter than usual.
She deserved something sweet.
The corridor was empty when she slipped inside. Too empty.
The lights along the walls glowed steady red, brighter than before. The hum beneath her feet wasn’t subtle anymore—it pulsed, deep and rhythmic, like a giant heartbeat.
“Lia?” she whispered.
No answer.
She followed the sound.
The door to the chamber was open.
Just a crack.
Cyan hesitated.
Then she smiled to herself. Heroes don’t stop halfway.
She pushed it open.

Inside, the air was hot and sharp. Runes covered the walls in layered spirals, some familiar, some not. Thin threads of light stretched across the room like spider silk, all of them converging at the center.
Lia stood there.
She was barefoot on the stone floor, eyes closed, arms held slightly away from her sides. Faint red light traced beneath her skin, pulsing in time with the chamber.
“Lia!” she said, relief flooding her.
Her eyes snapped open.
“Cyan—!” She took a step toward her and immediately winced, biting back a sound.
“Don’t move,” she said quickly. “You’re not supposed to be here.”
“I brought food,” she said, lifting the cloth proudly. “You forgot to eat yesterday.”
Her expression softened despite herself. “You’re going to get in trouble.”
“I always do,” she said cheerfully.
One of the light-threads flickered.
The hum deepened.
Lia stiffened. “Cyan. Please. Step back.”
She frowned. “Did I do something?”
“No,” she said. “You just—“
A symbol near the doorway wavered.
Cyan felt it immediately.
That wrong buzzing. The itch under her skin.
She glanced at the rune without thinking. It wasn’t stable. The curve was too sharp. Too tight.
Curves breathe better than corners.
She set the pastries down and crouched, tracing a small adjustment in the air—just like she’d done before. Careful. Gentle. Helpful.
The rune reacted.
Not the way she expected.
The light surged.

Lia cried out as the threads snapped tight around her, the red glow flaring violently beneath her skin. The chamber roared awake, alarms shrieking as containment patterns collapsed and rewrote themselves in rapid succession.
“CYAN!” she screamed.
She stumbled back, heart hammering. “I was just trying to fix it!”
The door slammed open.
Vera rushed in with two Rune Weavers behind her.
“Get her out!” she shouted.
One of the Weavers grabbed Cyan, pulling her backward as she struggled, eyes locked on Lia.
“Lia!” she yelled. “I’m sorry! I didn’t mean to—!”
She reached for him.
The light swallowed her hand.
The door sealed shut between them.
The last thing Cyan saw before being dragged away was Lia collapsing to her knees, runes burning brighter than ever.
The pastries lay crushed on the floor.
Cyan sat on the bench outside the chamber for a long time.
At first, she waited because she thought Lia would come out.
Then she waited because no one told her to move.

The corridor smelled sharp, like burned metal and hot stone. The red lights that had once pulsed were dim now, flickering weakly along the walls. Every so often, a Rune Weaver hurried past without looking at him.
She swung her legs.
She replayed the moment over and over in her head.
Curves breathe better than corners.
That was right. She knew it was right.
So why had Lia screamed?
The door finally opened.
Not for her.
Vera stepped out instead.
Her sleeves were stained dark at the cuffs. Her hair had come loose from its usual tie, strands clinging to her face. She looked smaller somehow, like the room had taken something from her.
Cyan jumped to his feet. “Vera! Is Lia okay?”
Vera stopped.
For a moment, she didn’t answer. She looked at him the way one looks at something fragile after it’s already fallen.
“She’s alive,” Vera said.
Relief crashed into her so hard her knees nearly buckled. “See? I told her it would be okay.”
Vera closed her eyes.
“She needs rest,” she said carefully. “And treatment.”
“Can I see her?”
“No.”
The word landed heavier than it should have.
“But— I didn’t mean to break anything,” she said quickly. “I was just helping. I swear.”
“I know,” Vera said.
She knelt in front of her, placing her hands firmly on her shoulders.
“This was my failure,” she said quietly. “I wasn’t watching closely enough.”
Cyan blinked. “You weren’t even there.”
“That’s why,” Vera replied.
Footsteps echoed behind her. Two Rune Weavers stood at the corridor entrance, their expressions tight and unreadable.
“She’s taken responsibility,” one of them said. “As agreed.”
Vera stood.
“You’ll stay away from this wing,” she said to Cyan, her voice steady now. “For a while.”
“How long is a while?”
“…I don’t know.”
She swallowed. “Can I at least give her the pastries?”
Vera’s breath caught for just a fraction of a second.
“No,” she said gently. “They were… destroyed.”
“Oh.” She stared at the floor. “She was going to like them.”
“I know.”
Vera rested a hand briefly on her head, a rare, almost parental gesture.
“You did what you thought was right,” she said. “That matters.”
“Heroes do that,” she said earnestly. “They fix things.”
Vera looked away.
“Yes,” she said. “They do.”
A guard appeared at the end of the corridor. “It’s time.”
Vera nodded once.
She took Cyan by the hand and led her away from the sealed door, away from the chamber, away from the place Lia had fallen.
Cyan looked back over her shoulder as they turned the corner.
“Tell Lia I’m sorry,” she said. “And that I’ll wait.”
Vera tightened her grip just slightly.
“I will,” she said.
She did not look back.
The room was not meant for arguments.
It was small, windowless, its walls etched with stabilization runes meant to dampen emotion as much as magic. The table at its center was plain stone. Three chairs were occupied.
Vera stood.
“She cannot remain here,” one of the Rune Weavers said calmly. “The feedback loop is unstable.”
“She is a child,” Vera replied.
“She is an asset,” another corrected. “And a dangerous one.”
Vera’s jaw tightened.
“You pushed the cycle too far,” she said. “You accelerated without clearance.”
“We acted under inspection pressure,” the Weaver replied. “Had we slowed, suspicion would have risen.”
“Suspicion from whom?” Vera asked sharply.
Silence.
“That doesn’t matter,” the first Weaver said. “What matters is containment. Both of them.”
Vera’s fingers curled at her side. “Cyan is not part of your project.”
“He interfered,” the Weaver said. “Twice.”
“He stabilized what you destabilized,” Vera snapped. “By instinct.”
“That makes him worse,” the other replied. “Untrained variables are unacceptable.”
Vera inhaled slowly.
“What are you proposing?” she asked.
The first Weaver folded his hands. “Separation. Immediate.”
“And Eclia?”
“She will be isolated. Monitored. Reconditioned if necessary.”
Vera’s voice went very still. “That will break her.”
“It may be necessary.”
Vera looked down at the stone table. For a moment, she said nothing.
Then she spoke.
“If you exile the boy,” she said, “you erase the trigger.”
The Weavers exchanged glances.
“He is attached,” one said. “She reacts to him.”
“Yes,” Vera agreed. “That is exactly why he must be removed from your reach.”
The silence stretched.
“You would take responsibility?” the first Weaver asked.
Vera met his gaze. “I already have.”
“And where would you send him?”
Vera answered without hesitation.
“To the North.”
One of the Weavers stiffened. “That is—”
“A neutral outcome,” Vera said. “A colonial orphanage. Anonymous. Forgotten.”
“You would hand him to your enemies,” the Weaver said quietly.
Vera’s lips curved into something sharp. “I would hand him to people who believe in heroes.”
The second Weaver studied her. “And what of your loyalties?”
Vera didn’t look away.
“My loyalty,” she said, “is to preventing a war that will kill her first.”
The room hummed softly as the runes adjusted.
Finally, the first Weaver nodded once.
“Very well,” he said. “The boy will be removed.”
“And Eclia?” Vera pressed.
“She will be told he was sent away for his own safety,” the Weaver replied. “No details.”
Vera closed her eyes.
“That will hurt her,” she said.
“Yes,” the Weaver agreed. “But less than the alternative.”
Vera turned toward the door.
“I will arrange the transfer,” she said. “And I will take responsibility for the breach.”
As she reached the threshold, one of the Weavers spoke again.
“You know,” he said, “this may cost you everything.”
Vera paused.
“I know,” she said.
She left the room.
Outside, in a quiet corridor far away, Cyan waited, humming softly to himself, still believing he would see Lia again tomorrow.
Vera did not go to him.
Vera found Cyan in the garden.
She was sitting on the low stone wall near the firefly corner, swinging her legs and humming to herself. The sun was just beginning to dip, turning the sky pale gold. Everything looked normal.
That made it harder.
“There you are,” Vera said.
Cyan looked up and smiled. “Is Lia awake yet?”
Vera stopped a few steps away.
“No,” she said. “Not yet.”
“Oh.” She kicked the wall lightly. “That’s okay. I can wait.”
Vera sat beside her.
For a moment, they watched the fireflies begin to stir in the grass. A few lights blinked on, hesitant, then more followed.
“Cyan,” Vera said carefully, “do you remember what you told Lia you wanted to be?”
She brightened immediately. “An adventurer!”
“Yes,” she said. “And adventurers… they travel.”
“Everywhere,” she agreed proudly.
Vera nodded. “There’s a place in the North. An academy. Not very fancy, but safe. They teach children how to read, how to survive, how to help people.”
She frowned slightly. “Why are you telling me this?”
She turned to face her fully now.
“Because,” she said gently, “they want you to go there.”
Her eyes widened. “Like… now?”
“For a while,” Vera replied. “Until things settle.”
“Can Lia come?”
The question landed exactly where Vera expected it to.
“No,” she said softly. “She can’t.”
She’s smile faltered, but only a little. “Then I’ll come back.”
Vera nodded immediately. “Yes. You will.”
“When?”
“Soon,” she said. “I promise.”
She accepted that without hesitation.
Heroes always leave and come back. Stories said so.
“But,” she added suddenly, “I should say goodbye.”
Vera’s chest tightened.
“She’s resting,” she said. “And she can’t be disturbed.”
“Oh.” She thought for a moment. “Then can you tell Lia something for me?”
Vera swallowed. “What?”
“Tell her… I didn’t forget the promise.” She smiled, small and certain. “And that I’ll get stronger.”
Vera reached out and squeezed her hand once.
“I will,” she said.
She nodded, satisfied.
“Good,” she said. “Then it’s okay.”
The fireflies rose higher, glowing softly in the growing dusk.
Vera stood.
“You should pack,” she said. “You’ll leave early.”
She hopped down from the wall, already energized. “I don’t have much stuff.”
“I know.”
As she ran off toward her room, Vera remained seated, staring at the place she’d been.
When she was alone, she whispered the part of the lie she could never say out loud:
You are not coming back.
She watched the fireflies until the last light faded.
The carriage waited at the side gate.
Not the main one. The small one used for supplies and servants, where no banners hung and no one bothered to look twice.
Cyan climbed inside on her own.
She carried a small pack slung over one shoulder. It wasn’t heavy. She’d packed carefully: spare clothes, the adventure book, the thin rune reference wrapped in cloth. Nothing she couldn’t carry.
Vera stood outside the carriage.
She adjusted the strap once, even though it didn’t need adjusting.
“You’ll be going north,” she said. “It will take a few days.”
She nodded. “That’s fine.”
“You’ll meet other children,” she continued. “Some older than you. Some younger. You’ll share rooms.”
“That’s okay,” she said again. “I’ve done that before.”
Vera’s mouth tightened, just barely.
“If anyone asks where you came from,” she said, “you say you don’t remember.”
She frowned. “But I do remember.”
“I know,” she said. “Just… say you don’t.”
She thought about it, then shrugged. “Okay.”
The driver cleared her throat softly.
Cyan leaned out of the carriage. “Can you tell Lia—“
Vera raised a hand gently. “I will.”
“—that I’ll come back,” she finished. “When I’m stronger.”
She met her eyes.
“I know,” she said.
That was all she trusted herself to say.
The driver climbed up and snapped the reins. The carriage lurched forward, wheels crunching softly against the stone.
She waved.
Vera lifted her hand in return, holding it there until the carriage rounded the corner and disappeared from sight.
Only then did she lower it.
The gate closed behind her with a dull final sound.
Eclia woke later that morning.
Her room was quiet. Too quiet.
She sat up slowly, every movement careful, like her body was made of glass. Sunlight filtered through the curtains, warm and ordinary.
“Cyan?” she called.
No answer.
She waited.
When Vera finally came, Eclia was sitting on the edge of the bed, hands clenched in the sheets.
“Where is she?” she asked.
Vera knelt in front of her.
“She’s gone somewhere safe,” she said gently. “For a while.”
Eclia stared at her. “Without saying goodbye?”
Vera didn’t look away. “Yes.”
Something in Eclia’s face cracked—not loudly, not all at once. Just a small, quiet fracture.
“…She promised,” she said.
Vera nodded. “I know.”
Eclia lay back down and turned toward the wall.
“Tell her,” she said softly, “that I’ll wait.”
Vera stayed until Eclia’s breathing evened out again.
She did not correct her.
Far to the north, the carriage rolled on.
She leaned her head against the window, watching the land change as the palace disappeared behind her. Fields gave way to roads, roads to open sky.
She smiled to herself.
Heroes always leave first, she thought.
That’s how the stories start.
She didn’t know this was the ending of her childhood.
Scene 3 — Vera’s Kitchen
The kitchen was Cyan’s favorite place in the palace.
It was warm, always smelled like bread, and nobody chased him out right away.
Vera moved between the counters with practiced ease, sleeves rolled up, hair tied back loosely. Pots simmered on rune-etched stoves, glowing faintly beneath iron grates.
Cyan sat on a stool near the wall, swinging his legs while Eclia perched on the counter, pretending she wasn’t watching everything Vera did.
“Hands off,” Vera said without looking.
Cyan froze mid-reach, fingers hovering dangerously close to a glowing symbol carved into the stove’s side.
“Oh. Sorry.”
He pulled back quickly.
Vera sighed, not angry, just tired. She set a pot aside and knelt, wiping a bit of flour from the rune with a cloth.
“That line’s cracked,” she muttered to herself. “No wonder it’s leaking heat.”
She reached for a piece of chalk and redrew a small curve, precise and careful.
The glow softened immediately.
Cyan leaned forward. “It stopped buzzing.”
“Yes,” Vera said. “Because it’s not angry anymore.”
Eclia tilted her head. “Runes get angry?”
“Only when you mistreat them,” Vera replied.
Cyan nodded solemnly, as if this made perfect sense.
Vera noticed his look and smiled faintly. “You don’t have to understand them,” she added. “Just don’t touch what you don’t know.”
“I can remember shapes,” Cyan said quickly. “I’m good at that.”
“I know,” Vera replied, surprising him.
She turned back to the counter, pulled a loaf from the oven, and cut it into uneven slices. One went straight into Cyan’s hands.
“Eat.”
He did, immediately.
Eclia watched him with quiet amusement. “You’re always feeding him.”
Vera shrugged. “He looks like he needs it.”
Cyan swallowed. “I do.”
That earned him a small laugh from both of them.

While Cyan ate, Vera moved to a cabinet and opened it with a soft click. Inside were folded cloths, jars of spices, and tucked carefully between them—a thin wooden panel etched with faint symbols. She hesitated before pulling it out, then stopped herself and closed the cabinet again.
Eclia didn’t notice.
Cyan didn’t either.
Instead, he hopped off the stool and peered at the stove again, careful this time not to touch.
“So if the line goes that way,” he said, tracing the air, “it stays calm?”
Vera glanced over her shoulder.
“…Something like that,” she said.
She wiped her hands and knelt again, adjusting his imaginary line with two fingers.
“Like this,” she corrected quietly. “Curves breathe better than corners.”
Cyan repeated the motion once in the air, then grinned. “I won’t forget.”
“I hope you don’t,” Vera said.
Eclia slid off the counter and hugged Vera around the waist without warning.
“Vera,” Eclia murmured into her waist, voice small.
Vera stiffened for half a second—then relaxed, resting a hand on Eclia’s head.
“Don’t cling, Lia,” she murmured. “You’ll wrinkle my clothes.”
Eclia didn’t let go.
Cyan watched them, feeling something warm settle in his chest. The kitchen felt safe. Solid. Like nothing bad could reach them here.
A soft knock came from the far door.
Vera’s hand stilled.
She straightened slowly. “You two,” she said gently, “stay here.”
“Are we in trouble?” Cyan asked, crumbs everywhere.
“No,” Vera said immediately.
Eclia relaxed.
Vera walked to the door, her posture calm, her face carefully neutral. Cyan watched her leave, then turned back to the stove, eyes drifting to the runes glowing quietly beneath the iron.
They weren’t buzzing anymore.
They felt… calm.
When Vera returned a few minutes later, she brought a small bowl of honey and said nothing about the conversation Cyan never heard.
“Dessert,” she announced.
Cyan decided she was the nicest adult in the world.
The palace at night felt like it was holding its breath.

Eclia stood just inside her room, fingers curled tight around the edge of the doorframe. The corridor beyond was dark, lit only by thin strips of moonlight spilling through high windows. Every sound—fabric shifting, a distant footstep, even her own breathing—felt impossibly loud.
Cyan didn’t seem to notice any of it.
She crouched low beside the door, peeking out like this was a game instead of a terrible mistake.
“They always leave the kitchen window open,” she whispered, grinning. “Something about heat and smoke. I checked.”
“You checked?” Eclia whispered back.
“Yesterday. And the day before that.”
Her eyes widened. “That’s… that’s not allowed.”
Cyan shrugged. “Lots of things aren’t allowed.”
That answer unsettled her more than the darkness.
She glanced behind them—at the safety of her room, the thick walls, the rules that had always told her where to stand and when to sleep. Stepping out meant stepping away from all of that.
Cyan was already moving.
Barefoot, light as a cat, she slipped into the corridor without hesitation. She paused a few steps in, turned, and tilted her head at Eclia.
“Coming?”
Eclia hesitated.
Her heart thudded painfully in her chest. She imagined alarms. Guards. Disappointment written across faces she wasn’t allowed to upset.
But nothing happened.
The corridor stayed quiet.
She swallowed and stepped out.
The stone floor was cold under her feet. That surprised her. She had never really felt it before.
They moved slowly, Cyan leading, stopping at corners to listen. She seemed to know when to wait and when to go, as if the palace itself had told her its secrets.
Eclia clutched her sleeves, watching her.
“How do you know when it’s safe?” she whispered.
“I don’t,” she whispered back. “I just go when it feels right.”
That sounded reckless. Dangerous.
And yet… here they were.
The kitchen window was exactly where Cyan said it would be. Open just enough to slip through. The smell hit her first—warm bread, sugar, something sweet baking hours ago and forgotten.
Cyan’s eyes lit up.
“There,” she whispered, pointing.
A plate of cookies sat on the counter, half covered with a cloth.
Eclia froze again. “We shouldn’t—”
“I’ll be fast.”
She climbed in without waiting for permission, landing softly on the counter. She reached for the cloth—
—and it slipped.
Eclia gasped.
Cyan froze mid-motion.
They waited.
Seconds stretched into something unbearable.
No footsteps came. No voices. The palace remained asleep.
Cyan let out a silent laugh and grabbed two cookies, hopping back toward the window. He held one out to her.
Eclia stared at it like it might bite her.
“It’s just a cookie,” she whispered.
Her fingers closed around it anyway.
They didn’t stop running until they were back in her room, door shut, backs pressed against it, both of them breathing hard.
Cyan laughed quietly, shoulders shaking.
Eclia covered her mouth, eyes wide.
They had done it.
Nothing bad had happened.
She looked down at the cookie in her hand. It was warm. Real.
She took a small bite.
It was sweeter than she expected.
Cyan watched her like this was the most important moment of the night.
“Well?” she asked.
Eclia hesitated—then nodded.
“It’s… really good.”
Cyan grinned, triumphant.
Eclia leaned back against the door, cookie crumbs on her fingers, heart still racing.
For the first time, the palace didn’t feel like a cage.
It felt like a place with hidden doors.
The garden became theirs after that.
Not officially, of course. Officially, it belonged to the palace. But Cyan decided that places didn’t really belong to adults if children could run through them without being stopped.
They played after lessons ended and before dinner bells rang—when the shadows stretched long and the guards grew lazy again.
“Rules,” she announced, standing on the edge of the fountain. “No touching the water, no stepping on the white stones, and no cheating.”
Eclia crossed her arms. “Those are terrible rules.”
“They’re very good rules,” she said seriously. “Heroes always have rules.”
Eclia laughed and stepped directly onto a white stone.
Cyan gasped. “You broke it already!”
“So?” she said, grinning. “What are you going to do?”
She jumped down after her, splashing water everywhere. “I’m going to catch you.”
She ran.

Eclia was fast in short bursts, light on her feet, darting between rose bushes and statues. Cyan was faster in straight lines. They circled the garden, laughter echoing off the stone walls, until Eclia tripped on the edge of a root and fell into the grass.
Cyan skidded to a stop beside her. “Hey—are you hurt?”
She shook her head quickly. “No! Look.”
She lifted her hand. A thin red line crossed her palm.
Cyan frowned. “You’re bleeding.”
“It’s just a scratch.”
She pressed her fingers together. The blood shimmered faintly—just for a moment—and the cut closed like it had never been there.
Cyan stared.
“That’s cheating,” he said finally.
Eclia burst out laughing.
“It doesn’t count if it’s me,” she replied. “It’s normal.”
Cyan accepted this explanation immediately. Palace kids had palace rules. That was just how the world worked.
They lay back in the grass, staring up at the sky. Clouds drifted slowly overhead, catching on the spires above.
“I’m going to be an adventurer,” she said suddenly.
Eclia turned her head toward her. “What’s that?”
Cyan’s face lit up immediately.
“They travel everywhere,” she said, sitting up as if this was important. “They fight monsters, explore ruins, help towns, and get really strong. Some of them save whole cities.”
Eclia blinked. “By themselves?”
“Sometimes!” she said proudly. “Sometimes with friends. There was a story I read once where an adventurer crossed the desert alone just to bring medicine back to a village.”
“Did they win?” she asked.
“Of course,” she said, smiling wide. “Heroes always win in the end.”
Eclia considered this quietly.
“Then,” she said slowly, “you should be one.”
Cyan beamed.
“I will be.”
Eclia smiled like she was picturing it already.
She nodded, satisfied. “Then I’ll watch.”
“Watch?”
“Yes,” she said softly. “From somewhere safe.”
Cyan smiled at the idea. “I’ll make sure you are.”
For a while, neither of them spoke.

A shadow passed over the garden. Cyan glanced up to see a group of adults crossing the far balcony, their robes dark against the pale stone. They were speaking quickly, voices low. One of them gestured sharply toward a sealed wing of the palace.
Eclia noticed her gaze and sat up. “What?”
“Nothing,” she said. “Just grown-ups.”
She relaxed immediately and leaned back again.
“Grown-ups are always busy,” she said. “They never play.”
“That’s because they forgot how,” Cyan replied.
Eclia smiled at that and closed her eyes, letting the sun warm her face.
From the kitchen door, Vera watched them for a moment longer than necessary.
When Eclia laughed again, Vera turned away.
The garden stayed quiet.
Eclia called it the floating room.

It wasn’t really floating, but the lights inside it were. Small runes drifted lazily through the air, glowing soft gold and pale blue, like bits of captured sunlight. The walls were smooth stone, etched with patterns that curved and looped into one another without any sharp edges.
Cyan walked in and stopped short.
“Whoa.”
“I like this one,” Eclia said, spinning slowly in place. “It doesn’t hurt.”
“That means some rooms do?” she asked.
She paused. Just for a moment.
“Some rooms are louder,” she said instead.
That explanation satisfied her.
Cyan reached out carefully, remembering Vera’s voice in her head. _Hands off._ He stopped his fingers just short of a drifting rune.
The symbol shifted away from him on its own, as if avoiding contact.
“It moved,” he whispered.
Eclia giggled. “They do that sometimes. They don’t like being poked.”
“Like grumpy cats,” Cyan said.
“Yes!” Eclia agreed immediately. “Exactly like that.”

They spent a long time chasing the runes without touching them, jumping and laughing as the symbols darted away just out of reach. Occasionally, one would dim or wobble, and Eclia would frown, instinctively tracing a small curve in the air with her finger.
The rune would steady again.
Cyan noticed.
Not in a _this-is-important_ way. Just in the way kids notice patterns when they play.
She tried it once.
She copied her motion clumsily, drawing the same curve in the air. The rune nearest her flickered… then settled.
Cyan froze.
Eclia gasped. “You did it!”
“I—“ She looked at her hand. “I just did what you did.”
“That means you’re good at listening,” she said seriously.
Cyan decided that sounded reasonable.
A soft hum filled the room, deeper now, like something waking up.
Eclia’s smile faded.
“We should go,” she said quickly.
“But—”
“Now,” she insisted.
They slipped out just as Vera appeared at the far doorway, eyes sharp as she took in the room, the runes, the children standing a little too still.
Her gaze lingered on Cyan’s hand.
She tucked it behind her back without knowing why.
“Did you touch anything?” Vera asked.
“No,” she said immediately.
Eclia shook her head. “We were just playing.”
Vera exhaled slowly, the tension leaving her shoulders in a way neither child noticed.
“Good,” she said. “Then play somewhere else.”
As they walked away, Cyan glanced back once more at the floating lights. One of the runes pulsed faintly, as if watching him leave.
He waved at it.
Later, as they sat on the steps outside, Cyan traced the curve again in the dust with a stick.
It didn’t do anything.
She shrugged and moved on.
Inside the rune room, a quiet recalibration began.
Eclia waited until the sky turned soft.
Not dark. Not bright. The moment when the light felt tired.
“That’s when they come out,” she said, tugging Cyan by the sleeve. “If we’re quiet.”

They slipped through the garden paths, past hedges and stone benches worn smooth by time, until they reached a place Cyan hadn’t noticed before. It was tucked between two old walls, half-hidden by climbing vines.
The air felt warmer here.
Eclia stepped forward and held out her hand.
At first, nothing happened.
Then a small light flickered to life.
Another followed. And another.
Fireflies rose gently from the grass, dozens of them, glowing gold and green, drifting upward like sparks that had forgotten how to burn.
Cyan sucked in a breath. “They’re everywhere.”
“They like it when it’s quiet,” Eclia said softly. “And when I’m calm.”
She stood perfectly still, eyes wide, afraid to scare them away. The lights hovered close to her, circling lazily, some settling briefly on her hair or sleeve before lifting again.
Cyan moved closer without thinking.
“They don’t run from you,” she said.
Eclia smiled, small and proud. “They never do.”
One drifted toward Cyan’s hand. She froze, afraid to breathe. The firefly hovered, then landed on her finger.
She laughed, unable to stop herself.
It lifted away immediately.
“Sorry,” she whispered.
Eclia giggled, clapping a hand over her mouth to keep the sound in.
They sat together on the cool stone, knees touching, watching the lights rise and fall. For a while, neither of them spoke.
“I wish you could stay here forever,” Cyan said quietly.
Eclia tilted her head. “Here?”
“In the garden. Where it’s quiet.”
She thought about that.
“…I’m not supposed to,” she said at last.
“Why not?”
She shrugged. “They say I have important things to do.”
“Like lessons?”
“Yes,” she said. Then, after a pause, “And tests.”
Cyan frowned. “Tests are boring.”
“I know.”
A breeze passed through the vines. The fireflies scattered briefly, then returned, clustering around Eclia again like they were drawn to her.
From the edge of the garden, Vera watched.
She didn’t step closer. She didn’t interrupt.
She simply stood there, hands clasped tightly together, as if afraid that moving might break something fragile.
Cyan lay back on the stone and stared up at the lights.
“When I’m an adventurer,” she said dreamily, “I’ll come back and take you somewhere like this. Somewhere no one can bother you.”
Eclia looked at her, eyes shining brighter than the fireflies.
“…Promise?”
“I promise.”
She leaned her head lightly against her shoulder.
For a long time, the world felt very small. Just light and warmth and quiet laughter.
Eventually, the fireflies began to fade, one by one, their glow dimming as the sky darkened.
Eclia watched the last one disappear.
“They don’t stay long,” she said.
“That’s okay,” she replied. “They’ll come back tomorrow.”
Eclia smiled.
Vera turned away before the children could see her face.
They didn’t plan it this time.
That was the strangest part.

Eclia was halfway through listening to the palace settle for the night—counting the distant steps of the guards, the soft click of doors being locked—when she realized Cyan was already looking at her.
She didn’t say anything. She just raised her eyebrows, the corner of her mouth twitching.
Her heart jumped.
“No,” she whispered immediately.
Cyan tilted her head. Are you sure?
She hesitated.
The memory of the last time rose uninvited—the cold floor, the fear, the warmth of the cookie in her hand afterward. The fact that nothing terrible had followed.
She glanced toward the door.
“…Just once,” she whispered back.
Cyan’s grin spread slowly, like she’d been waiting for that answer all along.
This time, Eclia stepped into the corridor first.
The stone was still cold, but it didn’t surprise her anymore. She paused at the corner and listened, just like she’d seen Cyan do before. Her breath slowed as she focused.
“Two guards,” she whispered. “Far end.”
Cyan blinked, impressed. “You hear better than me.”
She wasn’t sure if that was true—but she liked how it felt to be useful.
They moved together now, not rushing, not freezing. When a shadow passed under a doorway, they stopped without speaking. When it faded, they continued.
At the kitchen window, Eclia frowned.
“It’s not open as wide,” she said.
Cyan leaned over to check. “Huh. You’re right.”
For a moment, the plan stalled.
Eclia looked around, then pointed quietly. “That crate. If you stand on it, you can reach.”
Cyan followed her finger, then looked back at her, eyes bright.
“See?” she whispered. “You’re good at this.”
Her cheeks warmed—not from embarrassment, but something else. Something steadier.
Inside, the kitchen smelled different tonight. Less sweet. More bread than sugar.
Cyan lifted the cloth.
“No cookies,” she mouthed silently.
Eclia felt a flicker of disappointment—then shook her head.
“Wait,” she whispered, pointing to the cooling rack near the stove. “Those.”
Small pastries. Plain. Forgotten.
She nodded enthusiastically and grabbed them.
On the way back, a door down the hall creaked open.
Eclia didn’t panic.
She grabbed Cyan’s sleeve and pulled her into a narrow alcove, barely big enough for two children to breathe.
They stood there, pressed close, hearts pounding in sync.
A guard passed by, yawning, footsteps echoing once—twice—then fading.
Only when the corridor was empty again did Eclia realize she was smiling.
They made it back to her room without running this time.
Cyan flopped onto the floor, triumphant. “That was better.”
Eclia sat beside her, smoothing her sleeves.
“Yes,” she said. “It was.”
She broke a pastry in half and handed Eclia the larger piece without thinking.
Cyan noticed—but didn’t say anything.
As they ate in companionable silence, Eclia stared at the door, thoughtful.
“Cyan,” she said quietly.
“Yeah?”
“Do you think…” She paused, searching for the right words. “Do you think there are other places like that? In the palace. Places no one watches.”
She shrugged. “Probably.”
She nodded slowly, filing the thought away.
Tonight hadn’t felt like breaking rules.
It had felt like understanding them.
And understanding, Eclia was beginning to realize, could be just as powerful.
Eclia didn’t come to the garden that afternoon.
Cyan waited anyway.

He sat on the edge of the fountain, kicking his heels against the stone and counting the cracks between the tiles. When that got boring, he tried skipping stones across the shallow water. When that got boring too, he lay on his back and watched the clouds slide past the spires overhead.
She was never late.
By the time the sun dipped low enough to turn the walls gold, Cyan had convinced himself she was just hiding.
“Very funny,” he muttered, standing up. “You can come out now.”
Nothing answered him.

He wandered the paths they usually took, checking behind statues and hedges, peering into the vine-covered corner where the fireflies gathered. The garden felt larger without her. Quieter in a way that made sound feel rude.
Finally, he spotted Vera crossing the courtyard, her pace quicker than usual.
“Vera!” Cyan called, jogging over.
She stopped immediately, relief flickering across her face before she smoothed it away.
“There you are,” she said. “You shouldn’t wander alone.”
“Where’s Eclia?” he asked. “She didn’t come.”
Vera hesitated. Just long enough for Cyan to notice.
“She had an appointment,” Vera said.
“What kind?”
“…Lessons.”
Cyan frowned. “She has lessons every day.”
Vera crouched so they were eye level. Her hands rested lightly on her knees, steady, controlled.
“This one took longer,” she said. “She’ll be tired.”
“Oh.” Cyan nodded, accepting this easily. “I can wait.”
Vera’s mouth curved into something that tried to be a smile.
“Not today,” she said gently. “She needs rest.”

Cyan looked past her, toward the inner wing of the palace. A pair of guards stood near a sealed corridor he’d never been allowed to enter. Their armor gleamed too cleanly. Neither of them looked bored.
“Can I see her later?” he asked.
Vera followed his gaze and quickly shifted her body, blocking the view.
“Tomorrow,” she said. “I promise.”
That word again.
Cyan brightened instantly. “Okay!”
Vera stood and placed a hand on his shoulder, steering him toward the outer paths.
“Go home before it gets dark,” she added. “I’ll tell her you came.”
As Cyan left, he glanced back once more.
Far above, behind a narrow window he’d never noticed before, a faint red light pulsed, then dimmed.
He decided it must be sunset reflecting on glass.
That night, Eclia dreamed of fireflies she couldn’t reach.
The next morning, she came to the garden late.
She smiled when she saw Cyan, but it didn’t quite reach her eyes.
“Sorry,” she said. “I fell asleep.”
“That’s okay,” Cyan said quickly. “Vera said you had lessons.”
Eclia nodded.
Her sleeve slipped as she sat down.
Thin pale marks traced her wrist, fresh and careful, like lines someone had drawn and erased too many times.
Cyan stared for a second, then looked away.
“You wanna play?” he asked brightly.
Eclia smiled wider this time. “Yes.”
From the shadows near the archway, Vera watched them run.
She did not smile.
They weren’t supposed to go that way.
Cyan knew that because the floor changed color.
The stone shifted from pale gray to something darker, smoother, like it had been polished too many times. The air felt different too—cooler, heavier, like the palace was holding its breath.
“Hey,” she said, slowing. “This isn’t—“
“It’s faster,” Eclia replied, already walking ahead. “Vera uses it sometimes.”
That settled it.
If Vera used it, then it couldn’t be that bad.

The corridor stretched long and straight, lit by narrow strips of light along the walls. No windows. No decorations. Just doors—too many of them—set at regular intervals, each marked with faint runes she couldn’t quite follow.
She tried not to stare.
“So,” she said loudly, clapping her hands once, “race you to the end.”
Eclia smiled, but shook her head. “No running.”
“Why not?”
“Because,” she said, then hesitated, “…it echoes.”
Cyan stomped once, experimentally.
The sound bounced back sharper than it should have.
“Oof,” she muttered. “You’re right.”
They walked instead.
As they passed the first door, Cyan felt something prickle at the back of her neck. Not fear—more like the feeling of being watched when no one was there.
She laughed it off.
“Palaces are creepy,” she declared. “That’s why adventurers explore ruins, not live in them.”
Eclia hummed in agreement.

At the third door, voices drifted through the stone—muffled, urgent. Cyan couldn’t make out the words, only the tone. It reminded her of the adults arguing near the market back home, when something had gone wrong.
Eclia stopped.
“…We should turn back,” she said.
Cyan tilted her head. “Why?”
She glanced at the door, then away. “I don’t like this one.”
That was enough for her.
They turned.
Halfway back, a figure appeared at the far end of the corridor.
Vera.
She was standing very still, hands folded in front of her, eyes sharp in a way Cyan had never seen before.
“There you are,” she said.
Her voice echoed.
Eclia flinched.
“I was just—“ she began.
Vera raised a hand gently. “I know.”
She walked toward them, her steps measured. As she passed each door, the runes along the frames dimmed slightly, responding to her presence.
Cyan noticed. She didn’t think much of it.
“This corridor is closed today,” Vera said calmly. “You shouldn’t be here.”
“Sorry,” she said immediately. “We were just taking a shortcut.”
Vera looked at her for a long moment.
“…Shortcuts aren’t always faster,” she said.
She placed a hand lightly on Eclia’s shoulder and guided her away from the doors.
As they turned the corner, Cyan glanced back once more.
One of the doors was ajar now—just a finger’s width.
Something inside shifted.
The door slid shut with a soft, final click.
She decided the palace really needed better lighting.
Outside, the sun was bright and warm, and the corridor felt like a bad dream that faded the moment it ended.
Eclia squeezed his hand once, then let go.
They didn’t take that path again.
Scene 9 — The Wounded Creature
They found it behind the old storage sheds, where the palace gardens thinned into stone and moss.
Cyan noticed the smell first.
Not bad. Just sharp. Like metal after rain.
“What’s that?” she asked, slowing.
Eclia had already stopped.

Curled against the wall was a creature Cyan had never seen up close—small, no bigger than a dog, with too many joints in its legs and a hide that shimmered faintly like wet glass. One of its limbs was twisted at an angle that didn’t look right.
It hissed weakly when they approached.
Cyan took a step back. “Uh. Is it dangerous?”
Eclia knelt immediately.
“No,” she said softly. “It’s scared.”
The creature’s breathing was uneven. Its body jerked in small, painful motions.
Eclia reached out slowly, palm open.
“It’s okay,” she whispered. “We won’t hurt you.”
Cyan hovered uselessly behind her, unsure what to do with his hands.
“Should we get help?” he asked.
Eclia nodded, but didn’t move away. “Yes. But—”
The creature convulsed suddenly, a sharp cry tearing out of it. The air around it shimmered, runes flaring weakly along its skin—broken, unstable, flickering like dying embers.
Cyan felt it then.
That tight, wrong feeling. Like the room buzzing too loudly.
“That’s bad,” he said.
Eclia bit her lip. “It’s hurting.”
She pressed her hand gently to the creature’s side. The blood beneath her skin glowed faintly, warm and steady. The creature’s thrashing slowed—but the runes flared brighter, straining.
Cyan remembered the stove.
Curves breathe better than corners.
She didn’t think. She just moved.
Picking up a stick from the ground, she traced a shallow curve in the dirt beside the creature, copying the shape she’d seen Eclia draw in the air, the way Vera had corrected her once.
The flickering rune near the creature’s leg wavered… then steadied.
The buzzing eased.
Cyan froze.
“I didn’t touch it,” she said quickly. “I swear.”
Eclia looked at the ground. Then at him.
“You helped,” she said, quiet and amazed.
The creature let out a long, shuddering breath and went still—not dead, but resting.
Footsteps crunched behind them.
Vera was already there.
Her eyes took in the scene instantly: the creature, the faintly glowing runes, Eclia kneeling, Cyan holding a stick like he wasn’t sure why it was in his hand.
Her gaze snapped to the curve in the dirt.
For the first time, she didn’t hide her reaction.
Fear flashed across her face.
“Step back,” she said, sharper than usual.
Both children obeyed immediately.
Vera knelt, her movements precise and fast. She muttered under her breath as she reinforced the stabilizing marks properly, her hands steady despite the tension in her shoulders.
When she finished, the creature was breathing evenly.
Vera exhaled once, long and slow.
“Did it hurt?” Cyan asked.
Vera didn’t answer right away.
She looked at him. Really looked.
“…You should not do that again,” she said finally.
Cyan nodded hard. “I won’t.”
Eclia reached for Vera’s sleeve. “He was helping.”
“I know,” Vera said quietly.
She stood and placed herself between the children and the creature.
“I’ll handle this,” she said. “Go. Both of you.”
As they walked away, Cyan glanced back.
Vera was already pulling a cloth from her pocket, wiping away the curve she’d drawn in the dirt.
She didn’t look up.
Later that night, in a quiet room far from the gardens, Vera burned a small scrap of paper she had never meant to write.
The doors close.
The sound echoes longer than it should.
Eclia remains standing for several seconds, facing the empty space where Cyan stood.
She does not move.
Sol waits. Silent. Patient.
When Eclia finally turns, she does not stumble. She does not falter. She walks back to the throne and sits.
Only then does she close her eyes.
Her hand tightens slightly against the armrest.
Just once.
Sol speaks, low and respectful.
Sol: “He will not return.”
Eclia exhales.
A controlled breath. Measured.
“Good,” she says.
Her voice is steady.
Another pause.
Then, quieter:
“That means he will live.”
Sol inclines her head. “You ensured it.”
Eclia opens her eyes and stares ahead, unfocused.
“I removed her from the board,” she says. “I made her useless to me. To the North. To the war.”
She rests her palm flat against her chest.
Not clutching.
Grounding.
“If she had stayed,” she continues, “he would have died trying to save me.”
Sol does not interrupt.
“I will not allow that,” Eclia says. “Not again.”
A faint, almost imperceptible tremor passes through her fingers.
She stills them.
“Let her hate me,” she says. “Hatred is a direction. Grief is not.”
Sol finally looks at her fully.
“You chose loneliness,” he says. Not a question.
“Yes.”
She sits back against the throne.
The seat looks too large.
“I chose it a long time ago,” Eclia adds.
Silence stretches.
Then, softer — not to Sol, not to anyone in the room:
“Live well, Cyan.”
Her eyes close.
No tears fall.
The throne room remains lit long into the night.
The battlefield did not look like a battlefield anymore.

Cyan slowed as he stepped onto the cleared corridor, boots sinking slightly into softened earth. The ground here was warm—not from fire, but from something else. Life. New growth forcing itself through scorched soil in stubborn, impossible patches.
He recognized Lyrel’s work immediately.

Vines lay curled and brittle at the edges of the path, their glow faded, their purpose fulfilled. Flowers—too vibrant for a place like this—had bloomed and already begun to wither, petals scattered like exhausted applause.
“She did it,” Cyan murmured.
The wind carried no screams now. No psychic pressure. The maddening roar of the horde had vanished, replaced by a quiet so deep it rang in his ears.
He swallowed and kept walking.
Bits of shattered rune-stone littered the path. Defensive arrays, burned out completely. He crouched briefly, brushing ash from a familiar sigil.
Eve’s handiwork.
Precise. Ruthless. Overextended.
He could almost hear her voice.
You’d better not waste this.
“I won’t,” Cyan said aloud.
He straightened and jogged forward, urgency returning to his stride. Every step down the corridor felt earned—paid for in blood and exhaustion and promises he fully intended to keep.
They’d bought him time.
That was all this was. A tactical withdrawal. A calculated risk.
Eve would be hiding somewhere nearby, catching her breath, waiting for the signal. Lyrel would be recovering, drained but alive, the forest quiet around her at last.
They were strong. They always were.
And now it was his turn.

The southern palace loomed ahead, its silhouette rising from the horizon like an old memory dragged into the present. Cyan felt his chest tighten—not with fear, but with something dangerously close to relief.
She’s still there, he thought. I’m not too late.

He slowed near the outer rise, resting his hands on his knees for a moment, breathing hard. His fingers brushed against his gear—against the small tokens he carried, reminders of people waiting behind him.
“Just hold on,” he whispered, unsure who he meant it for.
Then he straightened, set his jaw, and looked forward.
This wasn’t a battlefield anymore.
This was a rescue.
They had cleared the path.
He just had to walk it.
And when this was over—when Eclia was safe, when the truth was explained, when everyone finally understood—
He would come back for them.
Certain of that promise, Cyan stepped into the open ground before the palace, carrying hope like a shield.
It would not protect him.
The throne room was quiet.
Not ceremonial.
Not hostile.
Simply prepared.

Cyan stood at its center, hands clenched at his sides, boots still dusted with ash from the battlefield. She felt like she had walked into the wrong place at the wrong time—like someone who had missed the cue and stepped onto the stage anyway.
Eclia faced her from the dais.
No crown.
No blade drawn.
Sol stood a step behind her, posture straight, eyes forward.
“You came here to save me,” Eclia said.
It wasn’t a question.
Cyan nodded. Her voice came out steady, carried by habit more than conviction.
“Yes.”
Eclia studied her for a moment, then gestured to the empty space beside her.
Eclia extended her hand.
“Stand beside me.”
Cyan stared at it.
Then her gaze drifted upward.
The hairpin caught the light—small, simple, almost wrong against the weight of her attire.
Her breath caught.
“…You still have that,” she said.
Eclia did not look away.
“Yes.”
Cyan laughed softly, once. It sounded broken.
“You used to freeze over cookies,” she said. “You remember that? You wouldn’t even breathe unless I went first.”
Silence.
“The first time, you were shaking,” Cyan went on. “The second time, you were listening. The third time—”
He stopped herself, swallowing.
“The third time you were already ahead of me.”
Eclia’s fingers curled slightly, then relaxed.
“You taught me how to step forward,” she said.
“That wasn’t what I meant to teach you,” Cyan replied.
“No,” Eclia said calmly. “It was what you showed me.”
She shook her head. “I just wanted you to be less afraid.”
“And I learned,” she said, “that fear is not what stops us. Obedience is.”
Cyan looked at her fully now.
“I thought we were sneaking out together,” she said. “I didn’t think you were learning how to burn the palace down.”
For the first time, something flickered in Eclia’s expression.
Not regret.
Recognition.
“That night,” she said, “you stepped forward when Vera found us.”
Cyan stiffened.
“You took the blame,” Eclia continued. “Without hesitation. Without asking if it would hurt.”
Her voice remained even.
“That,” she said, “is what bravery looked like to me.”
Cyan’s hands trembled.
“…That’s not bravery,” she said weakly. “That was me being stupid.”
Eclia shook her head once.
“No,” she said. “It was you choosing to be hurt so someone else wouldn’t be.”
She paused.
“I did the same.”
The space between them felt suddenly vast.
Eclia extended her hand again.
“Stand beside me,” she said. “As you did then.”
Cyan looked at her hand.
At the hairpin.
At the woman who had learned too well.
“I am ending this war,” Eclia continued. “The North will fall. Their systems, their heroes, their methods. All of it.”
She did not raise her voice.
“I want you with me when it ends.”
Cyan’s brow furrowed. “You’re asking me to help you destroy the North.”
“I am asking you to help me prevent the next one,” she replied.
She shook her head immediately. “No.”
The answer was reflexive. Honest.
“They’re not monsters,” Cyan said. “They’re wrong, but they can change. You don’t have to do this alone. You don’t have to become this.”
Eclia did not interrupt her.
“You don’t need to carry all of it,” he pressed. “Eve—Lyrel—they believed there was another way.”
That was the last time Cyan spoke with certainty.
Eclia inhaled slowly.
Then she raised her hand.
The air shifted.
A projection formed between them—not stylized, not symbolic. Raw. Untreated.
The river crossing.
Cyan recognized it instantly.

Lyrel stood at the center of the image, hands pressed to the earth, emerald light burning through her veins. The roots erupted around her, forming the cage. He saw herself pounding against it, mouth open in a scream the memory could not carry.
The light surged outward.
Bloomed.
And then—
Nothing.
The projection lingered on empty ground. Verdant. Silent.
Cyan took a step back.
The image changed.
A ruined courtyard.
Anne and Eve locked together—steel through flesh, daggers buried deep. Eve’s body slackened first. Anne collapsed a breath later.
Stillness.
No follow-up.
No aftermath.
Just death.
The projection vanished.
The throne room returned.
Cyan stood where he was, eyes fixed on the empty air.
Eclia waited.
Seconds passed.
Then she spoke again, using the same calm tone as before.
“Stand beside me,” she said.
The words were identical.
Cyan did not answer.
Her mouth opened slightly, as if something might come out—but nothing did.
Her hands trembled once, then went still.
Eclia watched her carefully.
Not with anger.
Not with disappointment.
With understanding.
“I gave you a choice before you knew the cost,” she said. “Now you know it.”
She waited again.
Cyan stared at the floor. At his boots. At the faint reflection of herself in the polished stone.
There was nothing behind her eyes now.
No refusal.
No acceptance.
Only absence.
Eclia exhaled.
It wasn’t a sigh of frustration.
It was the sound of a conclusion reached.
“Sol,” she said quietly.
Sol stepped forward.
“Take her beyond the walls,” Eclia continued. “Alive.”
Cyan did not react when Sol’s hand closed around her arm.
As he was turned toward the doors, Eclia spoke one last time—not to stop her, not to wound her.
“When you find your resolve,” she said, “you may return.”
Cyan did not look back.
The doors closed.
The sound echoed softly through the throne room.
Eclia remained where she was, crimson runes pulsing faintly beneath her skin.
She did not weep.
She had already lost everyone she loved.
They stopped before a sealed chamber.
The door bore older runes than the rest of the palace—precise, layered, reinforced far beyond necessity. Cyan recognized the style immediately.
Rune Weaver work.
Her stomach tightened.
Eclia placed her palm against the seal. It responded at once, lines of light folding inward as the door slid aside.
Inside was not a lab.
It was an archive.
Glass cases lined the walls, each holding objects sealed in stasis—documents, tools, fragments of runes too complex to be decorative. At the center stood a single pedestal.
On it rested a familiar item.
Cyan’s breath caught.
“That’s…” She stepped forward without thinking. “Vera’s.”
A small fox-shaped clasp lay on the pedestal, silver dulled with age. She had seen it a hundred times—fastened at her collar, hidden beneath layers of formal cloth.
“She favored that form,” Eclia said. “Foxians often do.”
Cyan swallowed. “Where is she?”
Eclia didn’t answer immediately.
She moved past her, stopping beside the pedestal.
“Vera was not my caretaker,” she said. “That was her cover.”
Cyan shook her head. “No. She watched over you. She helped us. She—”
“She reported to the North,” Eclia continued. “For decades.”
The words were quiet.
Precise.
Cyan laughed once, sharply. “You’re wrong.”
Eclia looked at her. “She was very kind.”
That sentence hit harder than denial would have.
“She believed,” Eclia went on, “that the South’s power would end the world if left unchecked. She believed killing me would save more lives than letting me live.”
Cyan’s vision blurred. “She wouldn’t—”
“She tried,” Eclia said.
She turned her palm upward.
A projection flared to life above it—rune arrays spiraling inward, containment fields fracturing under strain.
“Near the end of the experiment,” Eclia continued, “when my control was incomplete, she attempted to terminate me.”
Cyan stared at the image, chest tight.
“She failed,” Eclia said. “I killed her.”
Silence swallowed the chamber.
Cyan’s knees felt weak. She gripped the edge of a nearby case to steady herself.
“She was trying to protect you,” she whispered. “From them. From all of this.”
“Yes,” Eclia agreed.
Cyan looked up, hope flaring desperately. “Then you understand—”
“She was trying to protect the world,” Eclia corrected. “From me.”
The words slid neatly into place.
“No,” Cyan said hoarsely. “You’re twisting it. She loved you.”
Eclia regarded her evenly.
“She did,” she said. “That is why her hesitation cost her the moment.”
Cyan recoiled as if struck.
Sol shifted slightly behind them.
Not to threaten.
To acknowledge the truth had been spoken.
Cyan shook her head over and over. “She wouldn’t choose the North over you. Over us.”
“She did,” Eclia said calmly. “And I chose the South.”
She gestured toward the clasp.
“I kept this,” she said. “Not out of sentiment. As a reminder.”
“A reminder of what?” Cyan demanded.
Eclia met his gaze.
“That even love will try to stop me.”
Cyan closed her eyes.
Images crashed through her—Vera’s smile, her scolding, the way she always watched the doors first. The way she taught her runes meant for protection, not power.
All of it twisted.
When she opened her eyes again, her voice was barely there.
“You didn’t have to kill her.”
Eclia’s reply was immediate.
“Yes,” she said. “I did.”
She turned away from the pedestal.
“Come,” she said. “There is more you need to hear.”
Cyan stayed where he was for a moment longer, staring at the fox-shaped clasp.
Then, slowly, she followed.
Behind them, the archive sealed itself once more.
And the past, for the first time, stopped being safe.
They moved again.

Cyan barely noticed when the corridor changed. His feet followed Eclia out of habit, out of momentum. The palace no longer felt like a place — it felt like a current, pulling her forward whether he wanted to go or not.
His thoughts lagged behind his body.
Vera tried to kill her.
Vera is dead.
Eclia killed her.
No matter how many times the words formed, they refused to settle.
“You didn’t have to,” Cyan said suddenly.
Eclia did not slow.
“I told you,” she replied. “I did.”
“That wasn’t the only option,” he insisted, louder now. “You could’ve restrained her. Exiled her. Anything.”
“She was loyal to the North,” Eclia said. “That does not end with exile.”
Cyan clenched his fists. “You’re saying that because you had to.”
Eclia stopped.
Cyan nearly walked into her.
She turned, looking at her — not with anger, not with sorrow, but with something colder.
“You think I hardened myself afterward,” she said. “That I became this because of her death.”
She nodded, desperate. “Yes.”
Eclia shook her head once.
“I resolved myself because she was right,” she said. “If I had been weaker, she would have saved the world by killing me.”
Cyan’s breath hitched.
“That doesn’t make sense,” she whispered. “She believed in heroes. In prevention. In—”
“In containment,” Eclia corrected. “In control.”
She gestured ahead.
They had entered a long chamber lined with suspended glass slabs. Within each hovered images — records captured by runes. Scenes froze and replayed in silent loops.
Cyan’s eyes were drawn to them despite herself.
A village square.
A crowd cheering.
A figure standing at the center, radiant, elevated.
A hero.
Then the next slab.
The same square.
Bodies piled at the edges.
Runes embedded in flesh.
A teleportation array misfiring.
The hero still standing.
Unharmed.
Cyan staggered back a step. “That’s not— that’s not how it went.”
Eclia’s voice was steady. “That is the version that was recorded.”
Another slab flared.
Anne.
Cyan recognized her immediately — posture, blade, the way the air bent around her presence.
Then the next image.
Anne again.
Eyes vacant. Movements delayed. Blood soaking the ground around her feet.
Cyan swallowed hard. “She was sick.”
“She was used,” Eclia replied.
Another slab flared.
An arena.
Cyan stiffened.
Chains.
Cages.
Monsters forced to fight beneath roaring crowds.
Her breath caught. “The arena…”
She stepped closer without thinking.
“I was there,” she said. “I saw them.”
The image shifted.
A massive figure tore free of broken chains, eyes blazing with fury and disbelief.
Fenrir.
Cyan’s heart pounded. “He didn’t want to fight.”
“I know,” Eclia said.
The slab changed again.
The arena in chaos. Fighters fleeing. Chains shattered. Monsters and slaves pouring out together.
Cyan’s hands trembled. “We helped them escape.”
“Yes.”
“You were there,” Cyan said suddenly, realization hitting her like a blade. “That night. You spoke to me.”
Eclia inclined her head slightly.
“I did not show my face.”
“You told me,” he continued, voice cracking, “‘If you open one cage, you open them all.’”
“Yes.”
Cyan staggered back. “That was you.”
“You already chose them,” Eclia said calmly. “Before you knew my name.”
His thoughts spiraled.
“I felt sorry for them,” she said weakly. “They were being used. Broken.”
“As were the monsters,” Eclia replied. “As was I.”
Another slab ignited.
Northern alchemists.
Rune arrays identical to the ones Cyan had seen on his early quests.
Monsters dissected. Refined. Reused.
“I saw this,” Cyan whispered. “I thought it was corruption. Individuals.”
“You thought they were exceptions,” Eclia said. “Mistakes.”
Cyan pressed her hands to his temples.
“There are bad people everywhere,” she said quickly. “That doesn’t mean—”
“That the system is innocent?” Eclia finished.
She faced her fully now.
“They do not commit atrocities despite their ideals,” she said. “They commit them because of them.”
Cyan slid down against the glass, knees giving out.
Fenrir’s roar echoed in his memory. The fear in the slaves’ eyes. The relief when the chains fell away.
“I was already on your side,” he murmured.
“Yes,” Eclia said.
“But I didn’t know,” she whispered.
“That is how propaganda works,” she replied.
Cyan shook her head, backing away. “You’re showing me what you want me to see.”
“Yes,” Eclia agreed.
The admission hit like a blow.
“And it is still true,” she continued.
Cyan laughed weakly. “You expect me to believe you over everything I’ve known?”
“I expect you to believe what you have already seen,” she replied.
Her knees gave slightly. He leaned against the cold glass of a slab, breath coming too fast.
Vera’s face rose unbidden in his mind. Her careful hands. Her warnings disguised as lessons. The runes she taught her — all defensive. All meant to limit damage.
“She wouldn’t have tried to kill you,” she whispered. “Not unless she was desperate.”
“She was,” Eclia said. “Because she understood what I would become.”
Cyan looked up sharply. “And what is that?”
Eclia’s gaze did not waver.
“The end of the North,” she said. “And everything that stands like it.”
The chamber felt too small.
Too loud.
Too full.
Cyan slid down against the glass, sitting on the cold floor without realizing it. His thoughts tangled, hero stories clashing violently with blood-soaked proof.
“I just wanted to save you,” she said faintly.
Eclia looked down at her.
“I know,” she said.
For the first time since he entered the palace, her voice softened — not in regret, but in finality.
“That is why this hurts you more than it hurts me.”
She turned away.
“Come,” she said. “There is one last truth.”
Cyan didn’t answer.
But after a moment, he pushed herself up and followed — because stopping felt worse than moving.
And somewhere deep inside her, something vital had begun to fracture beyond repair
The room overlooked the battlefield.

Smoke rose in long, exhausted trails beyond the walls, drifting lazily across the horizon. The fighting there had quieted—not ended, just settled, like a wound that had stopped bleeding but not healed.
Sol stood beside a narrow table, fingers resting on a slate etched with fading runes.
Eclia joined her.
Cyan remained near the doorway, arms crossed tightly, eyes fixed on the distant line where she had last seen them.
“Well?” he asked.
Sol glanced down at the slate. “We’ve lost contact.”
Cyan nodded immediately. Too quickly.
“That makes sense,” she said. “Anne’s dead. The comm-runes would be fried.”
“They were,” Sol replied. “For a moment.”
He tapped the slate. A faint pulse flickered—then vanished.
“They didn’t reestablish,” Sol continued. “No signal followed.”
Cyan exhaled slowly. “Eve said she’d hide. She always does.”
Eclia said nothing.

“And Lyrel…” Cyan went on, words tumbling faster now. “She said she bought time. That means she’s still holding the field. The forest—” He gestured vaguely toward the horizon. “It’s quiet now, right? That means it worked.”
“The surge has stabilized,” Sol said. “Permanently.”
Cyan smiled, relief breaking through the tension.
“See?”
Sol hesitated—just a fraction too long.
“There are no remaining life signatures at the river crossing,” she said carefully. “Nor near the southern ridge.”
Cyan waved it off. “They moved. Of course they moved. Eve wouldn’t stay put, wounded or not.”
She looked at Eclia, expecting agreement.
She met her gaze calmly.
“They believed in you,” she said.
Cyan straightened at that. “I know.”
Silence stretched.
Sol closed the slate. “Anne’s energy signature dissipated completely. No residual interference.”
“That means Eve finished it,” Cyan said firmly. “She did what she always does.”
Sol did not respond.
The wind shifted outside, carrying the faint scent of ash and something greener beneath it—new growth, forced and sudden.
Cyan took a step toward the balcony, gripping the railing as she stared out.
“They’ll catch up,” she said, more softly now. “They told me to go ahead.”
Eclia joined her at the window, standing close—but not touching.
“Then you should not waste what they gave you,” she said.
Cyan nodded, swallowing hard.
“I won’t.”
Behind them, Sol remained still, eyes lowered—not in doubt, but in acceptance.
Outside, the battlefield lay quiet.
And Cyan, standing in that stillness, chose to believe that silence meant survival.
Bridge Scene — Cyan (After the Palace)
Cyan lay in the mud for a long time.
He wasn’t sure how long. Minutes, maybe. Long enough for the cold to seep through his clothes and into his bones. Long enough for the palace gates behind her to close, and stay closed.
His cheek pressed into wet earth. It smelled like iron. Like rain. Like blood that had already sunk too deep to wash away.
Her hands shook.
Not violently. Just enough that he noticed.
Vera’s voice kept trying to surface in his mind, and every time it did, he shoved it back down. Hard. Like forcing a lid onto something that wouldn’t stop boiling.
Later, he told herself.
I’ll think about it later.
He rolled onto his back and stared at the sky.
It looked exactly the same as it had before he went in.
That felt wrong.
His chest tightened, but he ignored it. She had learned how to do that. Orphanage nights. Empty stomachs. Days when thinking too hard meant not getting up again.
His fingers curled unconsciously, tracing a rune that never fully formed.
Ligära.
The snare that hadn’t mattered.
The snare that broke like it had never been there at all.
He stopped her hand.
“No,” he muttered. Her voice sounded strange to her. Too flat.
Later.
He pushed herself up to a sitting position. Mud clung to his palms, his knees, the edge of his cloak. He wiped none of it away.
If he stood up now—if he let herself think—he wasn’t sure he would keep standing.
A memory threatened to surface.
A tear on stone.
He crushed it before it could bloom.
