No gentle handling.
No conversation.
She laid ingredients out in straight lines. Meat. Grain. Water. Salt.
Only salt.
Cyan leaned closer. “Is that all?”
“It covers the essentials.”
Lyrel peered into the pot. “Where are the herbs?”
“Unnecessary.”
“The vegetables?”
“Optional.”
“The joy?”
Eve paused, knife mid-air. “Irrelevant.”
The food was ready in record time.
A dense slab of boiled meat. Plain grain paste. Clear broth.
No garnish. No aroma. No color.
It looked like it had been prepared for a siege.
Lyrel stared at her bowl.
“…Is this punishment?”
Eve sat down. “Eat.”
Cyan took a bite.
Immediately swallowed.
“…Wow.”
Lyrel tilted her head. “Good wow or bad wow?”
Cyan chose his words carefully. “I feel like I just fueled a machine.”
Lyrel burst out laughing.
“Oh my stars,” she said between giggles. “Helmethair, this isn’t food. This is a marching order.”
“It will keep you alive,” Eve replied.
Lyrel took a bite.
Her face went completely blank.
Then she swallowed and smiled brightly.
“I love how,” she said sweetly, “it tastes exactly like your personality.”
Cyan choked.
Eve didn’t even blink. “Efficient?”
“Emotionally unavailable.”
Cyan wiped his mouth. “I think it tried to fight me.”
Lyrel poked the grain paste with her spoon. “Did you cook this or interrogate it?”
Eve continued eating, unbothered. “You will not be hungry.”
“That’s true,” Lyrel said. “But I will be sad.”
Cyan nodded. “This meal has no childhood memories.”
Lyrel laughed again, openly now. “Treehugger food may be bland, but at least it doesn’t glare at you.”
Eve finally looked up. “You’re enjoying this.”
Lyrel beamed. “Immensely.”
Cyan leaned back. “I feel like we’re witnessing character development.”
Eve stood, collecting the bowls. “Tomorrow, Cyan cooks.”
Both of them froze.
Lyrel’s eyes widened. “You cook?”
Cyan scratched his cheek. “Uh. Yeah. Kind of.”
Eve nodded once. “Good.”
Lyrel leaned closer, whispering loudly, “If it tastes like feelings, I’m blaming you.”
Cyan grinned. “Deal.”
Eve walked away, already sharpening her dagger.
“Dinner,” she said over her shoulder, “is not a negotiation.”
Lyrel waved cheerfully. “Neither is taste!”
The rations finally broke them.
Cyan stared at the dried slab in his hands, poked it once, then sighed dramatically.
“If I die today,” he said, “tell history it wasn’t the monsters. It was this.”
Eve didn’t look up from sharpening her dagger. “You said that yesterday.”
“And yesterday I meant it.”
Lyrel, kneeling by the river and rinsing her hands, tilted her head. “If you dislike it that much… I could cook.”
Cyan’s eyes lit up. “You can cook?”
“I can prepare nourishment,” Lyrel corrected. “Cooking implies unnecessary aggression.”
Eve snorted. “Treehugger.”
Lyrel didn’t miss a beat. “Helmethair.”
Cyan grinned. “We’re off to a great start.”
Lyrel gathered ingredients with almost ceremonial care. Roots sliced thin and perfectly even. Greens washed and rewashed. Mushrooms cleaned like they were fragile artifacts.
Cyan leaned over her shoulder. “You know, you don’t have to apologize to the carrot.”
“I’m not apologizing,” Lyrel said. “I’m thanking it.”
Eve stared into the pot. “You’re thanking food now?”
Lyrel glanced up sweetly. “You thank your weapons. I thank my meals.”
“My weapons don’t rot if I ignore them,” Eve shot back.
The meal was… green.
Not burned. Not undercooked.
Just aggressively healthy.
Lyrel served Cyan first. “Tell me what you think.”
Cyan took a bite.
He chewed.
“…Wow,” he said carefully.
Lyrel leaned forward. “Good wow or bad wow?”
“It tastes like,” Cyan paused, “a forest politely asking me not to starve.”
Lyrel smiled proudly.
Eve took one spoonful.
Then another.
Then frowned.
“This has no salt.”
“It has herbs,” Lyrel said.
“Herbs are lies,” Eve replied. “Salt is truth.”
Cyan nodded solemnly. “I think my tongue is confused but my soul feels supported.”
Lyrel beamed. “That means it’s working.”
Eve pushed the bowl slightly away. “This will not sustain us.”
“It will,” Lyrel said. “Just not recklessly.”
“War doesn’t care about recklessness.”
Lyrel shrugged. “War also doesn’t care if you enjoy your lunch.”
Cyan raised his spoon. “Point to Lyrel.”
Eve exhaled sharply through her nose. “Fine.”
She finished the bowl.
Slowly.
In silence.
Then she stood.
“Tomorrow,” Eve said, “I cook.”
Lyrel blinked. “Is that a threat?”
“Yes.”
Cyan laughed. “I’m excited and afraid.”
As they packed up for the quest, Lyrel hovered by the pot, pleased.
“I’ll improve it next time,” she said cheerfully. “Maybe with actual seasoning.”
Eve glanced back. “If you add flowers, I’m burning the pot.”
Lyrel smiled. “Deal.”
Cyan watched them walk ahead, shaking his head.
“This is the healthiest argument we’ve had all week.”
EVE ROUTE — FINAL SUMMARY
✦ Core Theme:
“Mercy and destruction are two sides of the same sin.”
Eve’s route is a redemption story wrapped in a moral war crime — her attempt to make peace with her past turns into a choice that could either end a nightmare or restart it.
Act 1 – The Revenant’s Return
Setting:

The journey begins after the events of the common route, where the party (Eve, Cyan, Lyrel) heads northward following rumors about Vaelwood Forest’s forbidden zone reopening — the same site Eve once helped seal years ago.
Summary:

The player learns bits of Eve’s past — a covert Northern assassin who defected after the war. - Along the way, Eve shows moments of guilt and quiet fear when they pass through military ruins or hear “whispers” from the dead.

- Anne the cat acts as a strange comfort to her, instinctively staying close whenever Eve has nightmares. - The group encounters the Remnant Soldiers — half-mad survivors of the teleportation disaster — confirming the North’s involvement.
Key Emotional Points:

Eve confesses she’s been here before, but lies about the details. - Cyan and Lyrel see her as cold but oddly protective — especially toward Anne the cat. - They discover an abandoned research site with documents marked Lazarus Decree.
Hint: Eve recognizes the name, freezes, and insists they leave. - Cyan begins to suspect that Eve knows far more than she admits.
End of Act 1:
A ghostly memory sequence plays — Eve standing amid burning forest soil, voices screaming.
She whispers: “I made sure it would never happen again.”
Title fades: Act 2 — The Ash and the Echo
Act 2 – The Ash and the Echo
Setting:
The group travels deeper into the Valewood sector, uncovering ruins of the Lazarus Division, an old research corps of the North.
Summary:

They find a researcher’s journal describing how Anne’s body was preserved as a “reactor vessel” to stabilize mass teleportation. - The journal mentions Eve’s name in passing — as the commander who led the “containment and purification.” - Confrontation follows:

Cyan demands answers. - Eve finally admits she was tasked with erasing the site and ensuring Anne could not be resurrected. - She believed she was granting Anne mercy — not knowing part of the project survived.
Meanwhile, Anne the cat begins acting oddly — meowing and scratching at sealed doors, leading them toward a hidden lab deeper underground.
Key Emotional Points:

Eve breaks her usual stoicism, saying: “If she came back… she wouldn’t be Anne. Just another weapon.” - Lyrel argues that playing god with life and death only breeds suffering — foreshadowing her stance later.
- Roland makes her first move — appearing via intercepted message or hologram, taunting Eve for “running away from your salvation.”
End of Act 2:
The party discovers a still-functioning stasis tube deep beneath the ruins — empty but marked “Subject: A. Lysandria”.
A faint pulse of magic hums beneath the floor.
Eve realizes someone continued the work elsewhere.
Fade out with Roland’s recorded voice:
“You can’t kill what’s already immortal, my beloved commander.”
Act 3 – The Unfinished Task
Setting:
The party travels to a hidden Northern facility near the border — Roland’s domain.
This act is more thriller-like: stealth, infiltration, and moral confrontation.
Summary:
Roland greets Eve as if they were old comrades.

She reveres Eve as “the Saint of Mercy” who once burned the lab — believing that act was divine, not rebellion. - Roland reveals the Lazarus Project still thrives — and they’ve recovered Anne’s body. - “All that’s missing,” she says, “is your flame to wake her.”
Eve is torn. She believes Anne should rest, but part of her wants to see her again — just once. - The player witnesses flashbacks:

Eve and Anne as soldiers: Anne always smiling, guiding Eve to “believe the world can be better.” - Eve holding Anne’s body in the aftermath of the teleportation failure, whispering, “You’ve done enough. Rest now.”
Roland’s rhetoric cuts deep: “You burned her once out of mercy. Will you burn her again out of guilt?”
Key Emotional Points:

Eve’s internal conflict becomes unbearable. - Cyan tries to reason with her — “You can’t atone by erasing what’s left.” - Lyrel warns that any resurrection would twist the natural order. - The group splits temporarily after Roland provokes tension between them (Zemo-style).
End of Act 3:
Eve storms into the heart of the facility, sees Anne’s preserved body — serene and lifeless — and her resolve hardens.
She ignites her weapons, ready to destroy the chamber.
But the player gets control at this moment — the route’s critical choice.
Act 4 – The Choice
Branch Point:
The player chooses Eve’s final action.
Path A – Mercy (Bad End)
Eve burns the lab, killing Roland, the researchers, and Anne’s body once and for all.
Key Scenes:

Anne the cat cries in agony, meowing at Eve’s feet as flames rise. - Cyan pulls Eve out before the entire complex collapses. - Later, Eve watches Anne’s ashes scatter into the wind, whispering: “Sleep well… hero.”
Ending Tone:
Peaceful yet hollow.

Eve’s redemption feels earned but empty — she saved Anne from torment but killed the world’s last hope. - Northern morale collapses; without Anne, war halts — but only from exhaustion. - The cat disappears, leaving only her collar behind.
Final shot:
Eve sitting by the ruins, murmuring:
“I saved her… didn’t I?”
Then silence.
Title: Bad End – The Mercy That Burned the World.
Path B – Salvation (Good… until it’s not)
Eve hesitates. Cyan stops her. Lyrel and Anne the cat both plead silently.
She lowers her weapon and says:
“If she wakes… let her choose for herself.”
They spare the project — helping Roland stabilize the resurrection, despite moral doubts.
Key Scenes:

Anne awakens, frail but alive. - Her eyes are kind… but flicker with other voices. - She recognizes Eve — “You look tired, my friend.” - Roland kneels in awe, whispering that the goddess has returned. - Eve breaks down crying, holding her hand, whispering “Welcome back.”
Ending Tone:
Hopeful, even beautiful — until a faint echo of multiple voices whispers through Anne:
“…so many… lost… where am I…”
Final shot:
Eve smiles through tears as alarms sound in the background — Northern reinforcements arriving to reclaim their “miracle.”
Fade to black.
Title: Good End – The Resurrection of Hope.
But we know it’s the seed of the Convergence Route, where Anne becomes the unstable weapon of the next war.
They followed the corridor until the stone widened into a cavernous hall. The air was colder here, as if the earth itself kept its breath.
These runes… they’re old, but not the kind found in any archive I’ve read. Someone blended sigilcraft with mechanical thinking.
Looks like something someone wanted forgotten.
It was. I made sure parts of it were.
Her voice carried an edge Cyan had rarely heard — not anger, but the weight of a promise kept in darkness.

Pillars of veined crystal stood around the chamber; within the hollows of some, glass-like cylinders drooped with slow, inner light. Frost clung to cracked seals and ancient lacquered plates lay half-buried in dust.
Anne padded forward from Cyan’s shoulder and nosed at a seam in the floor — her tail twitching like a compass.
We don’t need to go down there. Whatever this was — I burned the essentials. I left nothing useful.
Then why is the place humming? Why did the air change the moment we stepped in?
Someone's been here more recently than you remember. If there’s a pulse, we should know what it is.
Eve didn’t answer at once. Her hands curled at her sides, knuckles white.
A carved panel at the far end flared — runes shifting like written breath. A line of light coalesced into letters: Incoming Transmission — and a voice threaded through the hall.
Eve. How nice of you to come see what you thought you buried.
Roland.
The name landed like a stone. No one here knew the Revenant Division's history except a few old ghosts.
You should be dead.
So should you, perhaps — but here we both stand. Funny, isn't it?
You set them on us. You dragged me back.
I arranged a door and left it unlocked. You opened it. That’s your choice, as always.
Burned...? What is he talking about?
Eve, who is this man?
Eve said nothing. Her eyes stayed fixed on the projection, every line of her body locked in ice.
Hello. My name is Roland Veyra. Once vice-commander of the Revenant Division — the unit Eve herself led into the dark.
We didn’t stumble on anything. We were led here—by chance, by her injuries, by—
By design. Everything circles back to her, sooner or later.
Enough riddles. Speak clearly.
Clarity is cruel, kid. You wouldn’t want it. Not yet.
If you came here to gloat, you’ve done it. Now vanish.
Still giving orders. I missed that tone.
Stop talking like you know my heart.
I don’t know your heart — I know your hands. They remember what to do.
As his image vanished with a crackle of static, a final door at the end of the hall slid open with a soft, clinical sigh.
The chamber beyond was circular and sterile. At its center stood a single, frost-rimmed stasis tube. A tiny monitor beside it rhythmically beeped, tracking a fragile life sign.
The Hero…
Inside floated a pale human form, her face horribly young. The hero from the songs.
Eve’s face changed as if the world had folded inward. She didn’t speak. The breath left her like a confession.
I burned it. I burned it with my own hands. I made sure—
Her practiced calm shattered into a thousand pieces. Grief, guilt, and a fresh, terrifying fury warred in her eyes as she stared at the ghost she had failed to put to rest.
The chamber hummed faintly, indifferent to sorrow.
Eve’s hand hovered over the purge console. The hum of the stasis cylinder was the only sound besides the frantic beating of Cyan's heart.
This was it. The moment where words failed. What Cyan did next wouldn't just decide Anne's fate. It would decide who they were.
Anne the cat pressed herself against the cold glass of the cylinder, letting out a soft, mournful cry. A plea that transcended language.
Cyan's thoughts raced. Could he trust Eve's broken promise... or Lyrel's desperate hope?

options.text: Side with Eve. Help her keep her promise.
Side with Lyrel. Stop Eve at any cost.

steps.text: The clearing smelled of ash and metal. The bandits were gone, their insignias charred beyond recognition.
Cyan tightened the last of Eve’s bandages. Her thigh wound still oozed faintly, but the bleeding had stopped.
That should hold. You’ll be limping for a few days, though.
I’ve had worse.
You also just burn d our entire paycheck.
You’re welcome. Those papers were poison.
Lyrel crossed her arms, but Cyan caught the tremor in Eve’s hands — the same one she’d been hiding since the fight.
Whatever that was, it’s over now. We’ll report what we found and head back.
Good. The less anyone knows about 'Lazarus', the better.
Anne let out a small chirp from Cyan’s shoulder — soft, questioning.
Eve glanced up, guilt flickering behind her calm mask. She didn’t answer.
Then, without warning, Anne leapt from Cyan’s shoulder and dashed into the fog.
Oh, great. The furball’s gone feral again.
Anne! Wait—
The cat didn’t stop. Her tail bristled, ears flat, sprinting deeper into Vaelwood’s shadows.
Eve cursed under her breath and followed limping. The others ran after her.
They pushed through thick mist and dead roots until Anne stopped at what looked like a collapsed ridge.
The ground there pulsed faintly with mana, humming like a buried heart.
Hold up. You feel that? The energy readings here are... fresh.
A mana reactor underground?
...No reactor. A containment site.
Her tone dropped, low and cold. She stepped closer, brushing aside the roots until her fingers touched iron — an old service hatch half-buried beneath moss.
I said we shouldn’t be here.
Then why does your cat look ready to claw her way through solid steel?
Anne scratched at the hatch, tail lashing, eyes glowing faintly in the dark.
A faint spark of magic rippled from her paw — the same blink energy she used to protect Cyan.
Anne... what are you trying to show us?
The ground vibrated softly. Something deep below responded — an echo from the dark.
Enough. We’re leaving. Now.
Cyan—
If someone’s still down there, we can’t just walk away.
You don’t understand what that place is.
Then maybe it’s time you explain it, Helmet Hair.
Later.
Eve’s voice cracked faintly on that word. Even Anne hesitated — ears twitching, eyes on the hatch.
Then Cyan knelt beside it and pressed their hand to the cold metal.
There’s a way down.
Eve exhaled sharply, resignation cutting through her calm.
Stop. Whatever it is — we don't need to go digging.
You sure? Those readings are… odd. Fresh mana, too.
Lyrel crouched and brushed moss aside, revealing scorch marks that were newer than the rest — and a faint overlay of a sealing glyph that hummed with residual energy.
These burn marks… they're recent. And this glyph — it's an overlay, more modern than the old Northern work. Someone topped up the seals not too long ago.
So it's not dead then.
Eve listened like someone being told their wound had reopened.
If someone tampered with it, I’ll make sure it’s closed. But we're not looting curiosity.
Deal.
With a hiss of rust and mana, the hatch creaked open, revealing a staircase descending into faint blue light.
The air was thick, sterile — reeking of dust, iron, and memories Eve wished she’d buried.
Anne stepped forward first, tail raised, vanishing into the dark.
Guess that’s our cue.
You’d better pray she’s wrong about this place.
The party descended — unaware that the shadows below were already stirring.
The stairs opened into a wide, ruined atrium. Pipes hung like broken ribs, and frost traced the edges of long-dead consoles. Somewhere under the dust a faint hum pulsed like a heartbeat.
This place still holds energy. Not full power — but someone fed it recently.
So somebody didn't forget this place like it was supposed to be forgotten.
They moved among ruined desks and shattered containers. Lyrel's hand brushed the corner of a scorched binder wedged beneath a console.
Field notes — 'Phase two reclamation. Transfer manifest…'
Cyan peered over. The manifest listed container IDs, dates, and destinations — and one line in particular snagged at him.
"Transfer record: Subject A. Lysandria — transferred to Vaelwood Relay — Received by: Unknown. Authorization signature: (redacted)."
Eve — this mentions Anne by name. Why was she a 'subject'?

She wasn't supposed to be any of that. I found out what they were doing after she was declared dead. They were trying to stitch people into engines. I burned the lab that was doing it. I thought— I thought that ended it.
Lyrel lifted a corroded hatch and peered into a maintenance conduit. A strip of clean metal — fingerprints recent, a sealing glyph overlay — glowed faintly.
Someone reopened a transfer channel not long ago. Whoever moved Subject A didn't use the old route. They moved her to somewhere else — perhaps this relay.
Then she isn't buried. Not in the way you thought.
If someone moved her… then they tried again.
Anne padded ahead, then skittered to the end of a corridor and pawed at a reinforced door. The metal around the seam had been recently cleaned as if someone had wiped away old scorch.
A small maintenance panel lit at the cat's touch — a service override glowing red with a single label: 'Containment: Local Override.'
There’s still someone who knows where the keys are.
Or someone had the forethought to leave a manual access. Either way…
They pulled the door aside with effort. A cold breath of stale air sighed out.

The chamber beyond was circular and sterile, ringed with inactive ports. At the center stood a single stasis tube still intact. A faint frosting traced the glass and a tiny monitor flickered with life.
Subject A. Lysandria — minimal but present neural signature. Vital stabilization: intermittent.
Is that— her? Anne…
Inside the tube floated a pale human form, small and still. Anne's face — the one from the songs and pictures — looked sleep-soft and horribly young.
No… I burned that place years ago. I left no name. I left no body.
Her fingers dug into the railing until knuckles blanched. The truth zapped through her — the unbearable possibility that she had failed to end it completely.

A lateral console blinked. A tiny log scrolled with timestamps: 'Reconstitution attempt: incomplete — transfer initiated — preserving vessel.' The last entry had a technician's handle — but the signature had been scrubbed.
They moved her. Someone moved Anne after you destroyed the first lab.
Who would do that? Why preserve her?
Eve didn't answer. Her face went stone-cold, and for the first time Cyan saw the iron behind her calm.
Then whoever did this will answer for it.
The stasis tube's faint heartbeat thrummed in the air; Anne the cat pressed her nose to the glass and looked up — as if feeling something only she could translate.

They stood there, three people and a cat, in the blue half-light of a machine that had swallowed a life. None of them knew who had done this — only that somebody had kept her alive when Eve had tried to erase that possibility.
A nearby console blinked, displaying a single log entry: 'Preservation protocol successful. Vessel stable. The Saint is ready for her second coming. - The Keeper.'
Silence. The only sound was the soft, rhythmic beep of the life support and the blood pounding in Cyan's ears.
Eve was still on her knees, her reflection trembling on the frost-coated glass beside Anne's serene face.
It can't be... 'Declared martyred at Lorthen's Gate.' Every history book says so.
But it is. That's her.
…Anne.
A flicker of memory—a smile through smoke, a hand slipping away. Then the present rushed back like a blast of cold air.
Eve? You knew her?
I buried her.
A figure stepped from the darkness — robes tattered, eyes bright with tired conviction.
Please… lower your blades. Her sleep is fragile.
Who are you? Are you 'The Keeper'?
That is what the logs call me. I am merely a caretaker. She has been sleeping peacefully for a long time. You need not disturb her.
Peacefully? This is necromancy. A perversion.
No. It is devotion. The Saint deserves rest until the world is worthy of her return.
Saint? Is that what the North is calling her now?
You speak her name as if you knew her. As an equal.
Eve pushed herself to her feet, her voice cracking under the weight of memory.
She fought beside me. And Gabe. She was my friend. She believed the world could still be kind.
But... you said you buried her…
I did. I made sure she could rest.
Then your efforts were in vain, child. The North wouldn't let their savior rest. When your fire was extinguished, they came to collect what was left.
They hired you? You worked for them on 'Project Lazarus'?
I was the lead researcher on the original project. She... she saved my village during the Lorthen campaign. I owed her a debt that could never be repaid.
When they came to me, proposing to... continue the work, I saw my chance. I took their funding. I used their labs.
You took their blood money to continue their defilement.

I took their resources to protect her! They saw a weapon; I saw a soul to be preserved. I delayed their progress with false reports and fabricated data for years. I told them the vessel was too unstable, that the spirit was gone, all while I worked to keep her safe here, hidden away.
I am not their pawn. I am her shepherd, using the wolf's own den to guard the lamb.
She's not a lamb, she's a person! And this is still a cage, no matter how much faith you wrap it in.
Faith is what keeps a soul alive when the body cannot! And it is my faith that has kept her pure, away from their generals and their battle plans!
By keeping her here? Like a relic in a tomb?
I kept her *pure*. The Northern generals sought to make her a weapon. I rescued the vessel and brought her here, to keep her soul safe until her purpose could be reclaimed by a world at peace.
That's still defilement, whatever faith you wrap it in.
Faith is what keeps a soul alive when the body cannot. Tell me, elf—is that defilement, or is it hope?
Eve took a step closer to the cylinder, her hand rising to touch the cold glass.
Anne...
Their voices clashed quietly, echoing through the chamber’s hollow hum.
She moved—!
Do not fear. It is her spirit remembering warmth. Nothing more.
No… she’s reacting to me.
Corin stepped forward, his expression torn between awe and fear.
Whatever binds her spirit to this vessel is fragile.
Fade? You mean die again.
And who decided that? You?
Rest… That’s all she ever wanted.
Then let her have it. Go. Don’t wake her before her time.
Eve said nothing, but her jaw clenched — torn between guilt and the echo of old duty.
Somewhere deep within the crystal, something stirred — or dreamed.
They retreated to a small alcove outside the chamber. Corin's voice — a prayer, pleading — had followed them, asking them to leave Anne to her sleep.
Eve — you have to tell us. What did you mean before when you said you 'buried' her?
Cyan's voice was steadier than his hands. Lyrel's eyes were flames.
You told us to burn the logs, to forget Lazarus — but you didn't tell us about this. You kept this secret.
Eve remains silent a beat, then closes her eyes as if drawing a wound inward.
You were... part of them? You led a covert unit?
I led the shadows that erased other people's sins. We were called when the kingdom needed someone to make terrible decisions.
She tried to make it small — three images, sharp as knives: Anne smiling through rain, the teleportation failing like a storm swallow, Eve carrying something that had been broken.
Anne was my friend. Gabe's fiancee. She was light. When the teleportation failed — when the Elder Tides spat them out — she was changed. Not just hurt. Used.
Used how?

They wanted to fix it. The northern labs wanted to patch what they'd broken and call it a miracle. They would have turned her into a stabilizer, a living anchor to move armies. I learned that after… after she was declared dead.
So you found out what they would do to her — and you burned the lab.
I burned what I could. I destroyed the tools and the orders. I left nothing for them to salvage. I made sure no one would take her name and make it an order again.
So you decided life or death for her? You played judge over life and death, Eve.
Her words landed like iron. Eve's eyes skimmed past Lyrel to the sealed chamber where Anne slept.
It wasn't judgment. It was mercy. I couldn't let them make her into that. She begged me to let her rest.
The memory hurt in the soft places — Eve kneeling in smoke, Anne's hand slack in her palm, the world reduced to an ember and a promise.
You did what you thought was right back then. But now — now that her body is here and someone kept it — destroying it again won't undo the past.
No. It won't. But leaving it will let others play god with her name.
Eve — you can't be the arbiter of all that. Mercy or murder, it's not for one person to decree.
Cyan steps closer, eyes searching hers.
We need to— we need to think. There might be another way. Burning everything won't heal you. It won't bring her peace for sure.
When I burned it, I thought I was putting a body to rest. I thought I had stopped the machine from using her. I told myself she could be buried in peace.
Her fingers found the hilt of her old blade, thumb tracing the worn edge as if it might remind her which self to be.
But if someone else keeps her alive, what then? If they wake her and she becomes something else — I can't let that happen. And yet... the thought of ending her again—
I don't know. I don't know which sin is smaller.
That's not an answer.
You don't have to decide now. But we need a plan — not just an oath to burn.
Eve's face was a map of old scars and fresh doubt. Her eyes flicked to the sealed glass once more, then to her hands.
I swore to end what tied her to that fate. I still believe that. But I won't throw myself into blind fury.
I am torn — half of me wants the fire to finish what it began. Half of me... wants to see if she can somehow be herself again.
The words hung between them like smoke. No resolution. No final verdict. Only a promise of hard choices to come.
Silence pressed down like old vows. Anne's crystal cylinder pulsed faintly. Dust motes moved in slow eddies. Eve's fingers flexed as if around an old wound.

You linger beautifully in the dark. But sentiment doesn't stop logistics. I thought you'd appreciate haste. A retrieval party moves tonight — northern battleguard tasked to recover the vessel before anyone can destroy it.
The words landed like an order. Corin's face drained; Eve's jaw tightened.
You called them? You brought the army here?
I did. Consider it a precaution. If someone intends to burn what history covets, better to secure the asset first. You forget how the world values a hero's body, Eve.
Something in Eve snapped like a brittle hinge. For a heartbeat she looked very old and very dangerous.
No. If they take her, they'll butcher her into an order. I won't let the north make a saint into a sword.
I'll end it. I will burn it all down again.
No! You cannot— You don't understand what it means for her—! I will not let you destroy what I kept.
Corin slammed both palms on a rune-altar. He chanted jagged syllables, hands trembling with fear and prayer.
Awake! Guardians of the ward — obey the keeper's oath!
Two hulking golems shifted from the gloom — iron-veined stone and crystal, runes along their joints flaring amber. They stepped between Eve and the cylinder, slow and absolute.
Please — leave. Take the child and go. I've kept her safe until now. I won't let her be taken or burned.
Eve — think. If you destroy this, you'll be doing the same thing you swore you'd never be.

Summary ### Act 4: Goal and Structure

Goal: To bring Eve's internal conflict to a head, forcing the player to make a definitive choice between her cynical pragmatism (mercy through destruction) and a fragile, newfound hope (salvation through faith). This choice will define her redemption and set the course for the future of the world.
Scene 1: "The Oath and the Accusation"
Objective: To establish the final stakes and solidify the ideological battle lines between Eve, Cyan, and Lyrel, making the player feel the weight of both arguments before the choice is presented.
How it Builds:

1. The Immediate Aftermath: The scene opens moments after the golems have fallen. The chamber is filled with dust and the heavy silence of betrayal. Corin is broken, weeping over his destroyed guardians. Eve stands before the stasis cylinder, her expression cold and resolved.
She is no longer just Eve; she is the commander of the Revenant Division, ready to finish a mission.

2. The Accusation: Lyrel is the first to speak, her voice trembling with rage and disappointment. She accuses Eve of becoming the very monster she fought against—someone who unilaterally decides life and death. "You burn labs, you kill guardians...
how is this any different from the orders the Northern Kingdom gave you?" This argument directly attacks Eve's justification of "mercy."

3. The Plea: Cyan steps between them, appealing not to Eve's logic, but to her heart. He reminds her of the friend she lost, not the "subject" she needs to erase. "This isn't about saving her from them, Eve. This is about saving yourself from your guilt.
Don't let the last thing you do for her be the same as what they did—taking away her choice."

4. Eve's Justification: Eve finally responds, her voice low and haunted. She describes, in chilling detail, what "Project Lazarus" truly entailed—not just making a weapon, but hollowing out a soul, creating a puppet that would wear Anne's face while committing atrocities.
She frames her actions not as murder, but as fulfilling a final, unspoken promise to her friend to never let her become that.

5. The Ticking Clock: Roland's voice cuts in via the comms, amused and detached. "A touching debate, but your time is running out. I can hear their boots on the stone above. Make your choice, Commander."
The scene ends with Eve raising her hand toward the cylinder's control panel, tuning them all out.
Scene 2: "The Final Choice"
Objective: To present the player with the clear, interactive choice at the peak of emotional tension.
How it Builds:
1. The Physical Action: Eve begins the process of overloading the stasis cylinder. A low hum builds, and the runes on the glass begin to glow erratically. This is the point of no return.
2. The Final Appeals: Cyan and Lyrel make one last, desperate attempt.
Cyan: "Eve, look! Look at the cat!" Anne the cat is at the base of the cylinder, pawing at the glass, letting out a soft, mournful cry. It's a pure, instinctual plea for the life inside.
Lyrel: "If there is even a fraction of a chance she can be herself again, we have to take it! That is the duty of the living!"

3. The Player's Intervention (The Choice Menu): As Eve's hand hovers over the final command, a memory flashes—Anne's voice, whispering from the past: "Promise me, Eve... if it ever comes to it... don't let them make me a monster." The screen freezes on this moment of decision.
[CHOICE]
"Fulfill your promise. Grant her peace." (This leads to Path A)
"Hesitate. Give her a chance to choose." (This leads to Path B)
Scene 3: "Ashes or Awakening"

Objective: To deliver the emotional and narrative consequences of the player's choice, providing a powerful, conclusive ending for Eve's route while setting up the future. This scene will have two completely different scripts based on the choice in Scene 2.
Path A Script (Mercy - Bad End):

1. The Inferno: Eve slams her hand down. The overload sequence is irreversible. Alarms blare. Roland's voice cuts out with a final, surprised curse. As the cylinder cracks and flames erupt, Anne the cat lets out a pained shriek and darts away into the shadows.

2. The Escape: Cyan grabs a stoic, unmoving Eve and physically drags her from the chamber as the structure begins to collapse. The last thing they see is the cylinder being consumed by white-hot energy.

3. The Aftermath: The scene cuts to the surface, dawn breaking over the smoking ruins of the Vaelwood site. Eve is sitting alone, watching the ashes rise on the wind. Cyan quietly places Anne the cat's collar beside her—it's all he could find.

4. The Hollow Victory: Eve whispers, "Sleep well... hero." Her voice is calm, but her eyes are empty. The war is averted for now, the North's weapon is gone, but her redemption feels like another ghost she must carry.
5. Final Shot: Eve sits in silence as the sun rises, murmuring to herself, "I saved her… didn’t I?" There is no answer.
[Title Card: Bad End – The Mercy That Burned the World]
Path B Script (Salvation - "Good" End):
1. The Hesitation: Eve's hand stops. Her resolve breaks. She whispers, "I can't." The overload sequence fails. At that moment, the doors to the chamber are blasted open and Northern soldiers pour in.
2. An Unlikely Alliance: Roland's voice returns, sharp and commanding. "Forget them! Stabilize the vessel! Now!"
Faced with a common enemy, Eve, Cyan, and even a reluctant Lyrel work frantically with Roland's remote instructions to initiate the resurrection protocol before the soldiers can seize the cylinder.
3. The Awakening: They succeed. The stasis pod hisses open. Anne Lysandria stirs, her eyes fluttering open. She is frail, confused, but she is alive.

4. The Reunion: Her gaze finds Eve. A faint, tired smile touches her lips. "Eve... you look tired, my friend." Overcome with relief and a decade of grief, Eve collapses to her knees, taking Anne's hand and crying for the first time. "Welcome back," she whispers.

5. The Seed of Doubt: The moment is beautiful, but as Anne looks around, her eyes flicker. A faint, discordant whisper is heard beneath her own voice: "...so many... lost... where am I..." It's a chilling hint that she didn't come back alone.

6. Final Shot: Eve is smiling through her tears, clutching her friend's hand—a picture of hope. In the background, the Northern commander is shouting orders to "secure the miracle." The alarms of the facility blend with the triumphant sounds of her reclamation.
[Title Card: Good End – The Resurrection of Hope]

Eve and Cyan confront Roland. He’s desperate — convinced redemption is impossible without erasing all witnesses. - Eve refuses to kill him this time. She stops Cyan too — proving she’s truly broken the Revenant cycle. She lets him live, even when he begs for death.

⚖️ Pros & Cons of Your “Roland Betrayal” Arc
✅ Pros

Grounded, human betrayal. No over-the-top villainy. - Mirrors Eve’s own guilt — he’s what she could’ve become if she didn’t leave. - Creates personal stakes separate from Lyrel’s mythic tone. - Builds emotional trust between Cyan and Eve naturally.
⚠️ Cons / Risks

If not paced right, Roland might overshadow Eve emotionally. - You’ll need to show why he still admired Eve until the end — makes his betrayal tragic, not petty. - Need strong dialogue to avoid “military cliché” traps (revenge, orders, etc.)

Anne.

Core Characterization — Roland

Role: Eve’s former second-in-command in the Revenant Division. - Personality: Devoted, precise, obsessive. A mirror of Eve’s old self, but without her conscience. - Belief: “Eve was perfection. We existed because she led us. Without her, we were nothing.”

What Happened After the War
After Eve’s disappearance:
The Revenant Division was dissolved quietly. - Official report: “Mission failed. All operatives presumed dead.” - In reality, the Division self-destructed out of grief.
Some took suicidal missions. - Some executed themselves after leaving their insignias behind. - Some were silenced by the kingdom to bury evidence.
Roland was the last one left — alive only because he was recovering from injury during the collapse. He woke up to find his entire team gone and a report saying Eve betrayed them.
That’s when the obsession began.
Roland’s Mindset
Roland is not evil — he’s broken.
He spent years replaying every command she ever gave, trying to find meaning.
He believes:
“You left us because we weren’t good enough. Because I wasn’t good enough.

His betrayal in the story isn’t done out of anger — it’s warped devotion.
He’s convinced that by exposing her, by “forcing” her to be Eve the Revenant Commander again, he’ll bring back the woman he worshiped.
Connection to Cyan’s Quest

Eve–Roland Dynamic

Roland speaks with reverence, always using “Commander.” - Eve hates it. She corrects him with “Don’t call me that.” - But he can’t — won’t — stop. - In his eyes, she wasn’t allowed to stop being their leader. When she deserted, she broke not just the army — she broke their reason for existence.
He’s the living embodiment of Eve’s guilt.
Endgame Confrontation Concept
When Eve finally faces him:
Roland’s dialogue turns from devotion to desperation.
“You were supposed to be our light. Our hand in the dark.

Eve answers quietly:

“You followed orders I never should’ve given. That’s not loyalty, Roland. That’s tragedy.”

⚙️ How He Sets the Trap
Let’s walk through it logically from his perspective:
Step 1: Gathering Fragments
Roland spends years reconstructing Eve’s mission logs, field reports, and operation patterns.
Every safehouse she used, every cleanup zone — he visits them all.
Everywhere he finds her handwriting, her orders, her traces.
He notices one consistent pattern:
Eve always erased herself clean — except for one thing.
She never destroyed the list of operatives she lost.
She kept them logged, like memorials, encoded into the safehouse symbols.
This obsession tells Roland something crucial — she feels guilt.
So he realizes: if he crafts a mission that mirrors one of their old “cleanup operations,” she might not resist helping.
Step 2: Forging the Bait
Roland uses old Revenant codes still buried in the guild registry system.
He forges a D-rank cleanup mission — something minor and forgettable —
with the coordinates of a defunct Revenant outpost once used by Eve’s squad.
The request:
“Investigate traces of old military material in the ruins near Frostmere Ridge. Possible contamination — hazard pay authorized.”
That’s it. Simple, unassuming — but Eve would know.
Those words are phrased exactly like the orders she used to give.
No one else could have written them that way.
Step 3: Waiting
Roland knows Eve doesn’t check the board anymore — but someone might take the quest for her.
When Cyan takes it (because it’s a cleanup near her area or guild), Roland’s scouts track them quietly.
When Eve shows up with Cyan, he knows.
“Only one person would come back here, Commander.
The one who taught us to erase the past — but couldn’t erase herself.”
🧠 His Mental Justification
Roland believes Eve didn’t abandon them — she was broken by guilt and manipulation.
He thinks if he shows her that the past still matters — that he’s still here, still loyal — she’ll return to who she was.
But his love is parasitic.
He wants her as she was, not as she is.
So his “backup plan” isn’t to imprison her out of hatred.
It’s containment out of devotion.
“If you won’t come back willingly, then I’ll keep you where I can still see you.
The world can’t have you, Commander. They don’t deserve you.”
He doesn’t even think he’s betraying her — he’s “saving” her from herself.
🕳️ Backup Plan: Military Leverage
Roland still has connections inside the army.
He leaks Eve’s “sighting” to the Northern military as an “unconfirmed deserter appearance.”
If Eve doesn’t agree to return voluntarily — he’ll let them take her “for her safety.”
In his twisted mind, prison means protection.
She’ll be alive. She’ll be “contained.”
He’ll finally be at peace — because his commander will no longer vanish.
💣 The Breakdown Moment
When Eve confronts him, she’ll realize the horror of it:
He doesn’t see her as a person anymore — he sees her as a memory to preserve.
Eve: “You didn’t look for me, Roland. You looked for a ghost.”
Roland: “I looked for the truth!”
Eve: “Then you never found me.”
That’s the moment his obsession turns desperate, leading to the final betrayal.

🌲 Lyrel’s Route – The Screaming Forest
Act 1 — Faith in Decay
Lyrel has been tagging along for a few quests, unofficially part of Cyan’s group. She’s helpful but distant — more interested in Anne’s teleportation magic than gold or glory.

As Cyan grows closer to her, Lyrel admits her true goal: she wants to heal the forest — the one that screams when the wind passes through. She joins to study Anne’s teleportation, insists the forest can still be saved.

Emotional Anchor
Lyrel is your hope in denial — the one who _still believes_ something beautiful can be salvaged from ruin. Her warmth and optimism become the player’s emotional center… until cracks start showing.

Hope versus decay
Idealism confronting harsh truth
The price of pretending things can still heal
Key Emotional Beats

1. Opening Mood — Hopeful Resolve Lyrel leads the group through the forest, determined to show Cyan and Eve “life still lingers here.” She hums softly, talks to the trees as if they can still hear — small, tender, almost childish habits from the _old Lyrel_.
Eve doesn’t mock her, but watches in silence, knowing exactly where this is heading.

2. The Dying Tree Scene They find the _Worldroot_, once sacred to elves — now blackened and hollow inside. Lyrel tries to use her magic to heal it. The bark splits. The sap bleeds red. The magic backfires, scarring her arm. Eve pulls her back.
Lyrel insists, “It can still heal,” but the audience knows — it can’t. That moment becomes the first crack in her denial.

3. Conflict with Eve That night, Eve confronts her: “You think clinging to fairy tales will change what we did?” Lyrel lashes out — her first emotional flare — accusing Eve of _giving up on everything worth saving_. It’s raw, emotional, but ends unresolved.

4. Echo of the Past — Whispers in the Trees Lyrel hears faint whispers — echoes of the elves lost in the failed teleportation, fused into the forest. She follows them alone, and finds one tree _crying_, sap leaking like tears. It calls her name.
She breaks down — part horror, part guilt, part desperate prayer that “they’re still alive somehow.” The player sees her denial begin to crumble.

5. Ending Beat — The Withered Dawn At dawn, the group leaves the forest. Lyrel doesn’t speak much — her smile forced, hope still clinging but visibly shaken. As they walk out, one leaf falls — alive, faintly glowing.

Act 2 — Shadows of Home

Lyrel’s hope turns into alienation. She’s no longer simply hopeful — she’s _defying_ both humans _and_ her own kin to protect that hope. The player starts to realize: her kindness isn’t just virtue — it’s stubborn self-destruction.

They reach the ancient elven sanctum — once Lyrel’s childhood home. The trees still sing faintly when she walks past, but their voices are cracked, distorted. She places her hand on an old wardstone. Flash of memory: the old Lyrel, joyful, running through sunlight with other elves.

That night, as the others sleep, Lyrel looks toward the glowing canopy. The forest whispers again — her name, faint, pleading. Eve wakes, watching her silently, seeing the same haunted look she once had in herself — the look of someone chasing ghosts.

Lyrel’s role shifts: from hopeful light → tragic intermediary.

Act 3 — The Screaming Woods
The Real Truth Behind the “Forest of Echoes”
The Northern Kingdom’s plan wasn’t an accident. It was _strategic coercion_: they wanted to force the elves’ hand. The teleportation ritual was meant to:
1. Instantly deploy 1,000 elite troops behind southern lines,
2. Establish a forward base inside the elves’ forest,
3. Corner the elves into siding with them “for protection” once the forest was compromised.

Eve’s role: she was part of the _Revenant Division_ — an elite black-ops unit under royal command. Her team wasn’t told the full plan; they were “securing the perimeter” for a “supply route,” unaware that the teleportation would tear open the forest’s ley lines.
When it went wrong, Eve’s squad was ordered to “contain the contamination” — which meant burning and killing everything left alive. She obeyed, until she realized _what_ she was killing.
The forest’s scream isn’t just magical residue — it’s the merged consciousness of soldiers and nature, all warped by the teleportation collapse. Every cry is a memory of that day.
💥 Why This Is the Peak Conflict

Lyrel’s revelation: the “accident” wasn’t just reckless human magic — it was _intentional political manipulation_. Her lifelong hope of reconciliation between elves and humans dies right there. Worse, the woman she grew to trust — Eve — was _part of it_.
Eve’s position: she becomes the living embodiment of that betrayal. She’s not lying, not defending herself — just existing as proof that Lyrel’s people were slaughtered for nothing.
Moral inversion: Lyrel, the pacifist, becomes the aggressor. Eve, the killer, refuses to fight back — showing growth through restraint. The player is forced to side emotionally:
Sympathize with Lyrel’s righteous anger?
Or with Eve’s guilt and her choice not to kill again?

Cyan: "Lia... wait. Where is she? Where is Vera?" Cyan: "She promised she'd hide you! She said she would be with you!"
(Eclia’s expression shifts. A flicker of genuine pain crosses her face, followed by cold, hard resolve. She signals Sol to step back.)
Eclia: "Vera." Eclia: "You came all this way... you killed your friends... and you are looking for the maid?"
Cyan: "She raised us! She saved me! If she's here, she can explain everything!"
(Eclia reaches behind her throne. She pulls out an object and throws it at Cyan's feet. It lands with a soft thud in the mud.)
(It is Vera’s signature apron. It is slashed down the middle and stained with old, dried blood.)
Cyan: "No..."
Eclia: "She didn't save you, Cyan. She exported you. You were a failed experiment she sent North to see if a commoner could hold a Rune."
Cyan: "That's a lie! She loved us!"
Eclia: "She loved the King. She was King's Eyes, Cyan. Just like the man who recruited you. Just like Brandt."
(Cyan reels. The connection snaps into place. The similar tactics. The magic training. The 'Hero' narrative.)
Cyan: "So... she's..."
Eclia: "Dead. I killed her myself."
(Flashback Image (Sepia): Young Eclia, crying, driving a dagger into Vera’s heart while Vera looks at her not with fear, but with a cold, professional nod.)
Eclia: "The day I awakened as the Sovereign... she tried to put a suppression collar on me. She tried to finish the job." Eclia: "So I hugged her. I hugged her, and I stopped her heart."
Cyan: "You... you murdered her? She was like a mother to us!"
Eclia: "She was a handler! And you are just another one of her puppets!"
(Eclia stands up, screaming now. The 'Cool Queen' mask cracks under the weight of the trauma.)

Eclia: "She told me you ran away! She told me you hated me! And she told you to be a Hero so you'd die for her Kingdom!" Eclia: "I killed the spy who ruined our lives. And you returned wearing her flag."
(Cyan looks at the bloody apron. He realizes that the magic he used to 'save' the town, the magic he used to fight his way here... it was all given to her by a spy to make her a useful weapon.)
Cyan: "I... I didn't know."
Eclia: "Ignorance is not innocence, Cyan. It is just another weapon."
(She sits back down, exhausted.)
Eclia: "Sol. Throw her out."
[SCENE END]
The scroll bore the King's Seal in red wax. It wasn't a request. It was a summons.
All B-Rank and above... mandatory assembly in the Capital Square at noon tomorrow. Failure to appear is desertion.
It's the Draft. Just like the Second War. They're going to feed us into the meat grinder to slow down the Beastkin.
We can't go. If we join the army, we're part of the problem. We saw what they did at the tunnel.
Refusal is logical, but dangerous. The penalty for desertion during a State of Emergency is death.
I'd rather take my chances running than dying for a lie. Pack your bags. We're leaving tonight. We'll head for the coast.
Heading for the coast, Eve? The ports are closed.
Brandt. Get out of my guild.
I am afraid I cannot. I am here to ensure the 'Heroes of Ironhold' attend the rally.
We're not going. We quit.
We had a deal. You play the Hero, you stay free. You try to run...
And I release the un-redacted report on Captain Vance's death. The one that implicates you in the murder of a Northern officer and conspiracy with the traitor Fenrir.
You... you're still holding that over us?
Until the war is won. Yes.
You will go to the Capital. You will stand in the front row. And you will cheer.
Fine. We'll be there.
Now hold on! You can't just bully them! They're my guild members!
I'm coming too. I know people in the Logistics Corps. I'm going to get you a safe assignment, guarding a warehouse or something.
Gabe, stay here. You don't want to see this.
I'm the Guild Master! I look out for my own. I'm coming, and that's final.
The more the merrier. The Capital needs every voice.
Gabe... you really shouldn't come.
I'm packing the wagon. We leave in ten minutes.
Gabe marched off to prepare, driven by loyalty.
Eve watched him go, a pit forming in her stomach. She knew the North didn't summon everyone to the Capital just for a speech.
They were planning a show.
Month Four. The rain hadn't stopped in three weeks.
General Anne was ten miles ahead, smashing another fortress. But the Strays weren't at the front. They were stuck in the mud, guarding the most valuable thing in the Kingdom.
How much longer to the outpost? The soldiers are getting restless.
Another ten miles. If the axle holds. Which it won't.
And we're out of booze. If I don't get a drink soon, I'm going to start biting people.
The magical pollution in this region is thickening. The land is rejecting us. The crops in the fields we passed were withered.
It's the 'Withering War'. Eclia... the South... they planned this. They knew we'd starve.
Hey... you're the B-Ranks, right? The 'Heroes'? You got any extra rations in your packs?
We're on half-rations too, soldier. I'm sorry.
Heroes. You eat in the command tent with Roland while we eat boot leather.
Ambush! Protect the food!
I can't see them! They're in the trees!
Guerilla tactics. They are not engaging. They are harassing.
NO! THE BREAD!
Stop! Get back in formation! You're exposed!
Let it burn.
Fenrir!
Go home, little fan. The snow is coming. General Anne can kill our forts, but she cannot kill the winter.
It's mine! I saw it first!
Back off! My squad hasn't eaten in two days!
Hey! Stop it! We're on the same side!
Stay out of it, mage! You don't know what hunger is!
Enough! Form up or I'll gut you both myself!
They were fighting over scraps. We're the 'Grand Army of the North'... and we're fighting over scraps.
We are winning the battles, Cyan. But we are losing the soldiers.
Get up. We have to report this to Roland. He'll just add it to the spreadsheet.
Is this what winning looks like?
No. This is what losing slowly looks like.
Cyan marched on. But she stopped looking for heroes. She just looked for her next meal.
This house... it feels lived in. Toys on the floor. Half-eaten meals.
They were families, Eve. Just like in Porthumming.
War doesn't care about families, kid. Keep searching. Intel says this was a safehouse for a high-ranking commander.
Eve. Look at this.
Lia...?
You know her?
It's... Eclia. My childhood friend. The one from the Blood Tribe estate.
I thought she escaped! I thought the Butler got her out!
Look at what they're doing to her. She's... she's bleeding. Crying.
So. You know the Vessel.
Vessel? That's Eclia! She's a person!
To you, perhaps. To the savages? She is a battery.
We've intercepted their communications. The Beastkin call her 'The Mother'. Not because she leads them... but because she feeds them.
Look at the binding runes. Southern Hemocraft. They have strapped her into a machine that amplifies her bloodline ability.
They are draining her life force to power their shields. To frenzy their soldiers. That 'hive mind' coordination you saw in the forest? That's her mind being ripped apart to control them.
They're... eating her alive?
Piece by piece. For years. That is the secret of the South's sudden power. They enslaved the last heir of the Blood Tribe and turned her into a generator.
I have to get her out.
Cyan, wait. Think about this. Why would they paint a shrine to a battery?
Primitives worship what they fear, Eve. Or what keeps them alive.
She is at the High Pass. That is where they are preparing the final ritual. If we do not break their line soon... there will be nothing left of her to save.
Then we break the line.
General Anne breaks the front. I punch through the middle. I'm getting her out of there.
A sound strategy. We move on the High Pass at the next moon.
Kid... Roland is playing you. I can smell it.
I don't care, Eve! Look at her!" (He points to the weeping painting). "She's dying! I left her behind once. I'm not doing it again.
Cyan took the painting down. He rolled it up and put it in his pack.
He wasn't fighting for the North anymore. He wasn't fighting for peace.
He was fighting to kill every single monster that had laid a hand on Eclia.
The painting lay open between them. In the flickering candlelight, the weeping girl looked even more desperate. Even more broken.
Alright, kid. Spill it.
You almost punched a General today. You stole evidence. And you've been staring at that painting for two hours.
Who is she? And don't give me the 'childhood friend' line. Lots of kids have friends. They don't try to invade countries for them.
Her name is Eclia. But I called her Lia.
She wasn't just a friend. She was... the only thing that mattered.
I grew up on the Blood Tribe estate in the South. I wasn't anyone special. Just the daughter of the groundskeeper.
The estate was huge, but it was quiet. Dead quiet. Except for the Tower.
The Blood Tribe... they were reclusive. Rumored to be obsessed with bloodline purity and ancient rituals.
They were obsessed with *her*. She was the last Heir.
They kept her locked up. They said she was 'fragile'. That the sun would hurt her. That she was too important to step in the dirt.
But she wasn't fragile. She was bored.
I used to climb the trellis to her window. I'd bring her things from the outside. Strange rocks. Flowers. Stories about the market.
She would listen for hours. She had this way of looking at you... like you were the only person in the world.
So you were the pauper, and she was the princess. A classic tragedy.
It wasn't like that. We were just... lonely. Both of us.
I promised her I'd get her out. I learned Rune Magic from one of the old guards—the only one who was kind to me—so I could be strong enough to break the locks.
But I wasn't strong enough. The scientists... the Rune Weavers... they took over the estate.
They started the experiments. I could hear her screaming from the gardens.
And you did nothing?
I tried! But the Butler—he was a spy for the North—he stopped me.
He told me that if I stayed, they would just kill me. He said my death would break her spirit completely.
He offered me a way out. He said: 'Go North. Become a Hero. Get strong enough to challenge a nation. Then come back and save her.'
Cyan... that Butler. He didn't save you. He exiled you.
He needed you gone so the scientists could work without distraction.
I know that now! I know I ran away!
That's why I have to go back. Look at the painting, Eve. She's suffering because I wasn't there to stop it.
She's waiting for me. She has to be.
Cyan looked at the painting of the Blood Sovereign—a figure of terrifying power and pain.
But she didn't see the Monster. She only saw the little girl in the tower who liked stories.
Cyan. The energy readings from the High Pass... the Crimson Tide ritual... it suggests she is not merely a battery.
She is the catalyst. To channel that much power requires a will of iron. The girl you knew... she may have changed.
She hasn't. She's the kindest person I know. She wouldn't hurt anyone unless they forced her.
Roland said they have her hooked up to a machine. That she's a prisoner in her own mind.
Just like Anne.
Trapped in a machine... being used by monsters to kill people she doesn't hate.
Yeah. I guess I know what that looks like.
Alright. We get her out.
Really?
We cut the wires. We break the machine. If she's a prisoner, we free her. If she's a weapon... we disarm her.
But Cyan? If we get in there, and she's not the girl you remember... if the torture broke her...
You have to be ready to do the hard thing.
She's still Lia. I know she is.
We march on the High Pass in three days. I'm going to be ready.
Cyan blew out the candle. The tent went dark.
She went to sleep dreaming of a garden and a promise.
She didn't know that the girl in the garden had burned it down years ago.
The battle for the Southern Outpost was fierce, but the Strays were S-Rank material in all but name. They moved through the Beastkin lines with surgical precision.
Two on the left! Lyrel, bind them!
Targets immobilized. They are secure.
I've got the right flank!
Cyan saw the fear in their eyes. She had the power to end them, or the skill to stop them.

options.text: Non-Lethal. Bind them with Rune Magic. (Mercy)
Lethal Strike. End the threat quickly. (Pragmatism)

steps.text: We don't have to kill them! Rune of Chains!
Chains of light erupted from the ground, wrapping around the Beastkin. They struggled, shouting curses, but they were unharmed.
Stay down! The battle is over! We aren't here to execute you!
You Northern scum! Just kill us and be done with it!
No. We're better than that.
They won't stop. I have to put them down. Rune of Impact!
Cyan blasted them back with a wave of force. They hit the wall hard and slumped over, unconscious or broken. It was clean, quick, and necessary.
Threat neutralized. Let's move up.
Something's coming. Something heavy.
General Anne! We secured the flank!
The enemy is neutralized. We can advance.
We took prisoners. They're secured and ready for transport.
Scan complete. Southern Biomass detected.
Status: Alive.
Directive: Total Purification.
Wait... what?
General! They're already down! There's no need!
No! Stop! They're tied up! They surrendered!
Obstruction of justice is treason. Stand aside.
It happened in a blink. One swing. The prisoners—the living, breathing people Cyan had just spared—were gone.
Reduced to silence.
You... you killed them. They were helpless.
The enemy is a contagion. Contagion must be burned.
Beautiful work, General. Efficiency rating: 100%%.
Why the long face, boy? You secured the targets. She processed them. That is called teamwork.
That's called a war crime, Roland.
It's called winning, Eve. Look at the map. We've taken three forts in one day. The South is crumbling.
Now, move out. The General needs to feed her blade.
I tried to be clean. But it didn't matter. The result is the same.
I saved them... I tied them up... just so she could kill them easier.
Your mercy became their executioner's block, Cyan.
This isn't a war. It's an extermination.
And we're helping them do it.
Cyan looked at her hands. They were clean of blood, but she felt dirtier than she ever had in her life.
The Hero had returned. And she was erasing the world, one swing at a time.
The Capital Square was a powder keg. Ten thousand armed adventurers, and none of them wanted to be there.
I'm not dying for the King's taxes! Let the nobles fight!
Where's the gold? The economy is dead!
This is bad. One spark and this turns into a riot.
Silence! You are called to serve your Kingdom! The South threatens our way of life!
Go home, old man! We want food, not war!
You are right to be angry. The North has been weak. The North has been sleeping.
But today... the North wakes up.
Roland. What is he doing on the stage?
Who?
The man who destroyed everything.
You ask for a reason to fight. You ask for hope. I give you... The Miracle.
Behold! The Hero of the Second War! Returned from the grave to lead us to salvation!
General Anne Lysandria!
Annie...?
Annie!?
Citizens of the North. The enemy is at the gate. They seek to erase our history.
I have returned to ensure that your children do not grow up in chains.
Who will stand with me? Who will bleed with me?
ANNE! ANNE! ANNE!
LEAD US! WE'LL FOLLOW!
They're cheering... a minute ago they were rioting.
Mass hysteria. Induced by a powerful charisma symbol.
Annie! It's me! Look down! It's Gabe!
You're back...
The morale is sufficient. Initiate deployment.
She... she looked right through me. Like I wasn't even there.
Gabe, stop. That isn't her. It's a puppet. A necromancer's doll.
Gabe, stop. That's what I tried to tell you. Roland... he wiped her. She doesn't know you.
To the Airships! Today we march! Today we reclaim our destiny!
You monsters. You stole her death.
We have to go, Gabe. The crowd is moving.
As the cheers deafened the capital, Cyan looked at the 'Hero' on the stage.
He saw the blankness in her eyes. He saw the fanaticism in Roland's smile.
And he saw Gabe, broken in the middle of the celebration.
Before we begin, please choose your character.
